nodes.rationale: ECharts draws into the host element itself, so the :host { display: block } style is what gives it a box to draw in.

nodes.label: Flame graph and waterfall trace views
nodes.norm_label: flame graph and waterfall trace views

nodes.label: TraceCarrier (injectContext / extractContext)
nodes.rationale: Key/Value-Map, die der Cluster-Transport automatisch in Wire-Envelopes legt. Ausserhalb des Actor-Systems (HTTP, Broker) inject/extract man manuell.

nodes.label: Span buffer
nodes.rationale: A bounded ring held on the server as well as in the panel, so a browser that connects late still gets it, flushed to the browser in batches rather than one span at a time because a busy system would otherwise turn a debugging aid into a firehose. On overflow the oldest spans are dropped and the panel says how many - a flame graph is about the recent past, so that is the half worth keeping.

nodes.label: TeeTracer
nodes.rationale: Attaching DevTools does not take your tracer away: if nothing is installed it enables a recorder, and if something already is it wraps it so both consumers see every span. Detaching puts the original back exactly as it was, which is what lets the panel run against a service that is also exporting traces for real.

nodes.label: Trace list
nodes.rationale: One row per trace with route, message, payload and duration. A message name is its kind when it has one, which is how this codebase tags its unions - constructor.name alone answers Object for every object literal and tells you nothing.

nodes.label: tracerOf
nodes.rationale: Returns the tracer installed right now. Held in a variable from before DevTools.attach it is still the noop, whose withActiveSpan runs your callback and records nothing, silently - so call it at the point of use.

nodes.label: actor.receive span
nodes.rationale: Opened once per message delivered to onReceive, carrying the actor path and the message type. On error the span records the exception and sets an error status - there is no error.message attribute.

nodes.label: Per-message tracing cost
nodes.rationale: Zero overhead with the NoopTracer, since the hot paths short-circuit without allocating spans or doing async-storage lookups. Enabled, each message adds one span allocation, a few attribute writes and one AsyncLocalStorage scope - roughly 5 to 10 microseconds.

nodes.label: Causal chaining across tells
nodes.rationale: tell snapshots the active span context onto the envelope; on receive the framework runs the handler inside the span so the chain is visible, and application spans appear as children of the auto-generated receive span.

nodes.label: cluster.envelope.received span
nodes.rationale: The infrastructure span for an inbound cross-cluster envelope carrying a parent trace context, with the sending address and the target path as attributes.

nodes.label: pipeTo does not propagate the active span
nodes.rationale: A known limitation: the target onReceive does not see the caller active span, so capture the carrier manually before piping.
nodes.norm_label: pipeto does not propagate the active span

nodes.label: W3C traceparent propagation
nodes.rationale: The same traceparent rides on the wire envelope across cluster nodes; the receiving node extracts it and its receive span links back to the sender.

nodes.label: OTel exporters
nodes.rationale: Pick by the backend preferred protocol; OTLP over HTTP is the most general because it works with the Collector, which then routes anywhere.

nodes.label: OTel resource attributes
nodes.rationale: Stamped on every span, and the most useful place for global context - service name, version, region, pod name.

nodes.label: OTel SDK version alignment
nodes.rationale: OpenTelemetry SDK versions need to align - major-version mismatches break, so pin both to compatible majors.

nodes.label: OtelAdapterOptions
nodes.rationale: withApi is mandatory: the adapter delegates to whatever you pass, and structural typing means the framework never imports the OpenTelemetry API itself. A pre-built tracer may be passed instead of a name and version.

nodes.label: otelTracer
nodes.rationale: The production-grade tracer, and a function rather than a class: you hand it the OpenTelemetry API namespace and install the result on the tracing extension, after which the framework auto-spans flow to whatever backend the SDK exports to.

nodes.label: RecordingTracer.recorded
nodes.rationale: A snapshot of every span that ended - a span is captured only when end is called, so one that was started but never ended never shows up.

nodes.label: RecordedSpan
nodes.rationale: Name, kind, context, parent, start and end times, attributes, status, status message and recorded exceptions - enough to verify causality chains as well as attributes.

nodes.label: RecordingTracer
nodes.rationale: The test counterpart to otelTracer: instead of exporting spans it stores them in memory for tests to assert on.

nodes.label: RecordingTracer.reset
nodes.rationale: Without a reset between tests, recorded spans accumulate across them.

nodes.label: injectContext and extractContext
nodes.rationale: The cross-wire pair - the cluster transport puts carriers into wire envelopes automatically, and outside the actor system you inject and extract manually to bridge tracing across services.

nodes.label: NoopTracer
nodes.rationale: The default: tracing disabled, every call short-circuited.

nodes.label: pipeTo does not propagate the active span (Tracer API)
nodes.rationale: The target handler runs in a fresh scope, so capture the carrier before piping.
nodes.norm_label: pipeto does not propagate the active span (tracer api)

nodes.label: Span interface
nodes.rationale: context, setAttribute, setStatus, recordException, end, and a readonly ended flag; after end further methods are no-ops.

nodes.label: SpanOptions
nodes.rationale: parent (undefined uses the active span, null forces a root), initial attributes, kind and a start-time override.

nodes.label: TraceCarrier
nodes.rationale: A key-value map, W3C-compatible so spans serialize to traceparent for downstream OTel services.

nodes.label: Tracer interface
nodes.rationale: startSpan, withActiveSpan, activeSpan, injectContext and extractContext - a minimal surface close to the OpenTelemetry API but smaller, with no SDK dependency since you bring your own.

nodes.label: withActiveSpan
nodes.rationale: Runs a callback with a span active so child spans auto-link as children; it uses AsyncLocalStorage under the hood, so the active span propagates across awaits.

nodes.label: Deliberately empty template file
nodes.rationale: The file exists rather than an inline empty string so every component in the tree is read the same way: markup lives in the .html beside it and there is no second place to look.

nodes.label: Kausale Verkettung ueber tell und W3C-traceparent
nodes.rationale: tell snapshottet den aktiven Span-Kontext auf den Envelope (tracer.injectContext); beim Empfangen laeuft tracer.withActiveSpan, damit onReceive die Kette sieht. Ueber Cluster-Nodes reitet derselbe traceparent auf dem Wire-Envelope - ein Trace pro logischem Request, auch ueber 4-5 Actor-Hops.
nodes.norm_label: kausale verkettung ueber tell und w3c-traceparent

nodes.label: Trace-IDs im MDC
nodes.rationale: Das Framework mergt traceId/spanId NICHT automatisch in den LogContext - Log-Zeilen tragen die IDs des aktiven Spans nicht von Haus aus. Wer von einem langsamen Trace zu den passenden Log-Zeilen springen will, kopiert sie selbst vom aktiven Span in den MDC.

nodes.label: pipeTo propagiert den aktiven Span nicht
nodes.source_location: pipeTo propagiert den aktiven Span nicht
nodes.rationale: Bekannte Limitation: das onReceive des Targets sieht den aktiven Span des Aufrufers nicht. Workaround ist ein manuelles tracer.injectContext() vor dem Pipen.
nodes.norm_label: pipeto propagiert den aktiven span nicht

nodes.label: Sampling auf SDK-Ebene
nodes.rationale: Das Framework zeichnet mit voller Rate auf, das SDK entscheidet was exportiert wird. Ungesampelte Spans propagieren weiterhin Kontext zur Korrelation, kosten das Backend aber nichts. Bei hohem Durchsatz immer samplen - 10 % ist typisch, manche Teams gehen auf 0,1 %.

nodes.label: Logs, dann Metriken, dann Traces
nodes.rationale: Jede Supervisor-Entscheidung, jedes Cluster-Event und jeder Dead-Letter wird geloggt, und LogContext-MDC fuegt einen Multi-Actor-Request in einer einzigen Abfrage zusammen. Metriken erkennen 'irgendwas laeuft schief' bevor Nutzer es merken; Traces geben die Ende-zu-Ende-Sicht eines einzelnen Requests.

nodes.label: Actors trace only messages that already belong to a trace
nodes.rationale: A cell opens an actor.receive span when the incoming message carries a trace context or a span is already active, and nothing in the framework starts the first one. So a plain tell records nothing and a system that is plainly busy can leave the panel empty; seed a span at your entry point and every tell inside it carries the context onwards.
nodes.norm_label: actors trace only messages that already belong to a trace

nodes.label: Tracing records from attach, with no button
nodes.rationale: The messages worth looking at are the ones that already went past, so tracing runs from the moment DevTools attaches and the recent history is there when you open the panel. Expect volume to match traffic: it opens a root span for every message and serialises each payload - that is the trade DevTools.attach makes, and a system that cannot afford it should not have a debugger attached to it.
nodes.norm_label: tracing records from attach, with no button

nodes.label: All-or-nothing auto-instrumentation
nodes.rationale: It is active whenever a non-noop tracer is enabled and there are no per-category toggles, so reduce span volume by sampling at the SDK level rather than turning categories off: turning auto-instrumentation off entirely means installing the NoopTracer, which also disables your manual spans since they route through the same tracer.

nodes.label: Trace IDs are not auto-merged into the MDC
nodes.rationale: Log lines are not stamped with the active span IDs out of the box; the MDC fields you set yourself still flow, and copying traceId and spanId from the active span into the log context yourself is what lets you pivot from a slow trace to the matching log lines.
nodes.norm_label: trace ids are not auto-merged into the mdc

nodes.label: Span attributes exclude message contents
nodes.rationale: The framework includes the message type but never auto-includes message field values, by design - message contents may contain PII or large payloads. Add custom attributes manually where it is safe and useful.

nodes.label: OTel sampling
nodes.rationale: Sampling is configured on the SDK, not the adapter: the framework records spans at full rate and the SDK decides which to export, and unsampled spans still propagate context for correlation at zero backend cost. At high throughput always sample - 10 percent is typical and some teams go to 0.1 percent.

nodes.label: Test-only by design
nodes.rationale: Memory grows unbounded because every span is kept forever, so this is never a production tracer. It also does not serialize context cross-wire: it works in single-process multi-node tests where every node shares the process, but cross-process tracing tests need a real OTel pipeline.

nodes.label: Span attributes and PII
nodes.rationale: Traces are typically less-protected than primary databases, so personal data, secrets and anything privacy-sensitive do not belong in attributes.

nodes.label: Span lifetime
nodes.rationale: Spans must be ended or the tracer leaks memory and the span never exports. The framework auto-ends the spans it creates for message handling; user code owns the ones it creates, and try/finally is the pattern.

nodes.label: Tracing off costs a field read
nodes.rationale: Since the message path resolves the tracer from a plain field on the ActorSystem rather than through the extension registry, an untraced message allocates nothing and makes no async-storage lookup on its account. This used to be documented as zero-cost and that was not true: the receive path resolved the tracing extension twice per message and the send path once more, each a map lookup plus two calls, on every message whether or not anything was tracing. The claim is now accurate rather than aspirational - a field read and a null check, not nothing.
nodes.norm_label: tracing off costs a field read

nodes.label: VoiceApp (Lit element)
nodes.rationale: Its reactive properties deliberately mirror the plain HTML reference's state shape; the file's stated job is to thread the same audio plumbing through Lit's reactivity so rendering follows state automatically. static/plain/index.html is named as the audio-plumbing canon.

nodes.label: beginPress
nodes.rationale: Target selection is sent before the first audio chunk, so the server always knows where a stream is going before any of it arrives.

nodes.label: drainQueue
nodes.rationale: Appends one chunk at a time and swallows appendBuffer throws (out-of-quota etc.); the next updateend retries, so a transient failure drops a chunk instead of killing the stream.

nodes.label: endIncoming
nodes.rationale: Teardown is delayed ~1.5 s so the already-appended buffer flushes audibly before the audio element and its object URL are revoked.

nodes.label: feedIncoming
nodes.rationale: The opus view is copied before queueing because it is a subarray onto a larger buffer that may be reclaimed, and SourceBuffer wants its own buffer.

nodes.label: resetToGate
nodes.rationale: Hard reload rather than incremental teardown: the simplest correct cleanup for a demo.

nodes.label: scheduleResume
nodes.rationale: Exponential backoff capped at 4 s over at most MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS tries, and only when a session token exists — a socket that closes without a token is a logout, not a dropout.

nodes.label: startMicMeterLoop
nodes.rationale: Peak deviation from 128 (the zero point of 8-bit PCM) is used as the level, sampled on requestAnimationFrame so the meter costs nothing when the tab is hidden.

nodes.label: state (app-level state bag)
nodes.rationale: Plain JS with no reactive framework: every change re-renders by hand, because for a multi-frontend comparison the load-bearing part is the WebSocket + audio plumbing, not the UI.

nodes.label: toggleRoomTalk
nodes.rationale: Room talk is open-mic, not push-to-talk: it stays on until toggled off or the room is left.

nodes.label: wirePttButton
nodes.rationale: Pointer events cover mouse, touch and pen uniformly, and the pointer is captured on press so an up-event outside the button still ends the transmission instead of leaving the mic open.

nodes.label: Phase machine: gate-mic to gate-login to app
nodes.norm_label: phase machine: gate-mic to gate-login to app

nodes.label: shared/frameCodec.ts (hand-duplicated codec)
nodes.rationale: The build-free frontends cannot import the TypeScript codec, so decodeIncoming is copied into each single-file app with an explicit keep-in-sync comment — the duplication is the price of having no build step.

nodes.label: Fresh MediaRecorder per press
nodes.rationale: The first chunk of every MediaRecorder run carries the WebM init segment and later chunks are media segments; receivers depend on that, so each voice-incoming-start opens a fresh MediaSource whose first append is the init.

nodes.label: [hidden] display:none !important specificity fix
nodes.rationale: The UA stylesheet maps the hidden attribute to display:none, but a class rule like .app { display: grid } outranks it and would leave the gate and the app pane visible at once; pinning [hidden] with !important makes the attribute do what its name says.

nodes.label: One-time mic gesture unlocking capture and playback
nodes.rationale: A single 'Enable mic' click does double duty: it grants the getUserMedia permission and it resumes the AudioContext, because modern browsers gate inbound playback behind a user gesture too — without it received audio would be silent even though capture worked.
nodes.norm_label: one-time mic gesture unlocking capture and playback

nodes.label: eventDispatcher
nodes.rationale: Typisierter Builder fuer PersistentActor.onEvent. Der Dispatcher ist ein reiner Wert - isoliert unit-testbar ohne Actor-Instanz.

nodes.label: EventDispatcherBuilder<S, E, Handled>
nodes.rationale: Der Typ-Parameter Handled verfolgt, welche Event-Arten bereits registriert sind; build() type-checkt nur, wenn jede Variante von E['kind'] abgedeckt ist.

nodes.label: EventDispatcherIncomplete
nodes.rationale: Der nicht-aufrufbare Rueckgabetyp bei unvollstaendiger Abdeckung. Das __unhandled-Phantom-Feld traegt die fehlende Art, damit die Fehlermeldung sie nennt und der Fix mechanisch wird.

nodes.label: FSM<SName, SData, Message>
nodes.rationale: In-Memory-Zustandsmaschine, DSL-getrieben. Uebergaenge werden im Subklassen-Konstruktor konfiguriert; das onReceive der Basisklasse routet jede Message zum Handler des aktuellen Zustands.

nodes.label: goto(state, data)
nodes.rationale: Uebergang: feuert onExitState fuer den aktuellen Zustand, setzt neuen Zustand + Daten, feuert onEnter fuer den neuen Zustand.

nodes.label: onEnter(state, hook)
nodes.rationale: Natuerliche Heimat fuer Timer-Setup beim Zustandseintritt. In diesen Callbacks geworfene Fehler werden abgefangen und als Warnung geloggt - sie erreichen den Supervisor nicht, und der Uebergang wird trotzdem abgeschlossen.

nodes.label: onExitState(state, hook)
nodes.rationale: Gegenstueck zu onEnter - der Ort, an dem in onEnter aufgesetzte Timer wieder abgebaut werden.

nodes.label: stay(data)
nodes.rationale: Kein Uebergang, aber Daten werden aktualisiert; weder onEnter noch onExitState feuern. Fuer unbehandelte Messages explizit stay(data) zurueckgeben.

nodes.label: applyEvent (reiner Fold)
nodes.rationale: Die einzige Quelle der Wahrheit fuer Zustands- und Daten-Updates. Laeuft sowohl zur Persist-Zeit als auch waehrend der Recovery, muss also deterministisch und frei von Seiteneffekten sein - ein Seiteneffekt darin feuert bei jedem Neustart erneut.

nodes.label: FsmStateData<State, Data>
nodes.rationale: Das kombinierte {state, data}; wird auch als Snapshot serialisiert - ein kompakter Blob, der den Replay begrenzt.

nodes.label: FsmTransitionMap<State, Command, Event, Data>
nodes.rationale: Als Klassenfeld deklariert, damit die Command-spezifische Typverengung an jeder Aufrufstelle funktioniert. transitions und Guards werden nur fuer Live-Commands herangezogen; das Replay treibt den Zustand rein ueber applyEvent. next ist hauptsaechlich informativ, aber eine Diskrepanz zu applyEvent wird auf warn geloggt, um ein Auseinanderdriften von Tabelle und Fold zu erkennen.

nodes.label: Multi-Event-Uebergang
nodes.rationale: Array-Events persistieren atomar in einem einzigen persistAll, applyEvent laeuft einmal pro Event, und nur der finale Zustand nach dem Replay wird gegen next geprueft. Ein leeres Array ist ein No-op. tagsFor wird ebenfalls einmal pro Event gefragt, sodass ein Uebergang mit unterschiedlich geformten Events jedes fuer sich taggt (#66).

nodes.label: onGuardRejected
nodes.rationale: Gibt der guard eines Eintrags false zurueck, wird das Command verworfen - auf debug geloggt, nichts persistiert. Ueberschreibbar.

nodes.label: onInvalidTransition
nodes.rationale: Gibt es keinen Eintrag fuer (Zustand, command.kind), ist es ein ungueltiger Uebergang - auf warn geloggt, nichts persistiert, keine Zustandsaenderung. Ueberschreibbar.

nodes.label: PersistentFSM<Command, Event, SName, Data>
nodes.rationale: Event-sourced, tabellengetriebene FSM ohne when/goto/stay-DSL. Es gibt kein Framework-Wrapper-Event - das Journal speichert die eigenen Domain-Events. Hat bewusst keine onEnter/onExit/onTransition-Hooks; die gehoeren zur In-Memory-FSM.

nodes.label: Zustands-Timeouts (_timeout)
nodes.rationale: Der Timer wird bei jedem Uebergang neu scharf gestellt - auch bei einem, der im selben Zustand bleibt - und beim Verlassen abgebrochen; genau das laesst die Idle-Session-Form funktionieren. Ein gefeuertes Timeout laeuft durch die Mailbox und kann hinter einem Command warten; das erneute Scharfstellen entwertet ein so eingereihtes Feuern (#143). Bei der Recovery wird relativ zur Wall-Clock neu armiert, damit eine lange gestoppte FSM ein frisches Fenster bekommt statt eines sofortigen Feuerns.

nodes.label: MigrationStep<From, To>
nodes.rationale: Upcaster sind einfache Funktionen und koennen ueber Konstruktor-Argumente des Actors schliessen - nuetzlich fuer Per-Instanz-Migrationskontext wie Per-Tenant-Defaults oder Per-Region-Waehrung.

nodes.label: this.state nicht direkt mutieren
nodes.rationale: Funktioniert zufaellig in manchen Store-Implementierungen, ist aber ein Footgun: das geladene State-Objekt wird vielleicht herumgereicht, und es wurde mutiert, bevor der Persist bestaetigt hat. Immer ein neues State-Objekt bauen. Ebenso: persist ohne await antwortet 'done', bevor der State durable ist.

nodes.label: Erschoepfungspruefung zur Compile-Zeit
nodes.rationale: Ein plain switch faellt fuer unbekannte Arten zu return state durch - das Event wird still ignoriert und das Replay produziert falschen State. assertNever wuerde es fangen, ist aber manuell und leicht zu vergessen; ts-patterns .exhaustive() ist ein Laufzeit-Check. eventDispatcher macht den Check ausschliesslich zur Compile-Zeit.

nodes.label: onEvent ist rein
nodes.rationale: onEvent laeuft bei jeder Recovery; Seiteneffekte darin duplizieren pro Neustart. Sie gehoeren in den persist-Callback in onCommand.

nodes.label: State-Daten immutable und serialisierbar halten
nodes.rationale: Pro Transition wird ein neues Objekt produziert; Mutationen funktionieren technisch, brechen aber Testbarkeit und Reasoning. Keine Closures und keine Actor-Refs in State-Daten - sie ueberleben keinen Neustart, koennen leaken und blockieren die spaetere Migration zu PersistentFSM.

nodes.label: FSM-Restart-Semantik
nodes.rationale: Beim Neustart laeuft der Konstruktor erneut und die FSM beginnt beim initialen Zustand + Daten. Kein Event-Log zum Abspielen - wenn der State Neustarts ueberleben muss, ist PersistentFSM das Werkzeug.

nodes.label: Endliche Zustandsmaschine (FSM-Muster)
nodes.rationale: Richtig, wenn ein Actor 3+ benannte Zustaende mit unterschiedlichem Verhalten hat, Uebergaenge explizit sind und Seiteneffekte zu Zustandsuebergaengen gehoeren. Fuer einen einzelnen Zustand oder Boolean-Toggle liest sich ein gewoehnlicher Actor sauberer; fuer hierarchische oder parallele Substates ist die bewusst flache FSM von actor-ts das falsche Werkzeug.

nodes.label: FSM vs. become
nodes.rationale: FSM hat benannte Zustaende, explizite Uebergaenge und typisierte Zustands-Inspektion; become sind anonyme Closures, die das aktuelle Verhalten nicht exponieren. Fuer 2 Zustaende ist become in Ordnung, ab 4 ist FSM einfacher zu lesen.

nodes.label: FSM vs. PersistentFSM
nodes.rationale: Fuer eine Saga, die ueber Stunden durch 10 Schritte laeuft, ist das Persistieren jedes Uebergangs kritisch. Fuer einen Connection-Actor, der ein paar Sekunden lebt, ist es verschwenderisch - bei einem Crash einfach von disconnected neu starten. Die beiden Varianten haben ausserdem unterschiedliche Formen: DSL-getrieben vs. tabellengetrieben.

nodes.label: Daten-Updates brauchen ein Event
nodes.rationale: Es gibt kein stay(newData): der einzige Weg, Zustand oder Daten zu aendern, ist ein Event zu persistieren, das applyEvent einfaltet. Ein reines Daten-Update, das einen Neustart ueberleben soll, wird als Event mit einem Uebergang modelliert, dessen next derselbe Zustand ist. Ausserdem: gleiche persistenceId fuer FSM und PersistentActor kollidiert im geteilten Journal.

nodes.label: Seiteneffekte nur fuer Live-Commands
nodes.rationale: onCommand laeuft waehrend des Replays nie - die Recovery treibt den Zustand allein ueber applyEvent - also feuert ein Seiteneffekt dort einmal pro echtem Uebergang. Fuer Arbeit nach dem Wiederhochfahren onRecoveryComplete verwenden.

nodes.label: Upcaster sind pur
nodes.rationale: Sie laufen bei jeder Recovery fuer jedes betroffene Event; Seiteneffekte wie API-Calls oder DB-Lookups verdoppeln sich pro Recovery und verlangsamen den Replay. Vorab berechnen und extern cachen, falls noetig.

nodes.label: DefaultsAdapterSpec<E>
nodes.rationale: defaults ist nach From-Version indexiert; jeder Key muss strikt kleiner als currentVersion sein, sonst wirft der Adapter. manifest muss dem On-Disk-Manifest entsprechen - ein Mismatch wirft beim Lesen MigrationError. Jedes defaults[v] ist ein Partial<E>, TypeScript erlaubt also Extra-Felder: Tippfehler in Feldnamen schlagen still fehl.

nodes.label: defaultsSnapshotAdapter
nodes.rationale: Identische Spec fuer Snapshot- und Durable-State-Datensaetze, gibt einen SnapshotAdapter zurueck.

nodes.label: writeVersion
nodes.rationale: Emittiert Events waehrend eines Rolling-Deploys in einer aelteren Version; spaeter hinzugekommene Felder werden beim Schreiben entfernt.

nodes.label: Versionierter Envelope { _v, _t, _e }
nodes.rationale: Unterstriche, damit die Felder nicht mit User-Feldern kollidieren; jedes Objekt mit genau diesen drei Keys gilt als Envelope.

nodes.label: Downcaster (addDown)
nodes.rationale: Waehrend eines Rolling-Deploys muessen v2-Nodes womoeglich weiterhin v1-Events emittieren, solange v1-Reader im Cluster sind. writeVersion muss <= currentVersion sein und die Chain braucht Downcaster fuer jeden Schritt auf dem Pfad currentVersion -> writeVersion, sonst wirft toJournal.

nodes.label: wrapEventAsEnvelope (Rezept 5 - Legacy-Journal nachruesten)
nodes.rationale: Ohne Envelopes hat die Chain keine Version, auf die sie schauen kann. One-Shot-Rewrite auf Version 1; danach uebernimmt die normale Chain. Idempotent, aber auf neuen Journals verschwendete Arbeit.

nodes.label: Envelope-Format { _v, _t, _e }
nodes.rationale: Das Format tritt erst in Kraft, wenn ein Adapter konfiguriert ist - vorher werden Events roh gespeichert, und das erste rohe Event wirft, sobald ein Adapter dazukommt.

nodes.label: manifestFor-Ableitung des _t-Diskriminators
nodes.rationale: Das erzeugte _t wird in den gespeicherten Envelope eingebacken; es muss dem manifest des spaeteren Adapters entsprechen und deterministisch aus dem Event abgeleitet sein.

nodes.label: wrapEventAsEnvelope
nodes.rationale: Pur und idempotent - ein Event, das schon wie ein Envelope aussieht, wird unveraendert zurueckgegeben, ein erneuter Lauf der Migration ist also sicher.

nodes.label: ATS1-Manifest-Header mit Kompressions-Flag
nodes.rationale: Die Dekompression wird ausschliesslich vom 2-Bit-Flag im Manifest gesteuert, nie von einem HTTP-Header. Weil jeder Body seinen Algorithmus selbst beschreibt, mischen none/gzip/zstd problemlos im selben Bucket.

nodes.label: Manifest-Prüfung auf dem Read-Pfad
nodes.rationale: Die Prüfung auszulassen ist der Weg, auf dem eine Row eines Event-Typs als ein anderer dekodiert wird — die Payload validiert, der statische Typ behauptet es sei das Erwartete, und nichts weiter unten kann es merken.

nodes.label: Mit Unterstrich präfixierte Keys sind framework-reserviert
nodes.rationale: Ein Event mit einem eigenen Feld _v kollidiert mit dem Envelope.
nodes.norm_label: mit unterstrich prafixierte keys sind framework-reserviert

nodes.label: Strikt beim Lesen (kein Mischen roher und eingewickelter Events)
nodes.rationale: Sobald ein Adapter gesetzt ist, wirft das Lesen eines Nicht-Envelope-Events MigrationError; Mischen für dieselbe pid geht nur über WrapLegacy.
nodes.norm_label: strikt beim lesen (kein mischen roher und eingewickelter events)

nodes.label: Operatives Rollout einer Migration
nodes.rationale: In Phasen: Adapter hinzufuegen und eine Version deployen, die alt und neu lesen kann; mehrere persistenceIds wiederherstellen und verifizieren; dann V2-Events schreiben; optional die Chain vereinfachen, sobald Snapshots die V1-Events abdecken und bestaetigt ist, dass keine V1-Events mehr verbleiben.

nodes.label: Einmal-Bulk-Migration vor der Recovery
nodes.rationale: Ein echtes Umschreiben der gespeicherten Daten, kein Read-Time-Shim. Muss gegen das Journal laufen, BEVOR ein Actor mit dem neuen Adapter recovert - sonst wirft das erste rohe Event MigrationError.

nodes.label: Level-Wechsel braucht keine Migration
nodes.rationale: Das Level steht nicht auf dem Wire (das Manifest haelt den Algorithmus fest) und der Decompressor braucht es nie - gzip- und zstd-Frames sind selbst-beschreibend.

nodes.label: Manifest check on the read path
nodes.norm_label: manifest check on the read path

nodes.label: Wrong-schema bytes decode plausibly, so the manifest is enforced
nodes.norm_label: wrong-schema bytes decode plausibly, so the manifest is enforced

nodes.label: Busiest mailboxes
nodes.rationale: Listet die tiefsten Queues von jetzt — der schnellste Weg von "irgendwo staut es sich" zu "dieser Actor staut sich".

nodes.label: Uebersichts-Panel
nodes.rationale: Common (Systemidentitaet, Uptime, Runtime, Cluster-Status), Numbers (Live-Zahlen) und Charts. Die Uptime wird ab ActorSystem.startedAtMs vom Server geschickt, ein Reload laesst das System also nicht juenger wirken.

nodes.label: Client-Frames
nodes.rationale: hello, subscribe, unsubscribe, request.

nodes.label: DevTools-Tap-Protokoll
nodes.rationale: Ein gemultiplexter WebSocket plus ein paar JSON-Endpunkte fuer alle Panels: ein Browser-Tab haelt genau eine Verbindung, ein Panel-Wechsel kostet keinen Reconnect, ein untaetiger Tab kostet nichts. Stabil genug, um einen eigenen Client dagegen zu schreiben.

nodes.label: Handshake (hello / welcome)
nodes.rationale: Der Client sendet zuerst hello; davor wird nichts akzeptiert. welcome traegt Protokoll- und Serverversion, Systemname, startedAtMs sowie streams und panels als Capability-Ankuendigung — ein Panel ist active, disabled oder unavailable mit Begruendung.

nodes.label: Server-Frames
nodes.rationale: welcome, event, response und error. Ein Fehler mit requestId lehnt diesen Request ab, einer ohne gilt fuer die Verbindung.

nodes.label: Tap-Endpunkte
nodes.rationale: GET / (UI-Shell), GET /assets/*, GET /api/info (Handshake-Daten als reines JSON, curl-bar) und WS /api/ws.

nodes.label: Busiest mailboxes list
nodes.rationale: The fastest way from something is backing up to this actor is backing up.

nodes.label: Charts over a chosen timespan
nodes.rationale: The series is recorded on the server from the moment DevTools attaches, so a panel opened an hour in shows that hour and a page reload does not lose it. Longer spans are bucketed; levels keep each interval peak so a spike survives summarising, and cumulative counters keep the interval last reading so the per-second maths stays correct however coarse the buckets are.

nodes.label: Hide DevTools actors
nodes.rationale: DevTools runs its own hub and taps as ordinary actors, so they are real and therefore listed - but marked at spawn with ActorOptions.withInternal() rather than matched by name, so their children (a websocket connection is a child of its hub) are hidden too.

nodes.label: Per-node figure breakdown
nodes.rationale: In a cluster every node runs a DevTools agent answering with its own numbers and the totals are their sum; a node that stops answering keeps its last reading marked not answering rather than disappearing, and is forgotten an hour later.

nodes.label: Capability advertisement
nodes.rationale: A panel is active, disabled because the operator switched it off, or unavailable with a reason - which the UI renders on the greyed-out nav entry, so a capability this system lacks is explained rather than silently missing.

nodes.label: decodeClientFrame
nodes.rationale: Rejects anything that is not a well-formed frame, including kinds it does not know: the ignore-what-you-do-not-recognise half of the compatibility rule applies to clients reading server frames, not to the server, which has no reason to accept frames from a client newer than itself.

nodes.label: DEVTOOLS_PROTOCOL_VERSION
nodes.rationale: Additive changes keep the version and clients must ignore frame kinds, streams and fields they do not recognise - that is what lets an older UI keep working against a newer server. Anything else bumps it, and a mismatch closes the socket with 4400: refusing beats negotiating, because a UI bundle from a different release rendering a half-understood actor tree is worse than a banner telling you to rebuild. The full surface is declared in version 1 from the start so each panel that lands is a pure addition.

nodes.label: Tap handshake
nodes.rationale: The client sends hello first and nothing else is accepted before it; the server answers welcome with the protocol version, server version, system name, start time, streams and panels.

nodes.label: Tap request methods
nodes.rationale: Pull operations namespaced by the panel that owns them. A method with no handler answers error code unavailable - the same signal the panel descriptor already gave, so a client that ignored the handshake still fails safely. Requests are answered off the tap mailbox so a slow journal read cannot stall other connected tabs.

nodes.label: Tap streams
nodes.rationale: Subscribing yields a snapshot first then deltas, and the server generates the snapshot on the same mailbox that publishes the deltas so it can never be built from a half-updated view.

nodes.label: Zusammenfassen laengerer Zeitraeume
nodes.rationale: Fuellstaende behalten je Intervall das Maximum, damit eine Spitze das Bucketing ueberlebt; kumulative Zaehler behalten den letzten Wert des Intervalls, damit die Sekundenrechnung stimmt, wie grob die Buckets auch sind.

nodes.label: Getrennte Diagramme fuer Fuellstand und Rate
nodes.rationale: Auf einer gemeinsamen y-Achse drueckt ein Rueckstau von 400 eine 2/s-Linie auf null, deshalb teilen sich Fuellstand und Rate nie eine Skala.
nodes.norm_label: getrennte diagramme fuer fuellstand und rate

nodes.label: Kumulative Zaehler, abgeleitete Raten
nodes.rationale: Zaehler sind auf dem Draht kumulativ und die UI leitet die Sekundenraten selbst ab, damit ein Browser, der sich neu verbindet, im Hintergrund gedrosselt wird oder einen Tick verpasst, korrekte Zahlen statt einer Phantom-Spitze zeigt.

nodes.label: Zaehler sind kumulativ, nie Deltas
nodes.rationale: Der Client berechnet Raten aus aufeinanderfolgenden Samples, sodass ein Reconnect oder ein verpasster Tick die Zahlen nicht verfaelschen kann.

nodes.label: decodeClientFrame
nodes.rationale: Der Server lehnt alles ab, was kein wohlgeformtes Frame ist, inklusive unbekannter Kinds: die Ignoriere-was-du-nicht-kennst-Haelfte gilt fuer Clients, die Server-Frames lesen — der Server hat keinen Grund, Frames eines neueren Clients zu akzeptieren.

nodes.label: Versionierungsregel
nodes.rationale: Additive Aenderungen behalten die Version und Clients muessen Unbekanntes ignorieren; alles andere erhoeht sie. Eine Abweichung schliesst den Socket mit 4400, weil ein UI-Bundle, das einen halb verstandenen Actor-Baum rendert, schlimmer ist als ein Banner, das zum Neubauen auffordert.

nodes.label: Sequenznummern und Luecken
nodes.rationale: Eine Luecke heisst, Frames wurden verworfen und der inkrementelle Zustand ist geraten — die UI abonniert dann neu fuer einen frischen Snapshot, statt einen Baum zu zeigen, der still von der Realitaet abweicht.

nodes.label: Span-Puffer und Batching
nodes.rationale: Spans gehen gebuendelt (Default alle 250 ms) statt einzeln, weil eine Nachricht mehrere Spans erzeugen kann und ein ausgelastetes System sonst eine Sturzflut ergaebe. Laeuft der Puffer ueber, fallen die aeltesten Spans und das Panel sagt wie viele — ein Flame-Graph handelt von der juengsten Vergangenheit.

nodes.label: Cumulative counters on the wire
nodes.rationale: Counters are cumulative on the wire and the UI derives per-second rates itself, so a browser that reconnects, throttles in a background tab or misses a tick still shows correct figures rather than a phantom spike.

nodes.label: Live actor state dot
nodes.rationale: Lifecycle events only announce births, deaths and restarts and nothing announces a suspension, so the tap re-inspects the tree each second and sends the cells that moved. A restart flashes the row because the path survives a restart and nothing else would move.

nodes.label: Removed members kept for an hour
nodes.rationale: The node that drops out of membership is the one you want to look at, and it used to disappear at exactly that moment; the record lives on the server, so reloading the page - often the first thing you do - does not erase it.
nodes.norm_label: removed members kept for an hour

nodes.label: Ring topology layout
nodes.rationale: Every node gossips with every other, so the membership graph is complete and a force-directed simulation would only produce a slowly settling circle; a ring draws the same membership the same way every time.

nodes.label: A level and a rate never share a y-axis
nodes.rationale: On one scale a backlog of 400 flattens a 2-per-second line to nothing, so the three plots are split.
nodes.norm_label: a level and a rate never share a y-axis

nodes.label: Stopped-actor tombstone
nodes.rationale: A stopped actor stays greyed out with a stopped-Ns-ago badge for 30 seconds because the actor you want to look at is usually the one that just died; removing its row the instant it stopped meant you never saw it. Remote trees get the same thirty seconds when an actor stops appearing in a round.

nodes.label: Per-stream sequence numbers and gaps
nodes.rationale: A gap means frames were dropped, so the client incremental state is now a guess: the bundled UI re-subscribes for a fresh snapshot rather than rendering a tree that quietly disagrees with reality. Counters in stream payloads are cumulative since attach, never deltas, so a reconnect or a missed tick cannot corrupt the figures.

nodes.label: One multiplexed WebSocket
nodes.rationale: One socket rather than one per panel means a browser tab holds a single connection, switching panels costs no reconnect, and an idle tab costs the system nothing.

nodes.label: DevTools actors excluded from traces
nodes.rationale: Never a root span and never a child one either: its probes receive event-stream publishes during an application message and would otherwise reappear in the middle of that message route. Without the internal marking the hub publishing the spans it just recorded would feed every batch back in as the payload of the next one.

nodes.label: actor-ts.io.broker.email-bridge
nodes.rationale: target hat kein Blatt - eine ActorRef kann nur aus dem Code kommen.

nodes.label: Three-layer settings resolution
nodes.rationale: Constructor argument beats HOCON beats builtInDefaultOptions; preStart merges, validates against requiredOptions and throws early so the actor takes the supervisor failure path before it ever connects.

nodes.label: EmailBridgeOptions
nodes.rationale: Options merge one level deep, so supplying the imap or smtp group in code replaces the configured group wholesale rather than overriding single fields.

nodes.label: Settings precedence
nodes.rationale: Constructor argument, then HOCON under a protocol-specific key, then built-in defaults.

nodes.label: HOCON root key difference
nodes.rationale: Both frameworks use HOCON with the same format and conventions; only the root key and specific leaves differ — akka { cluster { seed-nodes ... } } versus actor-ts { cluster { gossip-interval ... } }.

nodes.label: The system dead-letter queue behind the panel
nodes.rationale: A message becomes a dead letter when the recipient was stopped, never existed, or the path was wrong; nothing throws and nothing logs by default.
nodes.norm_label: the system dead-letter queue behind the panel

nodes.label: Filtering by recipient subtree
nodes.rationale: Filtering happens on the server over the ring it already holds, and the summary counts what the filter selected rather than what the page shows.

nodes.label: Live tail of the system event bus
nodes.rationale: Per-session seq column where a gap means events were dropped; pause discards rather than buffers, because resuming into a wall of everything that happened meanwhile is not what the button promises.
nodes.norm_label: live tail of the system event bus

nodes.label: DeadLetter
nodes.rationale: A tell to a stopped ref, a selection that resolved to nothing, a behavior answering unhandled, a singleton with no host. Every dead letter names its recipient, which is what makes one distinguishable from another.

nodes.label: Die Bloecke imap und smtp ersetzen, sie mischen nicht
nodes.rationale: Optionen werden nur eine Ebene tief zusammengefuehrt, eine im Code uebergebene Gruppe ersetzt die konfigurierte also vollstaendig.
nodes.norm_label: die bloecke imap und smtp ersetzen, sie mischen nicht

nodes.label: Changed-from-defaults-only filter
nodes.rationale: If the filter leaves the table empty the panel says so, because nothing overriding the defaults is a worthwhile answer in itself and a different one from "no key matches that filter".

nodes.label: Code options are not HOCON
nodes.rationale: Per-consumer XOptions builders override HOCON at the call site and never pass through the configuration tree, so a key shown here may still be overridden by code this panel cannot see. What it shows is the HOCON resolution, exactly.

nodes.label: Redaction by key, not by value
nodes.rationale: Anything matching pass, secret, token, key, credential or auth is replaced before it leaves the process — by key, because a password that happens to look ordinary is still a password and the key is what names it. Blunt on purpose: a redacted tree still reveals hosts, ports, seed nodes and storage paths, so switch the panel off where that matters.
nodes.norm_label: redaction by key, not by value

nodes.label: The three HOCON layers
nodes.rationale: A merged tree answers what a setting is now; the question that brings you here is why it is not what you wrote, and that needs the layer as well as the value. Naming where application.conf was read from separates "my file is being ignored" from "my file says something else".

nodes.label: Payload sanitisation and exposure
nodes.rationale: Depth, entry count and string length are capped; a message cut to fit says truncated and one the queue could not keep says why, rather than showing a null that reads like an empty message. The panel exposes whatever your messages carry.

nodes.label: store setting: off, memory, persistent
nodes.rationale: Off by default because capturing every undelivered message costs memory. With store off the panel stays in the navigation and reports itself unavailable naming the setting, because an empty table cannot tell you whether nothing is broken or nothing is being recorded — opposite answers.

nodes.label: Why the panel polls
nodes.rationale: The queue is a bounded ring the server already keeps, so a request is cheap — and pushing every capture would put DevTools on the delivery path of the very failures it is watching.

nodes.label: Event payloads are your data
nodes.rationale: The tail shows event contents, so switch it off with panels: { eventStream: false } anywhere that matters — the same call as for the time-travel and dead-letter panels.

nodes.label: What DevTools costs
nodes.rationale: Unused, nothing: creating the extension opens no port and installs no taps, and each panel collects only while a browser is subscribed. While attached it switches the metrics registry on, because throughput, mailbox drops and handler latency read 0 against the default noop registry; detach puts the noop back, and a registry you enabled yourself is left alone in both directions.

nodes.label: Per-panel switches
nodes.rationale: A disabled panel is disabled for good — its data never leaves the process, whatever a client asks for. Time travel is the one to think about first because it surfaces raw persisted events, followed by dead letters and event stream, which both show message payloads.

nodes.label: Two switches, only one a security decision
nodes.rationale: Hiding a view and making a system writable are different decisions, so they are different settings. With the acknowledgement unset the panel still appears as a disabled entry naming the setting to change, rather than silently absent.
nodes.norm_label: two switches, only one a security decision

nodes.label: actor_dead_letters_total counter
nodes.rationale: Minted by the queue, so it exists only once the store is not off; recipient is unbounded in principle and bounded in practice by the per-family cap, and it pays for itself because this counter only fires when something is already wrong. A loss signal, not a backlog one.

nodes.label: system.deadLetterQueue
nodes.rationale: withDeadLetters is the only way to configure the queue the system uses — new DeadLetterQueue(system, options) builds a valid object that nothing installs as the capture sink, because there is one sink slot and the system owns it.

nodes.label: What happens by default
nodes.rationale: Every dead letter is wrapped and published on the event stream, and that is the whole default. The framework does not log them — DeadLetterRef holds no logger — so if nothing subscribes the letter is gone, which is fine for a development run and a poor answer to what did we drop last night.

nodes.label: Degraded payloads
nodes.rationale: The tagged-JSON encoder refuses functions, symbols, Promise, weak collections and cycles rather than corrupting them silently, so a persistent queue keeps the provenance instead of losing the letter — and such an entry cannot be replayed, because there is nothing left to send.

nodes.label: Why a metrics-only store exists
nodes.rationale: Retaining a payload is a different decision from observing a rate: a ring holds a strong reference to every undeliverable message, which is a data-protection question the moment a payload says anything about a person, and a counter is not. You cannot approximate it with a tiny ring, because max-entries must be positive.

nodes.label: Graceful-shutdown durability, not crash durability
nodes.rationale: The stream is derived from the system name so two systems sharing a journal keep separate queues; writes are issued as letters arrive and settled twice at shutdown, because teardown itself produces dead letters after the last phase. A hard kill loses the whole outstanding backlog, not just one write, because tell is synchronous and appends are fire-and-forget onto a serialized chain.

nodes.label: Poison messages cannot grow the queue
nodes.rationale: A replayed message that dead-letters again comes back as the same entry with a higher replayCount; without that, retrying a message the recipient cannot handle would add an entry per attempt while every attempt still looked like a first.
nodes.norm_label: poison messages cannot grow the queue

nodes.label: Replaying a captured letter
nodes.rationale: Replay resolves the recipient path again rather than reusing a ref captured at failure time, because the whole point is that the actor has come back at the same address as a new instance. Every outcome is named, so nothing fails quietly.

nodes.label: Replaying to a different recipient
nodes.rationale: Only the destination changes — the sender stays the recorded one; the recorded path is not resolved at all, because redirecting is most useful exactly when the original address is gone for good; and the replay cap still applies, since alternating between two paths would otherwise hand back the unbounded retry loop the cap exists to close.

nodes.label: Four stores on one axis: off, metrics, memory, persistent
nodes.rationale: Every key in this block decides what is retained, which is why they live under actor-ts.dead-letters and not beside the eventual logging and rate-limiting knobs: those decide how loudly a letter is announced, are read on the publish path, and sit downstream of capture so a suppression setting can never quietly make this record incomplete.
nodes.norm_label: four stores on one axis: off, metrics, memory, persistent

nodes.label: Symptom: shutdown dropped my messages
nodes.rationale: terminate() drains /user first, but not past the drain budget, not a parked mailbox (a throttle or a suspended mailbox counts as quiet), not work not yet in a mailbox, and not anything addressed to /system. Subscribing to DeadLetter has to happen before shutting down, because publishing is all that happens by default.

nodes.label: Actor.displayName()
nodes.rationale: Resolved on every record rather than captured once, so it may be derived from state and follows a restart. Added to the line rather than substituted for the path; a throw falls back to the path.

nodes.label: Class channel (instanceof matching)
nodes.rationale: Subclass instances reach base-class subscribers, which is what makes hierarchical event taxonomies work — subscribers pick their level.

nodes.label: DeadLetter event
nodes.rationale: Publishing is all that happens to a dead letter — nothing logs or keeps it, so with no subscriber it is gone.

nodes.label: EventKey.of<T>(kind)
nodes.rationale: Gives a plain kind-discriminated type the call shape a class gets for free, carries the event type into predicates, and makes the kind string checkable where a bare string quietly never matches on a typo.

nodes.label: SchedulerError on the event stream
nodes.rationale: Carries the cause and nothing else, because a scheduled task is an anonymous closure and a system has exactly one scheduler; the message-delivery forms do not publish here.

nodes.label: JsonLogger
nodes.rationale: One newline-terminated JSON object per record for aggregation pipelines; Error instances serialise as name/message/stack because Error enumerable surface is empty, and circular refs, BigInt and functions are sanitised so a log call never throws. Writes to stdout by default — the right pipe for Docker, Kubernetes, vector, fluent-bit and jq.

nodes.label: LogContext.run / with / get
nodes.rationale: get() returns the live readonly context — the same reference for the whole scope, so never hold onto it past the scope or hand it to something that might mutate it.

nodes.label: LogContext.snapshot
nodes.rationale: Returns a fresh copy on every call — the one to reach for at a boundary, safe to keep, mutate or serialise.

nodes.label: LogContextEntry<T>
nodes.rationale: Exported so a queue that outlives the turn which filled it can be typed; capture the context at enqueue time, the only moment it is still current.

nodes.label: Logger interface
nodes.rationale: Calls below the configured level emit nothing, but the arguments are still evaluated first because they are ordinary function arguments — guard expensive payloads with a manual level check.

nodes.label: MDC propagation across tell
nodes.rationale: The runtime snapshots the current context onto the envelope and the receiver runs under a fresh run() of that snapshot; across nodes the snapshot rides on the wire envelope, so one correlationId stitches a multi-actor multi-node request together.

nodes.label: otelLogger (OTLP logs bridge)
nodes.rationale: @opentelemetry/api-logs is an optional peer dep the framework never imports — you bring your existing namespace import; the active span traceId/spanId link automatically when tracing runs in the same process.

nodes.label: withFields (static structured fields)
nodes.rationale: Bind it in preStart rather than a field initializer — this.context is not available until the actor is attached, so a field initializer would throw at construction.

nodes.label: withDisplayName
nodes.rationale: The spawn-site counterpart to overriding the method — for an actor with no subclass of yours to override: a Behaviors actor, a sharded entity, a singleton. Purely cosmetic; the path stays the identity everywhere that routes or correlates.

nodes.label: system.scheduler (Scheduler)
nodes.rationale: Three legitimate cases: initiating work from outside the actor world, work that must outlive a specific actor, and framework code with no actor context.

nodes.label: DispatcherError
nodes.rationale: Fires for faults supervision structurally cannot see, so the channel is quiet by design — traffic on it means something is wrong underneath your actors; treat one as a page, not a counter. Caught at the actor cell, so it works for third-party dispatchers the system never sees.

nodes.label: Synchronous dispatcher anti-pattern
nodes.rationale: Synchronous execution defeats actor-model invariants — tell stops being fire-and-forget and the receiver await stalls the caller stack.

nodes.label: EventStream
nodes.rationale: A system-wide bus for one-to-many messaging that fits neither parent-child nor sender-receiver: the publisher does not know how many subscribers exist and subscribers do not know who publishes — loose coupling for cross-cutting concerns.

nodes.label: Kind channel
nodes.rationale: A kind channel matches exactly one kind — kinds have no base, so there is no way to say every billing.* event. A key and its string are the same channel; a class and a kind are two channels even when the class instances carry that kind, so holding both yields two deliveries per publish.

nodes.label: Predicate filtering on the bus side
nodes.rationale: Cheaper than filtering in each subscriber for high-frequency channels. Predicate-bearing subscriptions are never deduped because predicate functions have no identity contract; a throwing predicate counts as no match; predicates run at publish time on the publisher stack.
nodes.norm_label: predicate filtering on the bus side

nodes.label: Stopped subscribers are released
nodes.rationale: A stopping actor drops its subscriptions as part of termination, so a short-lived subscriber needs no unsubscribe in postStop. The recipient set is fixed when publish is called, so a removal takes effect from the next event on.

nodes.label: Context is per envelope, not per async resource
nodes.rationale: A delivery carries the context its tell snapshotted, or none — never whatever was ambient in the timer, socket callback or dispatcher tick that woke the actor. ReceiveTimeout, timer ticks, every Scheduler schedule, preStart/postStop and a context-free inbound frame all run with the MDC emptied, so a framework-delivered message never inherits the previous request.
nodes.norm_label: context is per envelope, not per async resource

nodes.label: displayName()
nodes.rationale: A path is an address, not a name, and under sharding it is unreadable. The name is added rather than substituted so source stays the path and nothing you correlate on moves; it is a label for humans, never an identity. Resolved per log call so it can read state and follow a restart — keep it cheap and side-effect free.

nodes.label: LogContext (MDC)
nodes.rationale: Backed by AsyncLocalStorage so the context propagates across awaits, tells and cluster hops. Static withFields and dynamic MDC merge at emit time with dynamic winning on collision (innermost-scope-wins).

nodes.label: LogContext.runEach
nodes.rationale: Entries run sequentially, each in its own scope, ambient context ignored rather than merged. It returns Promise<void> because handing back results would read like Promise.all and invite use as a concurrency helper; an error propagates immediately and abandons the rest, since swallowing it would be a supervision decision inside a diagnostics primitive.

nodes.label: LogContext.runFresh
nodes.rationale: The inverse of with(): where with inherits and adds, runFresh starts from empty. That fails safe — a field nobody set cannot leak — and is easier to reason about than remembering which keys to strip. Use it where work stops being attributable to the caller that started it.

nodes.label: MDC values must be JSON-safe
nodes.rationale: Values are string|number|boolean, enforced by the type, because across cluster hops the context serializes to JSON and arbitrary objects do not round-trip safely.

nodes.label: Deferred work and tenant isolation
nodes.rationale: AsyncLocalStorage binds a store when the async resource is created, so a promise started inside a turn keeps that turn context forever and every tell its continuation makes stamps it onto the envelope. When the deferred work serves a different principal, one tenant identifiers travel with another tenant messages — a data leak, not just a confusing log line.

nodes.label: ReceiveTimeout carries no diagnostic context
nodes.rationale: The handler runs with the MDC empty rather than under the last real message context, and a tell from it carries nothing either. You never arm this timer yourself — the framework re-arms it after every message — so there is no call site at which the context could have been cleared. Idleness belongs to no request.

nodes.label: SchedulerError
nodes.rationale: The function-form schedules run in a raw timer callback with no cell and no supervisor above them, so a throw is caught and reported twice over — system logger plus event stream — instead of escalating; a repeating schedule keeps ticking past it. The message-delivery forms never publish one, because a throw inside the target handler is the parent business.

nodes.label: A tick carries no diagnostic context
nodes.rationale: Whatever armed a schedule, the schedule does not belong to it. Without this, one setInterval armed while handling one tenant request would pin that tenant identifiers to every tick for the life of the process and — because a tell re-snapshots its context — forward them to whoever the tick messaged next.
nodes.norm_label: a tick carries no diagnostic context

nodes.label: CompressionConfig (none / gzip / zstd)
nodes.rationale: Es gibt bewusst kein brotli und kein deflate. Level sind rein encoder-seitig, werden geclamped und stehen nicht auf dem Wire.

nodes.label: gzip-Kompression (Store-Default)
nodes.rationale: Store-Default, weil es keine native Runtime-Unterstuetzung und keine Zusatz-Dependency braucht - node:zlib laeuft auf Bun, Node und Deno.

nodes.label: zstd-Kompression
nodes.rationale: Bestes Verhaeltnis bei konkurrenzfaehiger Geschwindigkeit und asymmetrisch guenstigem Decode auf jedem Level - deshalb stark fuer lese-lastigen State.

nodes.label: encryptionByPrefix (Per-persistenceId-Resolver)
nodes.rationale: Gibt jedem Tenant seinen eigenen Schlüssel ohne Wrapper oder eigenen Store, wenn ein Tenant auf ein pid-Präfix abbildet.

nodes.label: Body-Integrität (HMAC-SHA256, 16 Byte Tag)
nodes.rationale: Verschlüsselung ist keine Integrität: ein unverschlüsselter Body ist schlichtes JSON, und dazu gehört das revision-Feld, auf dem der Compare-and-Swap aufsetzt. Der integrityKey ist bewusst vom Encryption-Master-Key getrennt, denn die Bedrohung ist Manipulation, nicht Offenlegung.

nodes.label: Rollback-Schutz (Durable State)
nodes.rationale: Ein Replay desselben Bodys am selben Key ist für jeden Authentifikator unsichtbar — die revision liegt in den Bytes, die das Tag abdeckt. Der Store merkt sich die höchste gesehene Revision pro persistenceId; die Untergrenze gilt je Store-Instanz, ein Shard-Rebalance übergibt daher eine kalte Untergrenze.

nodes.label: withAllowUntaggedBodies (Migrationsfenster)
nodes.rationale: Solange die Option gesetzt ist, steht der Downgrade-Weg offen; Snapshots migrieren über keepN von selbst, DurableState braucht load + upsert pro persistenceId.

nodes.label: withRejectRevisionRollback
nodes.rationale: Standardmäßig aktiv; Opt-out für den legitimen prozessübergreifenden Delete-and-Recreate, bei dem ein neuer Record wieder bei Revision 1 beginnt.

nodes.label: FilesystemObjectStorageBackend
nodes.rationale: Gleicher Code-Pfad wie Produktion, mit lokalen Dateien - Tests und lokales Dev ohne MinIO-Container.

nodes.label: Vorhersagbares Object-Key-Layout
nodes.rationale: state/<persistenceId> und snapshots/<pid>/seq-<n>; das Framework verwaltet das Layout, Keys werden nie manuell gebaut. Verteilt Schreiblast ueber Prefixe gegen S3s Per-Prefix-Limits.

nodes.label: ObjectStorageBackend (PUT / GET / DELETE / LIST)
nodes.rationale: Bewusst kleine Oberflaeche - passt zu AWS S3, MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi; die meisten S3-kompatiblen APIs passen exakt.

nodes.label: encryption()-Hook pro Actor
nodes.rationale: PCI / HIPAA / GDPR-Scope: als sensibel klassifizierte Daten verwenden einen separaten Master-Key UND einen separaten HKDF-Kontext, sodass die Kompromittierung eines Keyrings den anderen nicht exponiert.

nodes.label: integrity()-Hook pro Actor
nodes.rationale: Der dritte Hook neben compression() und encryption() - lohnt auch fuer Daten, die nicht geheim sind, weil er Manipulation an Ort und Stelle beim Lesen erkennbar macht.

nodes.label: Faehigkeit durch Aufrufen pruefen, nicht durch Existenzcheck
nodes.rationale: Auf Deno exportiert node:zlib zstd-Einsprungpunkte, hinter denen kein Binding steht. Ein Existenzcheck waere dort falsch positiv; das Aufrufen laesst die Meldung die fehlende Faehigkeit benennen und haelt den fzstd-Fallback darunter erreichbar.
nodes.norm_label: faehigkeit durch aufrufen pruefen, nicht durch existenzcheck

nodes.label: Komprimieren vor dem Verschluesseln
nodes.rationale: Ciphertext zu komprimieren ist sinnlos (hochentrop), und die feste Reihenfolge vermeidet zudem CRIME-artige Seitenkanaele.

nodes.label: Dekompressions-Limit (512 MiB Bomb-Schutz)
nodes.rationale: Security audit #3: wenige KB, die sich auf viele GB aufblaehen, duerfen beim Recovery nicht den Speicher sprengen. gzip und zstd reichen die Grenze ueber zlibs maxOutputLength an den Decoder durch, der Body wird also abgelehnt BEVOR sein Output allokiert ist; auf den beiden Pfaden ohne Option (Bun.zstdDecompressSync, fzstd) greift die Grenze erst nach dem Output und ist eher Korrektheitspruefung als Bomb-Schutz.

nodes.label: fzstd-Pure-JS-Decompress-Fallback
nodes.rationale: Kann nur dekomprimieren, nie schreiben, und deckelt die Backreference-Distanz bei 2^25 (32 MB) - zstd-Ultra-Level (>= 20) sind darauf evtl. nicht lesbar. Level <= 19 halten, wenn irgendein Leser ohne natives zstd laufen koennte.

nodes.label: Kompression auf winzigen Objekten lohnt nicht
nodes.rationale: Unter ~100 Bytes uebersteigen die Header des Compressors die Einsparungen; der Output kann groesser sein als der Input.
nodes.norm_label: kompression auf winzigen objekten lohnt nicht

nodes.label: Das Tag ist Pflicht, nicht bloß geprüft
nodes.rationale: Das Bit, das 'dieser Body hat ein Tag' festhält, liegt im Body — hieße ein fehlendes Tag 'Prüfung überspringen', schützte die Prüfung niemanden, denn ein Tag zu entfernen ist weit einfacher, als eines zu fälschen.
nodes.norm_label: das tag ist pflicht, nicht bloß gepruft

nodes.label: CAS ueber ifMatch / ifNoneMatch
nodes.rationale: Laesst ObjectStorageDurableStateStore nebenlaeufige Writer ohne separate Koordination erkennen. Einige aeltere S3-kompatible Stores beachten die Header nicht - die Backends werfen dann klar, statt still zu ignorieren.

nodes.label: Object Storage sitzt zwischen SQLite und Cassandra
nodes.rationale: Fuer Single-Node ist SQLite einfacher, fuer High-Throughput-Multi-Node ist Cassandra schneller. Object Storage ist cloud-freundlich mit anstaendiger Performance und vielen Features - geteilte Persistenz ueber Cluster-Nodes, ohne Cassandra zu betreiben.
nodes.norm_label: object storage sitzt zwischen sqlite und cassandra

nodes.label: Gleiche Verschluesselungs-Config ueber alle Cluster-Nodes
nodes.rationale: Sonst koennen Sharded Entities nach der Migration auf einem anderen Node nicht gelesen werden - Key-Rings von derselben Quelle auf jedem Node hereinreichen.

nodes.label: Nur die Object-Storage-Stores lesen diese Hooks (#960)
nodes.rationale: Zehn der elf Snapshot-Stores und neun der zehn Durable-State-Stores nehmen PersistenceOptions entgegen und sehen sie nie an. Auf SQLite, Postgres, Cassandra, Mongo, DynamoDB und dem In-Memory-Referenz-Store bringt ein Override keine Manipulationserkennung und wirft keinen Fehler - die Direktive wird fallen gelassen.
nodes.norm_label: nur die object-storage-stores lesen diese hooks (#960)

nodes.label: Override gibt bei jedem Aufruf ein neues Objekt zurueck
nodes.rationale: Fuer die Korrektheit in Ordnung, aber pro Persist allokiert - bei Perf-Sensitivitaet zu einer statischen Konstante hochheben.
nodes.norm_label: override gibt bei jedem aufruf ein neues objekt zurueck

nodes.label: Reads folgen dem selbstbeschreibenden ATS1-Manifest, nicht den aktuellen Overrides
nodes.rationale: Ein unter pciKeyRing verschluesseltes Objekt wird ueber pciKeyRing entschluesselt, egal was encryption() aktuell sagt - das Rotieren einer Actor-Policy bricht alte Daten also nicht, solange die noetigen Keys verfuegbar sind.
nodes.norm_label: reads folgen dem selbstbeschreibenden ats1-manifest, nicht den aktuellen overrides

nodes.label: Labels
nodes.rationale: Labels machen aus einer Metrik viele Zeitreihen - jede eindeutige Label-Kombination ist zur Export-Zeit eine separate Serie.

nodes.label: maxSeriesPerFamily (Kardinalitaetsgrenze)
nodes.rationale: Auffangnetz fuer Labels die niemand beschraenkt hat: ab der Grenze (Default 10000) faltet die Familie alles weitere in eine Overflow-Serie und loggt einmal pro Familie. Der Marker steckt im Label-WERT, nicht im Label-Namen, weil Prometheus Label-Namen mit __-Praefix beim Ingest entfernt und die Overflow-Serie sonst still in eine echte Serie mischen wuerde. Default 10000 statt ~1000, weil actor_mailbox_size{path} und ein Per-pid-Projektions-Fan-out genau waehrend einer Stoerung am breitesten sind - dem Moment, in dem man sie lesen muss. 0 schaltet ab (nicht Infinity: die Grenze ist eine Ganzzahl).

nodes.label: GET /metrics ueber die Management-Routen
nodes.rationale: Opt-in via enableMetricsEndpoint. Laeuft auf einem separaten Port vom Haupt-HTTP-Server (App 8080 oeffentlich, Management 8558 nur intern), weil Scrapes periodisch sind und Metriken internen Zustand offenlegen - Request-Volumina, Fehlerraten, Nutzerzahlen.

nodes.label: Counter / Gauge / Histogram / Timer
nodes.rationale: Jede Metrik hat Namen + Labels; Labels erlauben, dieselbe Metrik nach Dimensionen zu zerlegen. Timer baut auf Histogram fuer timing-spezifische Ergonomie auf.

nodes.label: bucketize
nodes.rationale: Maps a value that comes from outside onto a fixed allow-list before it reaches the registry, returning the value when it is allowed and other otherwise - so the family can never hold more series than the allow-list length plus one, no matter what an attacker sends.

nodes.label: Counter
nodes.rationale: Monotonic - negative increments throw, and it resets on process restart. For things that go down, use a gauge.

nodes.label: Gauge
nodes.rationale: Settable and bidirectional; represents a point-in-time value such as active sessions, mailbox depth or queue size.

nodes.label: Histogram
nodes.rationale: Counts how many observations fell into each bucket, from which Prometheus computes percentiles at query time. There is no dedicated timer primitive - observe an elapsed duration instead.

nodes.label: Histogram bucket choice
nodes.rationale: Pick buckets that capture your SLO, bias toward fewer in the noise floor and more around the target; the defaults are seconds-scale and need overriding for millisecond-scale observations.

nodes.label: Metric labels
nodes.rationale: Turn one metric into many time-series - each unique label combination is a separate series, read in Prometheus or Grafana as filters or group-by axes.

nodes.label: MetricsRegistryOptions
nodes.rationale: Raises or disables the cap when the registry is installed; 0 disables it - 0 rather than Infinity, because the cap is an integer count.

nodes.label: Noop metrics registry
nodes.rationale: The default until enable is called: the framework own instrumentation resolves against it and records nothing.

nodes.label: Reading metric values in-process
nodes.rationale: value is a readonly property rather than a method; histograms expose count, sum, buckets and counts directly - useful for tests and custom exporters.

nodes.label: prom-client peer dependency
nodes.rationale: Only required if you use this adapter.

nodes.label: PromClientAdapterOptions
nodes.rationale: client and registry are mandatory - the bridge has nothing to publish into without them - plus an optional name prefix and the per-family cap.

nodes.label: promClientRegistry
nodes.rationale: Returns a MetricsRegistry that writes straight through to prom-client, so one scrape endpoint emits framework and application metrics together. Use it when you already run prom-client; otherwise prefer the framework native exporter and skip the dependency.

nodes.label: exportPrometheus
nodes.rationale: Turns the in-process registry into a single string in Prometheus 0.0.4 exposition format, ready to serve from a scrape endpoint.

nodes.label: Prometheus naming conventions
nodes.rationale: Counters end in _total, histograms carry the unit in the name, _count and _sum are framework-appended suffixes, and labels are snake_case. The framework does not enforce these, but Prometheus tooling expects them.

nodes.label: Prometheus text exposition format
nodes.rationale: One line per series for counters and gauges; for histograms one bucket line per bound plus count and sum.

nodes.label: Scrape cadence versus gauge update rate
nodes.rationale: Prometheus only sees a value at scrape time and computes counter rates from successive scrapes, so a fast-changing gauge may be stale when scraped - that is fine, since Prometheus is eventually consistent with its samples. Storage scales with series count times scrape interval, so bound label cardinality before adding labels.
nodes.norm_label: scrape cadence versus gauge update rate

nodes.label: MetricsExtension
nodes.rationale: Counter, gauge, histogram and timer, each with name plus labels, exported through PrometheusExporter or PromClientAdapter.

nodes.label: otelLogger
nodes.rationale: The logging counterpart to otelTracer, with the same pass-in-the-namespace shape, emitting through the SDK LoggerProvider.

nodes.label: Kardinalitaetsdisziplin
nodes.rationale: Unbeschraenkte Labels (Request-ID, User-ID, Zeitstempel) produzieren unbeschraenkte Serien und lassen dem Monitoring-System den Speicher ausgehen. Ziel: unter 100 Serien pro Metrik.

nodes.label: Kardinalitaetsgrenze der prom-client-Bruecke
nodes.rationale: Dieselbe Grenze pro Familie wie die In-Process-Registry, aber dringender gebraucht: prom-client legt bei jedem .labels(...) eine Serie an und laesst sie nie verfallen, ein unbeschraenktes Label laesst also den Resident-Speicher wachsen, nicht nur den Scrape-Body. Jenseits der Grenze wird das Tupel auf die DEKLARIERTEN Label-Namen umgeschrieben (Werte auf __overflow__), weil prom-client die Label-Namen bei der Konstruktion festlegt und bei einem .labels(...) mit anderen Namen wirft - ein synthetischer Marker-Name wuerde genau den Aufruf sprengen, der den Schaden begrenzen soll.

nodes.label: Prometheus-Namenskonventionen
nodes.rationale: Counter enden auf _total, Histogramme tragen die Einheit im Namen, Labels sind snake_case. Das Framework erzwingt das nicht - aber Prometheus-Tooling erwartet es.

nodes.label: Keine OTel-Metrik-Bruecke
nodes.rationale: Fuer Metriken gibt es keine OTel-Bruecke - nimm den Prometheus-Exporter (scrape ihn in einen Collector, wenn er in die OTLP-Pipeline soll) oder den prom-client-Adapter. Fuer Logs existiert mit otelLogger das Pendant zu otelTracer.

nodes.label: Per-family cardinality cap
nodes.rationale: bucketize is the fix; the cap is the backstop for the labels nobody bounded. A family stops minting series at maxSeriesPerFamily and folds the rest into one overflow series, warning once per family rather than per call. The marker lives in the label value, not a label name, because Prometheus reserves double-underscore label names and strips them at ingestion, which would silently merge the overflow into a real series. The default is 10 000 rather than the ~1 000 that would look sufficient, because an incident is exactly when the widest families are at their widest and exactly when you need to read them.

nodes.label: Cardinality discipline
nodes.rationale: Unbounded labels such as a request id, a user id or a timestamp produce unbounded series and your monitoring system runs out of memory. Bounded labels only - route names, environment, status kinds, pod names where the pod count is bounded - and aim for under 100 series per metric.

nodes.label: Bridge cardinality cap
nodes.rationale: The bridge needs the cap more urgently than the in-process registry: prom-client mints a series inside its own metric on every labels call and never expires one, so an unbounded label grows resident memory rather than only the scrape body. Past the cap the bridge rewrites the tuple to the family own declared label names with every value set to the overflow marker - reusing the declared names is not cosmetic, because prom-client fixes label names at construction and would throw on the very call meant to contain the damage.

nodes.label: Write-through bridge
nodes.rationale: Every framework counter, gauge and histogram mutation lands in the prom-client registry synchronously: no background sync, no interval and no second copy of the values. prom-client holds the canonical state and the existing metrics route emits everything.

nodes.label: No OTel metrics bridge
nodes.rationale: The SDK ties traces, metrics and logs together via shared context, but the framework ships no OTel metrics bridge: use the Prometheus exporter, scraped into a Collector if you want it in an OTLP pipeline, or the prom-client adapter. For logs there is a bridge.

nodes.label: maxPendingQuorumRequests cap
nodes.rationale: Bounds the unsettled set rather than the mailbox. Without a cap, a partition that stops quorums completing lets promises, timers and target sets pile up and then expire together as a timeout storm; the cap converts that into immediate rejections still attributable to the caller that made them.

nodes.label: maxQuorumTimeout ceiling
nodes.rationale: Clamps a caller-supplied timeoutMs down to a ceiling so one call cannot park a record indefinitely.

nodes.label: DistributedData quorum metrics
nodes.rationale: Fixed label sets keep the series count to a handful. A rising rejected_total means callers are outrunning the cap; a rising dropped_values_total means a broken or hostile peer, not a tuning problem.

nodes.label: BoundedMailbox
nodes.rationale: Constructing one yourself defaults to reject, because you built a bound and nothing else can be assumed about what is safe to lose; withMailboxOverflow defaults to drop-head, the policy that suits the workloads people reach for a bound to protect.

nodes.label: DropReportingMailbox / observeDrops
nodes.rationale: Registration is additive, so your own onDrop keeps firing alongside the stock counter.

nodes.label: undroppable envelope flag
nodes.rationale: Read by removeOldest, so a drop-head-shaped bound built on that seam steps over it for free without having to know why. Undroppable is not queue-jumping — it keeps its place in line and merely cannot be discarded from it.

nodes.label: ActorOptions.withMailbox(factory)
nodes.rationale: Called once per actor instance including on restart, so each restarted actor gets a fresh empty queue. It replaces rather than configures, so combining it with withMailboxCapacity is a configuration error rather than a silent precedence rule; never return a shared instance from two factories.

nodes.label: withMailboxCapacity / withMailboxOverflow
nodes.rationale: Capacity is what creates the bound; a policy without a capacity is rejected rather than silently ignored, since an unbounded mailbox never overflows. There is no system-wide mailbox setting — every bound is chosen per actor.

nodes.label: withMailboxCapacity
nodes.rationale: This is the call that introduces message loss: the mailbox is otherwise unbounded, and a bound discards the oldest queued message unless you name another policy.

nodes.label: Fixed-rate semantics (no catch-up, no compression)
nodes.rationale: A still-queued tick when the next interval elapses gives two ticks in the mailbox; there is no built-in missed-firing detection — record the last-fire timestamp yourself.

nodes.label: High-frequency timers are mailbox pressure
nodes.rationale: Pick an interval slower than the worst-case handler latency, or bound the mailbox and accept dropped ticks — mailboxes are unbounded, so the queue grows until the heap does.

nodes.label: maxBufferedBytes / onBackpressure
nodes.rationale: When a client cannot keep up its send buffer grows; past the bound the connection drops frames or is closed. Broadcasts to many slow clients are where this bites.

nodes.label: WebsocketRouteOptions
nodes.rationale: Precedence is route options > HOCON (actor-ts.http.websocket) > built-in defaults.

nodes.label: Subscriber tracking and topic fan-out
nodes.rationale: subscribeRef registers and death-watches a local ref; unsubscribeRef matches on the ref path rather than the ref object, so a different ref for the same actor still unsubscribes.

nodes.label: Subscriber fan-out to a target ref
nodes.rationale: Subscription semantics differ per protocol, but the pattern is constant: point the actor at a target ref and receive protocol messages as actor messages.
nodes.norm_label: subscriber fan-out to a target ref

nodes.label: Actor lifecycle and message metrics
nodes.rationale: actor_created_total, actor_terminated_total, actor_restarted_total, actor_messages_delivered_total and actor_message_handler_seconds, each a single unlabeled series.

nodes.label: DistributedData metrics
nodes.rationale: Five families in eight series over the CRDT quorum path, its wire decoder and its gossip packer; operation is write or read and reason is oversize or unserialisable, those values and no others.

nodes.label: Symptom: HTTP latency high under load
nodes.rationale: An actor monopolizing the event loop starves HTTP handlers; the fix is dispatcher-side.
nodes.norm_label: symptom: http latency high under load

nodes.label: Symptom: memory grows unboundedly
nodes.rationale: A mailbox with a slow consumer, subscriber sets that never unsubscribe, DistributedData keys accumulating, or persistent stash and ask buffers.

nodes.label: Dispatcher heuristics
nodes.rationale: HTTP plus actors takes the default; compute-heavy without HTTP takes microtask; batch processing with many actors takes ThroughputDispatcher; a single bottleneck actor takes the default plus withThroughput.

nodes.label: Per-actor dispatcher
nodes.rationale: Mix freely — a compute-only actor on microtasks while HTTP handlers stay on the default. What it is not good for is batching.

nodes.label: System-wide dispatcher
nodes.rationale: Overrides the default for every actor that does not specify otherwise; useful for batch-only systems with no HTTP traffic.

nodes.label: Mailbox as one layer of backpressure
nodes.rationale: The mailbox enforces the local boundary; sender retry logic and upstream rate-limiting (HTTP 429, broker push-back) are the rest, and no bound fixes a handler that is simply too slow.
nodes.norm_label: mailbox as one layer of backpressure

nodes.label: Unsettled quorum-request set
nodes.rationale: Each pending request keeps a promise, a timer and a target set alive until its deadline passes; the replicator mailbox itself stays unbounded, so nothing is discarded on the way in.

nodes.label: Extensions (lazy plugin system)
nodes.rationale: Extensions do not initialize until reached for, which keeps single-process apps small — you adopt a feature by reaching for it and drop it by not reaching.

nodes.label: Terminated is exempt from every discard policy
