nodes.label: Origin/Referer same-origin gate
nodes.rationale: Whole origins are compared - scheme, host and port - on both arms, so https://app.example accepts neither http://app.example nor https://app.example:8443, and an opaque Origin: null is always rejected. A request never tells you its scheme (TLS may terminate at a proxy and a forwarded scheme header is client-set), so expectedScheme supplies that missing half; it defaults to https and reads http when the Secure cookie attribute is explicitly turned off.

nodes.label: serializeCookie
nodes.rationale: Strict by omission — an unmentioned attribute resolves to Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ — so the two-argument call is already shippable and loosening is what you write down. Path is always emitted because otherwise the browser derives scope from the request URI. It refuses a Path or Domain that could break out, since both reach the header verbatim and the last Domain is the one that counts.

nodes.label: waitFor Deterministic Deadline Helper
nodes.rationale: Every wait-until step goes through it because it fails with a deterministic deadline message instead of a flaky 30-second timeout.

nodes.label: Control-Port Ping Healthcheck
nodes.rationale: Nodes are considered healthy only once /test/ping answers, which is what other nodes' and the controller's depends_on conditions wait on.

nodes.label: PEERS List for Shutdown-Trace Hook
nodes.rationale: A comma-separated list of all node hostnames so a shutting-down node can post a marker to a peer that is still alive.

nodes.label: In-Memory Transport Blind Spots
nodes.rationale: Synthetic partitions and deterministic ordering cannot surface TCP-layer timing, OS scheduler pressure under real concurrency, kernel-buffer / Nagle interactions, or real-DNS dual-stack behaviour.

nodes.label: integration.yml CI Gating
nodes.rationale: Runs only on pull requests targeting main (the release PR) and nightly: the suite is expensive and the fast unit suite catches most regressions, so develop pushes and feature PRs skip it.

nodes.label: Management HTTP Endpoint
nodes.rationale: Auth-protected with BearerTokenAuth via the MGMT_TOKEN env var, unlike the test-control port.

nodes.label: Real-Network Multi-Node Integration Suite
nodes.rationale: The in-memory transport suites give tight feedback loops but never exercise the kernel; a Docker-compose topology of 5 cluster nodes plus a controller is what makes TCP timing, scheduler pressure and real DNS observable.

nodes.label: Real TcpTransport Cluster Join
nodes.rationale: Bound on 0.0.0.0:9000 and identified by the compose hostname, so joins traverse a real socket and real DNS rather than an in-process transport.

nodes.label: Test-Control HTTP Surface
nodes.rationale: Unauthenticated on purpose: it is only reachable from the compose bridge network, so the scenarios need no credential plumbing to install or heal a partition.

nodes.label: Controller Exit Code as Test Result
nodes.rationale: `--exit-code-from controller` in the npm script bubbles the controller's status back up, so the compose run itself is the pass/fail signal.
nodes.norm_label: controller exit code as test result

nodes.label: Per-Container NET_ADMIN Capability
nodes.rationale: Each cluster node gets NET_ADMIN so it can install iptables and tc rules inside its OWN namespace — no host-level privileged mode and no docker-socket access.

nodes.label: x-node-defaults YAML Anchor
nodes.rationale: Each node overrides only container_name, hostname and NODE_NAME; the anchor keeps the per-node block to ~5 lines instead of duplicating the whole stanza five times.

nodes.label: Seed-of-Self Bootstrap Node
nodes.rationale: An empty SEEDS list means be the seed; every other node seeds back to the first, which is what makes the mesh converge from a single well-known address.

nodes.label: Symmetric iptables Partition Injection
nodes.rationale: Drops are installed in each container's own network namespace and applied in both directions between A and B, so there is no half-open weirdness and a container can only affect its own peers.

nodes.label: JsonLogger Container Logging
nodes.rationale: Chosen so the docker logs are jq-friendly when a scenario fails in CI.

nodes.label: tc netem Latency Injection
nodes.rationale: Latency is injected with `tc qdisc add ... netem delay` rather than simulated in the transport, so the delay is real kernel queueing.

nodes.label: Unpublished Control Port
nodes.rationale: Deliberately not published to the host so nothing in the scenarios can reach through it; the same configuration then runs identically in CI and locally, and debugging goes via `docker compose exec`.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ service (AMQP suite)
nodes.rationale: ~10s boot, slower than MinIO/Mosquitto, but the de-facto AMQP 0.9.1 reference broker. Healthcheck is rabbitmq-diagnostics check_running, faster than check_port_connectivity because it needs no management plugin. The image relaxes the loopback-only restriction so guest:guest works from any client on the compose bridge.

nodes.label: AMQP runner service
nodes.rationale: Built from the repo-root context, gated on service_healthy, connects as AMQP_URL amqp://guest:guest@rabbitmq:5672/ over the amqpnet bridge.

nodes.label: DynamoDB Local service
nodes.rationale: AWS's own local emulator, the image the AWS docs recommend for tests. Run with -inMemory -sharedDb: the suite creates its own tables on first use, and a fresh instance per run is exactly what makes it reproducible.

nodes.label: DynamoDB runner service
nodes.rationale: DYNAMODB_ENDPOINT http://dynamodb:8000; dynamodb-local ignores credentials but the SDK refuses to sign without them, so any non-empty pair will do.

nodes.label: GreenMail service
nodes.rationale: Apache-2.0 mail server speaking both halves of the bridge - SMTP 3025 and IMAP 3143 in one container - so a scenario can send a message and watch the same server hand it back. The user is declared up front rather than left to GreenMail's auto-create: the bridge authenticates, and a server that invents accounts on demand would make a wrong credential look like a pass.

nodes.label: Email runner service
nodes.rationale: EMAIL_HOST greenmail with SMTP 3025 / IMAP 3143, logging in as the full address bridge@example.test.

nodes.label: gRPC runner service
nodes.rationale: The single service in the suite: GRPC_BIND 0.0.0.0:50051, GRPC_ENDPOINT localhost:50051, GRPC_PROTO_PATH pointing at the suite's echo.proto.

nodes.label: k3s API server service
nodes.rationale: Privileged because it mounts its own cgroups and iptables for kube-proxy - a test-only container on a dev/CI host, so the security trade-off is acceptable for the test scope. traefik, servicelb, metrics-server and network policy are disabled; the kubeconfig file appearing under /output is the readiness signal, since it is written when the API server is up.

nodes.label: k8s runner service
nodes.rationale: Mounts the shared kubeconfig volume read-only and rewrites the server URL at runtime: k3s writes 127.0.0.1, the perspective of its own container, while on the compose bridge it is reachable as https://k3s:6443.

nodes.label: Redpanda service
nodes.rationale: Minimal dev-container flags: one core, 512M, overprovisioned, listener on 9092 advertised as redpanda:9092 so the runner can reach it by service name. Healthcheck is rpk cluster info.

nodes.label: Kafka runner service
nodes.rationale: KAFKA_BROKERS redpanda:9092, KAFKA_CLIENT_ID actor-ts-runner.

nodes.label: Mosquitto service
nodes.rationale: Anonymous auth via a read-only mounted mosquitto.conf; the broker is only reachable on the compose bridge, never published to the host. The healthcheck uses mosquitto_sub, which ships with the image and exits 0 once a subscription succeeds, so compose waits for the broker to actually accept traffic.

nodes.label: MQTT runner service
nodes.rationale: MQTT_BROKER_URL mqtt://mosquitto:1883, client id actor-ts-runner; exercises real MQTT 3.1.1 and 5.0 traffic.

nodes.label: NATS service
nodes.rationale: Boots in well under a second - the fastest broker in the suite. No auth, no clustering, standalone server on 4222.

nodes.label: NATS runner service
nodes.rationale: NATS_SERVERS nats://nats:4222; depends_on service_started because the scratch image has no readiness probe, so waitForPort is the actual gate.

nodes.label: Redis service
nodes.rationale: Redis 7 ships streams in the open-source build; single-node ephemeral instance with --save '' and --appendonly no, so no persistence and no clustering.

nodes.label: Redis Streams runner service
nodes.rationale: REDIS_URL redis://redis:6379, gated on the redis-cli ping healthcheck.

nodes.label: MinIO service
nodes.rationale: Single node, single drive - no HA, this is a test. MINIO_ROOT_USER / MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD are the runner's credentials; bucket creation is an init step inside the runner so cleanups stay co-located with the test rather than split across compose hooks.

nodes.label: S3 runner service
nodes.rationale: S3_ENDPOINT http://minio:9000 - MinIO is reachable by service name, not localhost - with forcePathStyle because virtual-host style would need DNS for bucket.minio wired up separately. The runner keeps its own waitForPort as belts-and-braces for runtimes where compose healthcheck propagation is unreliable (Bun on Windows + Docker Desktop).

nodes.label: tests/integration/brokers/package.json
nodes.rationale: Runner images install from a dedicated manifest declaring every adapter peer-dep plus fastify/ts-pattern as plain dependencies - the shape an end user has after bun add actor-ts + bun add @aws-sdk/client-s3. A fresh manifest with no peerDependencies block side-steps two bun traps that fire only inside this repo. Failure mode is loud: the first import of a missing package throws Cannot find module before any scenario starts.

nodes.label: integration-brokers.yml CI matrix
nodes.rationale: Runs the broker suites as a job matrix; skipped on PRs touching only docs or unit tests via the same paths filter as integration.yml.

nodes.label: OptionalPeerDeclarations.test.ts
nodes.rationale: The loud import failure only covers peers that have a suite here; a driver with no suite directory is declared in no manifest at all and nothing says so. This test is the quiet half: every optional peer must be declared either in this manifest or in root devDependencies, so the gap is a failing test rather than a discovery years later (#676).

nodes.label: Own-scenarios suites
nodes.rationale: The nine broker suites - s3, mqtt, kafka, amqp, nats, redis-streams, grpc, k8s, email - add a scenarios/ directory that the runner imports before calling runScenarios().

nodes.label: Three-file suite directory layout
nodes.rationale: Every suite has docker-compose.<name>.yml, Dockerfile.runner and Runner.ts; three also carry a config file their image needs (mqtt/mosquitto.conf, amqp/rabbitmq.conf, grpc/echo.proto).

nodes.label: Adding a new broker suite
nodes.rationale: Prefer an image with a tini-style PID 1 so it exits cleanly on docker compose down instead of leaking zombies; create the three files; add an npm script (stale - the discovery script replaced them); optionally extend the CI matrix; guard readiness with waitForPort.

nodes.label: Broker live-integration suites
nodes.rationale: Unit suites cover the broker adapters against hand-rolled fakes - right for fast feedback, blind to protocol corners, auth/connection bring-up and operational shape. Each suite brings the real broker up in Docker and runs scenarios against the live socket; same pattern as the #313 cluster setup, one container per suite instead of a 5-node mesh.

nodes.label: rabbitmq.conf transient-queue permission
nodes.rationale: Mounted read-only to permit transient non-exclusive queues; without it RabbitMQ 4.x rejects the test scenarios' ephemeral-queue declarations.

nodes.label: service_started gate (bare JRE image)
nodes.rationale: No service_healthy gate: the image is a bare JRE with no shell utilities to probe with. The runner waits on the port itself via waitForPort and the SDK retries its first call.

nodes.label: Mailpit rejected: no IMAP
nodes.rationale: The other obvious candidate is out because its maintainer has explicitly declined IMAP support, and IMAP is the inbound half of the bridge.

nodes.label: Two-port readiness gate
nodes.rationale: service_started rather than a healthcheck - a slim JRE with no curl or nc, so compose cannot probe from the inside. The runner's waitForPort gates on BOTH ports from the outside: a two-port service is only ready when both listen, and SMTP comes up before IMAP.

nodes.label: greenmail.users.login=email
nodes.rationale: greenmail.users=<local-part>:<password>@<domain> creates the mailbox but authenticates under the local part alone - GreenMail's default since 1.6.1. Setting users.login=email lets the bridge log in with the full address the way a real provider expects; bending the client to a test server's default would be fitting the wrong way round.

nodes.label: No external broker (framework is both ends)
nodes.rationale: Unlike every other suite here there is no broker container: GrpcServerActor is the server, GrpcClientActor is the client, and both run in the same runner against a local echo.proto.
nodes.norm_label: no external broker (framework is both ends)

nodes.label: k3s over kind
nodes.rationale: kind needs nested Docker, which is brittle in CI (Docker-in-Docker pitfalls, slow boot). k3s ships as a single binary, runs in one container, boots in ~5s and presents the full K8s API - and the suite tests the API surface the seed provider reads, not workload scheduling.

nodes.label: Redpanda over a real Kafka cluster
nodes.rationale: Redpanda is Kafka-protocol-compatible and boots in ~2s versus a real Kafka cluster's ~30s+ Zookeeper boot. For broker-level correctness against the Kafka protocol it is the right cost/coverage trade: the adapter speaks pure Kafka protocol through kafkajs, so it cannot tell the difference.
nodes.norm_label: redpanda over a real kafka cluster

nodes.label: No compose healthcheck (distroless sqld image)
nodes.rationale: The sqld image is distroless-ish and ships neither a shell nor curl, so a compose healthcheck has nothing to run. The runner waits on the port itself via waitForPort, then retries its first statement.

nodes.label: Scratch image has no readiness probe
nodes.rationale: The NATS image is built on scratch and ships no shell, curl, wget or nc, so docker-compose has no way to probe readiness from inside the container. The runner's waitForPort polls the client port until it accepts a TCP connection - the same readiness shape, just from the OUTSIDE.
nodes.norm_label: scratch image has no readiness probe

nodes.label: Auth / connection bring-up
nodes.rationale: Credential format, TLS and lazy reconnect after a transient drop are never exercised by an in-process fake.

nodes.label: bun add no-ops on an already-declared optional peer
nodes.rationale: bun treats a package already listed in peerDependencies with optional true as declared and silently does nothing.
nodes.norm_label: bun add no-ops on an already-declared optional peer

nodes.label: Container-started-but-broker-not-ready race
nodes.rationale: The single most common source of flake in these suites; every scenario guards against it with waitForPort(host, port).

nodes.label: scripts/integration-compose.mjs suite discovery
nodes.rationale: There used to be a package.json script per suite - 34 of them, the same two docker compose invocations with a different path - so the backend set was maintained in four places and missing one meant a suite that silently never ran (#559). A suite is now just a directory holding docker-compose.<dir>.yml; a wrong name prints the ones that exist. up stops at the first failing suite, teardown deliberately does not so one broken suite cannot strand later suites' containers and volumes.

nodes.label: Operational shape
nodes.rationale: Broker config the code assumed exists but is not on by default - Mosquitto's allow_anonymous, RabbitMQ's definitions.json import.

nodes.label: Per-suite container lifecycle
nodes.rationale: One broker container per suite rather than per test; fine for the current scenario count, revisitable if each it() should ever get a fresh broker.

nodes.label: Protocol-level corners
nodes.rationale: Quoting, escaping and header serialisation where the project's spec-reading and what the real broker accepts diverge - a fake agrees with the code by construction.

nodes.label: Why not testcontainers/node
nodes.rationale: Bun compatibility is best-effort (the library expects Node's child_process event ordering); the stated requirement was locally runnable like tests/integration and compose YAML is the universal shape every developer already has muscle memory for; the compose files are ~20 lines each, so the abstraction cost outweighs the boilerplate saved.

nodes.label: stream-node-max-entries 10
nodes.rationale: What makes the MAXLEN ~ scenario deterministic. ~ trims whole macro nodes and never a partial one, and a node is sealed at whichever of stream-node-max-entries (default 100) or stream-node-max-bytes (default 4096) is reached first. The scenario writes 50 entries of roughly 80 bytes - about 4000 total, sitting on the byte threshold - so whether a second node existed to trim decided the result and the assertion flipped between runs with nothing changing. Ten entries per node puts it well clear of the boundary, in the direction the scenario means to test.

nodes.label: Built-in test KMS for SSE-AES256
nodes.rationale: MinIO since ~mid-2025 refuses server-side-encryption PUTs - even plain AES256 - unless a KMS backend is configured; older releases accepted SSE without one, and pinning latest is what surfaced the policy change. The key is <keyname>:<32-byte base64 secret>, the same string every run so re-runs can read back previously-encrypted objects.

nodes.label: MinIO over LocalStack
nodes.rationale: MinIO boots in ~1-2s versus LocalStack's 10-15s so CI minutes stay tight, its S3 implementation is closest to the AWS spec (fewer quirks than R2/B2), and the images are stable and tagged. LocalStack S3 stays an optional secondary target that can be layered on later (#297).

nodes.label: Probe the container's own address, not 127.0.0.1
nodes.rationale: YSQL listens on 5433, not 5432, and comes up well after the process starts. yugabyted binds every service to the node's advertise address, so loopback never listens and a 127.0.0.1 probe fails forever even once the cluster is fully up. That is what happened: the container went unhealthy after a clean YugabyteDB Started line, compose refused to start the runner on the unmet service_healthy condition, and this certification silently never ran at all while looking like a slow image.
nodes.norm_label: probe the container's own address, not 127.0.0.1

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.rationale: System-Level-Scheduler fuer verzoegerte und periodische Tasks; unterscheidet sich vom per-Actor TimerScheduler.

nodes.label: bun:test
nodes.rationale: Drop-in-kompatibel mit Jests API; TestKit funktioniert direkt.

nodes.label: Buns Timer-Quantum (15,625 ms unter Windows)
nodes.rationale: Ein setTimeout, dessen Deadline knapp unter einem Tick-Vielfachen liegt, feuert einen ganzen Tick zu früh — setTimeout(30) wurde mit 18,67 ms gemessen. Die Uhr ist nicht das Problem, die Toleranz war falsch; eine sichere Obergrenze gibt es nicht (derselbe Timer wurde unter Last mit 201 ms gemessen), also virtuelle Zeit prüfen.

nodes.label: Feuer-Reihenfolge in einem advance
nodes.rationale: Aufgaben feuern in ihrer geplanten Reihenfolge (frueheste zuerst, Gleichstaende nach Einfuege-Reihenfolge), sequenziell bevor advance zurueckkehrt. Plant eine Aufgabe beim Feuern weitere, feuern die mit, wenn ihre Zeit ins selbe Fenster faellt — ein re-armender Heartbeat feuert in advance(3500) ab t=0 dreimal.

nodes.label: ManualScheduler
nodes.rationale: Virtual-Clock-Scheduler: Timer von context.timers und system.scheduler feuern nur, wenn der Test die Zeit vorstellt — kein echtes setTimeout, keine Flakiness.

nodes.label: TestKit
nodes.rationale: Frisches ActorSystem mit NoopLogger plus createTestProbe, within und shutdown; tk.shutdown() ist kritisch, sonst bleibt ein lebendes System mit laufendem Dispatcher zurück und der Test-Prozess kann hängen.

nodes.label: expectMessage(expected)
nodes.rationale: Wartet-dann-assertet deep-equal und gibt die Nachricht zurueck; jeder Aufruf KONSUMIERT eine Nachricht aus dem Buffer, ein zweites Assert auf dieselbe Nachricht braucht den Rueckgabewert.

nodes.label: expectMessageType(Class)
nodes.rationale: Fuer Success/Failure-Envelopes aus pipeTo oder beliebige klassenbasierte Message-Typen.

nodes.label: expectNoMessage(timeoutMs)
nodes.rationale: Assertet, dass im gegebenen Fenster NICHTS ankommt; Default 300 ms — kurz genug fuer schnelle Tests, lang genug, um die meisten unerwuenschten Sends zu fangen.

nodes.label: fishForMessage(predicate)
nodes.rationale: Verwirft Nachrichten, bis eine das Praedikat erfuellt — verworfene sind weg und koennen spaeter nicht mehr assertet werden.

nodes.label: probe.sender / probe.reply
nodes.rationale: Nach dem Konsumieren haelt probe.sender den Sender der eben empfangenen Nachricht; reply(message) ist die Abkuerzung dorthin — gaengig in Tests, die Zwei-Wege-Konversationen simulieren.

nodes.label: receiveOne / receiveN
nodes.rationale: Nachrichten holen OHNE zu asserten — fuer variierende Formen, die der Test mit eigener Logik inspiziert.

nodes.label: tk.createTestProbe(options?)
nodes.rationale: Gibt eine auf das System dieses Kits gescopte Probe zurueck, damit das System nicht durch jeden Probe-Konstruktor gefaedelt werden muss.

nodes.label: tk.shutdown()
nodes.rationale: Immer im Fixture-Teardown aufrufen — ohne ihn leakt der Test-Prozess ein lebendes System, das die Event-Loop am Leben haelt; manche Runner erkennen das und lassen die Suite fehlschlagen, andere haengen.

nodes.label: TestKit
nodes.rationale: Duenner Convenience-Wrapper um ActorSystem mit Test-Defaults. Rohes ActorSystem.create funktioniert genauso und liest sich bei komplexen Setups (eigener Logger, mehrere Systeme, spezifische Extensions) manchmal klarer.

nodes.label: tk.within(durationMs, callback)
nodes.rationale: Weiche Deadline: der Callback laeuft auch bei Ueberziehen zu Ende und wirft nur im Nachhinein — fuer SLA-artige Assertions, ohne vom Per-Test-Timeout des Runners abzuhaengen.

nodes.label: TestKit.withManualScheduler()
nodes.rationale: Gibt Kit und ManualScheduler zurueck, damit der Test virtuelle Zeit voranbringen kann.

nodes.label: advance and advanceToNext
nodes.rationale: Tasks maturing in the advanced window fire in scheduled order (ties by insertion) before advance returns, and tasks they re-arm join the same window if their time falls inside it; advanceToNext skips an idle gap and is a no-op when nothing is scheduled.

nodes.label: clearInbox
nodes.rationale: Drops everything queued so a later phase asserts only on what comes next.

nodes.label: expectMessage
nodes.rationale: Waits for the next message and deep-equals it, returning it so assertions can chain. It consumes from the buffer, so asserting twice on one message means capturing the return value.

nodes.label: expectNoMessage
nodes.rationale: Asserts nothing arrives in a window; the 300 ms default is short enough to keep tests fast and long enough to catch most spurious sends.

nodes.label: fishForMessage
nodes.rationale: Discards messages until a predicate matches - useful against a stream of traffic, at the cost that discarded messages cannot be re-asserted.

nodes.label: probe.sender and probe.reply
nodes.rationale: The sender of the just-consumed message, plus a shortcut that tells it back - the shape for simulating a two-way conversation.

nodes.label: TestProbe
nodes.rationale: An ActorRef that runs no user code - every tell lands in a buffer the test asserts on - so it can stand in for any downstream actor or reply-to target.

nodes.label: TestProbeOptions
nodes.rationale: Optional default timeout (3 s otherwise) and a name that makes the probe visible in logs.

nodes.label: TestKit
nodes.rationale: A thin convenience facade over ActorSystem for tests: quiet system, one-line probe creation, deterministic shutdown.

nodes.label: TestKit.shutdown
nodes.rationale: Without it the test process leaks a live system that keeps the event loop alive - some runners detect it and fail the suite, others simply hang.

nodes.label: TestKit.within
nodes.rationale: A soft deadline: the callback still runs to completion and the assertion throws afterwards, so it expresses an in-test SLA without depending on the runner's per-test timeout.

nodes.label: TestKitOptions
nodes.rationale: Extends ActorSystemOptionsType with quiet (default true); quiet false restores console logging while debugging a failing test.

nodes.label: Date.now() wird nicht virtualisiert
nodes.rationale: ManualScheduler virtualisiert den Scheduler des Actor-Systems, nicht Date.now() oder new Date(): zeichnet ein Actor Zeitstempel auf, sind das echte Wall-Clock-Werte. Fuer deterministische Tests eine Clock injizieren und in Tests () => scheduler.now() uebergeben. Ebenso duerfen rohe setTimeout-Aufrufe nicht mit dem Manual-Scheduler gemischt werden.

nodes.label: Warum virtuelle Zeit
nodes.rationale: Die Toleranz aufzuweiten rettet einen Wall-Clock-Test nicht, denn Timer feuern ebenso ZU FRUEH: unter Windows sind 15,625 ms das Quantum, ein 30-ms-setTimeout wurde unter Bun mit 18,7 ms gemessen und unter CPU-Last mit 201 ms. Ein nominales Delay, eine Zehnerpotenz Streuung — keine Grenze ist gleichzeitig eng genug, um etwas zu bedeuten, und weit genug, um zu halten, und eine praezisere Uhr hilft nicht: zu frueh ist der Timer, nicht die Messung.

nodes.label: Kein createTestProbe<T>()
nodes.rationale: Der Wert einer Probe liegt darin, fuer Empfaenger mit unterschiedlichen Nachrichtentypen einzuspringen — ein festes T muesste an den meisten Aufrufstellen wieder aufgeweitet werden. Stattdessen sind die zurueckgebenden Methoden generisch (expectMessage<T>, expectMessageType<T>, fishForMessage<T>).

nodes.label: Probe als Stellvertreter fuer einen Downstream-Actor
nodes.rationale: Die Probe ersetzt einen echten DB- oder Downstream-Actor; der Test sieht den Call, ohne dass die Abhaengigkeit existieren muss. Zweite Rolle: Reply-to-Ziel fuer Ask-artige Nachrichten.
nodes.norm_label: probe als stellvertreter fuer einen downstream-actor

nodes.label: Synchrone Reads nach tell sehen meist 0
nodes.rationale: tell plant nur; die Verarbeitung passiert in der naechsten Event-Loop-Runde, also ist messageCount direkt nach einem tell meist 0 — das asynchrone expectMessage wartet auf Zustellung. Lange Timeouts verstecken umgekehrt langsamen Code.
nodes.norm_label: synchrone reads nach tell sehen meist 0

nodes.label: Fixture-Muster (per-Test vs geteilt)
nodes.rationale: Ein frisches Kit pro Test kostet etwas Zeit, ist die Isolation aber wert; ein geteiltes Fixture ist schneller und nur sicher, wenn Tests keine geteilten Actor mutieren. Eindeutige System-Namen vermeiden Cluster-Identitaets-Konflikte.

nodes.label: Leises Logging als Default (NoopLogger)
nodes.rationale: Log-Aufrufe sind No-Ops, was die Test-Ausgabe sauber haelt; einschalten nur zum Debuggen.

nodes.label: Date.now is not virtualized
nodes.rationale: ManualScheduler virtualizes the actor system's scheduler only, so an actor that stamps timestamps still reads the real clock; inject a clock and pass () => scheduler.now() in tests.

nodes.label: Don't mix real timers with ManualScheduler
nodes.rationale: A raw setTimeout runs on the real clock the manual scheduler knows nothing about, so everything time-based in a test should go through context.timers or system.scheduler.
nodes.norm_label: don't mix real timers with manualscheduler

nodes.label: Always call stop()
nodes.rationale: Orphaned worker threads leak and can starve later tests; the runner may clean up after a crash, but explicit teardown is what guarantees it.

nodes.label: No createTestProbe<T>
nodes.rationale: A probe's value is standing in for recipients whose message types differ - the same probe is handed to actors with unrelated protocols in one test - so pinning it to a single T would be widened back at most call sites; expectMessage, expectMessageType and fishForMessage are generic individually instead.

nodes.label: Quiet NoopLogger default
nodes.rationale: Log calls become no-ops so test output stays clean; turning logging on is an explicit opt-in for debugging.

nodes.label: Unique system names per test
nodes.rationale: Two systems with the same name on the same network would join each other once clustering is enabled, so per-test names avoid a latent identity conflict.

nodes.label: Logo-derived docs theme and fonts
nodes.rationale: Indigo primary, Slate background, Red for cautions; JetBrains Mono is chosen because it matches the font-family already in the logo's wordmark.

nodes.label: Guarantee-carrying cache entries
nodes.rationale: A setIfAbsent claim or an incr counter with a finite TTL: for these the cache IS the source of truth, so losing one voids a guarantee rather than costing a round-trip. A set picks a guarantee up only when it replaces a live claim under the same key, which is the shape idempotent uses; a claim with no TTL is not protected, because protecting one would make it permanent.

nodes.label: InMemoryCache
nodes.rationale: The default Cache: a Map with LRU eviction, lazy per-entry TTL and an optional background sweep. Single-process only, so multi-pod deployments each keep their own copy; setIfAbsent is atomic here for a structural reason (read and write in one synchronous block) rather than a protocol one.

nodes.label: InMemoryCacheOptions
nodes.rationale: maxEntries (default 10000) and cleanupMs (default 60000), validated once at construction on the merged settings so the builder, a plain object and HOCON all hit the same check and a bad value throws OptionsError.

nodes.label: LRU eviction bounded by maxEntries
nodes.rationale: Keeps a flood of distinct never-re-read keys (attacker-chosen idempotency or rate-limit keys) from growing the map without limit. Only a read counts as a use, so an entry written once and never read back ages towards eviction from the moment it is stored.

nodes.label: Opportunistic cache entries
nodes.rationale: Everything written by set or mset has a source of truth behind it, so losing one is a cache miss the caller already handles; eviction drains this half first, least-recently-used end onwards.

nodes.label: Lazy TTL with a background sweep
nodes.rationale: Expiry is checked on every read path, and a sweep every cleanupMs reclaims expired entries nothing touches again so they do not sit in the Map waiting for a read; setting cleanupMs to 0 or Infinity relies on lazy expiry alone.
nodes.norm_label: lazy ttl with a background sweep

nodes.label: MemcachedCache
nodes.rationale: Right when you already run Memcached or need a pure cache: simpler protocol, smaller footprint, zero persistence. mget/mset are parallelised single-key operations because Memcached has no multi-key commands.

nodes.label: memjs peer dependency
nodes.rationale: memjs supplies SASL auth, hash-distribution across servers and its own connection pool, which the framework does not manage directly.

nodes.label: acquireLock token-guarded lock
nodes.rationale: Writes a random 128-bit token and deletes the key only if that token is still there; the naive delete-in-finally evicts the new owner once a holder overruns its TTL. ttlMs is required because expiry is the recovery path from a crashed holder. Not a consensus lock: the compare-and-delete is a get then a delete, not one atomic step, so guard with a fencing token where two holders would be a correctness bug.

nodes.label: Atomic increment (incr)
nodes.rationale: Returns the new count; the TTL is applied only when the counter is created, which is the right semantics for a fixed-window rate limiter.

nodes.label: Bulk cache operations (mget / mset)
nodes.rationale: Round-trip optimisation, critical for shared-entity hydration after a sharding rebalance: one call instead of N.

nodes.label: Cache interface
nodes.rationale: Seven operations (get, set, incr, setIfAbsent, delete, mget, mset) cover about 95% of real cases; deliberately no pattern scans and no pub/sub, since the cluster has its own.

nodes.label: setIfAbsent atomic compare-and-set
nodes.rationale: Atomicity is a guarantee, not best effort: every backend maps it onto a single native compare-and-set (Redis SET NX, Memcached ADD, an uninterleavable Map read/write pair in-process). No backend implements it as get-then-set, which would let two callers both observe the key absent. ttlMs applies only to the winning write, so a retry loop cannot extend someone else's hold.

nodes.label: Redis Cluster mode
nodes.rationale: For horizontal scale beyond one server's memory; cross-slot MGETs fan out per slot, so hash-tagging related keys keeps them in one round-trip.

nodes.label: ioredis peer dependency
nodes.rationale: Handles the cluster protocol (MOVED/ASK redirects, slot tracking) and pipelines commands issued in the same JS turn into a single TCP write.

nodes.label: RedisCache
nodes.rationale: The multi-pod default: pods share cache state, MGET/MSET are single round-trips, AOF/RDB survive a restart, and it is the best-supported backend for locking because a key lives on one logical keyspace.

nodes.label: actor-ts documentation site
nodes.rationale: A self-contained Astro Starlight sub-project with its own package.json, node_modules and build pipeline; CI builds it on every push to main and deploys to GitHub Pages.

nodes.label: Three-tier reading model for doc pages
nodes.rationale: What you can do with it, a minimal example, how it works, when (not) to apply it, common pitfalls, related concepts, API reference: the reader can stop after any tier and still have learned something, which keeps newcomers oriented while carrying depth for experienced users.
nodes.norm_label: three-tier reading model for doc pages

nodes.label: What a dropped guarantee costs
nodes.rationale: Nothing surfaces when the cap reaches one: a rate limit resets without anyone hitting it, an idempotency record vanishes so an honest retry runs the handler twice (a double charge on payments), and a lock is handed out twice while the original holder is still inside the critical section. The holder's release() then returns false, which reads like a TTL overrun and here means the opposite.

nodes.label: One cache per consumer
nodes.rationale: The eviction policy only re-orders victims inside one instance and does not rank guarantees against each other, so each named cache gets its own instance and its own maxEntries under its own HOCON block, per-name winning over global leaf by leaf. It narrows the blast radius rather than removing it: a consumer whose own key space is attacker-controlled can still evict its own entries.

nodes.label: ADD is atomic per server, not per cluster
nodes.rationale: ADD is atomic on the one server a key hashes to, which makes setIfAbsent correct in steady state; a topology change rehashes the keyspace, the key can land on a server with no entry, and the lock is handed out twice. There is no client-side fix without reaching into memjs's internal hashring, so keep the server list fixed for a lock's lifetime or use a fencing token; Redis is the better locking backend.
nodes.norm_label: add is atomic per server, not per cluster

nodes.label: Server-side LRU eviction
nodes.rationale: The decision is made in the server and the client is not consulted, so there is no equivalent of InMemoryCache's guarantee-aware ordering: an entry written by setIfAbsent can disappear with most of its TTL left and nothing in the API reports it. Needs only memory pressure, unlike the topology hazard.

nodes.label: Opportunistic, lossy-by-design cache semantics
nodes.rationale: A None means "not cached" and the caller falls back to the source of truth; implementations return defaults on transient failures rather than throwing, and only misuse throws.

nodes.label: keyPrefix namespacing
nodes.rationale: Applied to every key; without it two unrelated apps sharing a Redis collide on the same key names and corrupt each other.

nodes.label: Akka 2.8.8 / Pekko 1.6.0 — dieselbe Linie beiderseits des Lizenzwechsels
nodes.rationale: Weil sich diese Arme nur in ihrer Abhängigkeit unterscheiden, ist jeder die Kontrolle für den anderen; auf einer OSI-konformen Lizenz zu bleiben kostet höchstens 6 %, meist unter 2 %.
nodes.norm_label: akka 2.8.8 / pekko 1.6.0 — dieselbe linie beiderseits des lizenzwechsels

nodes.label: ask-Roundtrip p50
nodes.rationale: 0,9 µs gegen 3,2-5,5 µs der anderen Arme; die frühere Erklärung über geparkte Threads trug weit mehr Gewicht, als die Messung hergab — unter Linux liegen dieselben JVM-Arme bei 3,5-3,7 µs.

nodes.label: benchmarks/comparison-Harness
nodes.rationale: Eigenes Manifest, damit die gemessenen Frameworks nie in die ausgelieferte Abhängigkeitshülle gelangen; bench:compare misst, bench:compare:report validiert und generiert RESULTS.md neu.

nodes.label: nact 7.6.2
nodes.rationale: Erzeugt Aktoren synchron und kennt keinen ambienten Sender; faktisch nicht mehr gepflegt, die Zahlen sind eine Momentaufnahme.

nodes.label: Orleans 10.2.2
nodes.rationale: Virtual-Actor-Runtime mit der am stärksten abweichenden Semantik; drei von vier Zeilen messen ein benanntes Näherungsäquivalent. Starke ask- und schwache tell-Zeile sind dieselbe Tatsache: Request/Response ist ein Grain-Aufruf.

nodes.label: Ping-Pong, 10k Wechsel
nodes.rationale: Der frühere Gleichstand war eine Aussage über die Messung, nicht über die Frameworks: hundert Runden bringen die Streuungen von ±27-82 % auf ±2-3 %, und bei dieser Auflösung führt actor-ts den besten JVM-Arm um Faktor 1,4.

nodes.label: spawn → gestartet → gestoppt
nodes.rationale: Die einzige Zeile, auf der actor-ts im JavaScript-Feld zurückliegt, und der Grund ist strukturell: gewartet wird auf ein bestätigtes preStart, ein stop() und ein bestätigtes postStop samt Eltern-Benachrichtigung — ein Benchmark, der das ausließe, würde etwas anderes messen.

nodes.label: tell-Durchsatz (Batch 1k / 10k)
nodes.rationale: actor-ts 0.16.0 bei 13,82M/s (±15 %) bzw. 19,05M/s (±6 %) auf Bun 1.3.14, 10 Kernen eines i9-12900K unter Linux.

nodes.label: XState 5.32.5
nodes.rationale: Eine Statechart-Bibliothek, deren Aktoren das Transportmittel sind; kein Request/Response-Primitiv und synchrone Ereignisverarbeitung, die tell-Zeilen messen also keine Mailbox.

nodes.label: Overhead pro Nachricht (~53 ns tell, 0,9 µs ask)
nodes.rationale: 53 ns ist der ganze Pfad — einreihen, einplanen, zustellen, behandeln — bei einer Mailbox mit Tiefe; der tell()-Aufruf selbst kehrt schneller zurück. Cross-Cluster-tell ist noch nicht gemessen.
nodes.norm_label: overhead pro nachricht (~53 ns tell, 0,9 μs ask)

nodes.label: Bun-Performance (grobe Zahlen)
nodes.rationale: ~10M msgs/s tell auf MicrotaskDispatcher, ~150K req/s HTTP, ~50K SQLite-Events/s; Start unter 100 ms gegen Nodes 300-500 ms.

nodes.label: Dequarantänisierungs-Checkliste
nodes.rationale: Flag aus drei Workflows, die drei describeMns-Guards, der coveragePathIgnorePatterns-Block, --exclude=worker im Benchmarks-Smoke, und die Neubewertung von COVERAGE_LINE_FLOOR samt Modul-Untergrenzen — src/cluster/ misst unter seiner echten Line-Coverage, solange LeaseMajority nicht laufen kann.

nodes.label: flaky gegen durchgehend rot
nodes.rationale: Ein Test, der einmal umfällt und beim erneuten Lauf grün ist, ist keine Kategorie, sondern eine Beobachtung mit Stichprobengröße eins; ein durchgehend roter Test ist kaputt, und Wiederholung sagt nichts Neues.

nodes.label: Selbsttests des Harness
nodes.rationale: Vier CI-Tests prüfen Aggregation, Klassifikation, Quarantäne-Guard und Watchdog gegen Eingaben, deren Antwort vorher feststeht — sonst sähe ein falsch liegender Klassifikator wie eine überraschende Messung aus. POSIX-, Windows- und absolute Pfade müssen zu einer Identität zusammenfallen, sonst werden aus einem flaky Test drei Rot-Meldungen.

nodes.label: Lokale Messung der drei Suiten (15 Wiederholungen)
nodes.rationale: Je 1/15 für LeaseMajoritys Partitionstest und ParallelMultiNodeSpecs partition+heal, sonst 0/15, kein Hänger — lokale und Hosted-Runner-Geschichte sind wirklich verschiedene Fehler. 'Reproduziert lokal nicht' war für die Fehlschläge selbst zu stark: LeaseMajority erzeugte denselben falschen Split-Brain, nachdem seine handgeschriebene 25-s-Deadline-Schleife still durchgefallen war.
nodes.norm_label: lokale messung der drei suiten (15 wiederholungen)

nodes.label: nightly-flakes.yml und das Ausstiegskriterium
nodes.rationale: 14 aufeinanderfolgende grüne Nächte (42 Ausführungen), weil der Fehler eine Eigenschaft des Runner-Pools ist und vierzehn Tage Wochentags- und Wochenendpools abdecken; der Job ist continue-on-error, damit eine bekannt rote Messung kein roter Pflicht-Check wird. Der Zähler wird von Menschen aus Annotationen abgelesen — automatisiert ist er nicht, weil beide Wege Rechte brauchen, die WorkflowHygiene verbietet.

nodes.label: Drei quarantänisierte Multi-Node-Suiten
nodes.rationale: Bun kann auf GitHubs Hosted Runnern nach dem ersten Worker-Test keine funktionsfähigen Worker-Threads mehr starten, und dieselbe Ressourcen-Knappheit verzögert LeaseMajoritys Renewal-Timer über die Lease-TTL hinaus, sodass beide Partitionsseiten acquiren. Ein grüner CI-Check sagt über diese drei nichts aus.

nodes.label: bun run test:stress (Repeat-Run-Harness)
nodes.rationale: Lässt die Suite N-mal laufen, hebt JUnit-Report und Log auf und aggregiert Fehlschläge nach Test-Identität; Reports, Logs und summary.json landen in .stress/.

nodes.label: Benchmarks (Vergleich)
nodes.rationale: Beantwortet den Vergleich mit Messungen statt Adjektiven und sagt genauso deutlich, was nicht gemessen wurde — ein Vergleich, der nur seine Siege auflistet, ist Werbung.

nodes.label: Verschränkte Runden, gemittelt
nodes.rationale: Runde 1 jedes Arms, dann Runde 2, damit Hintergrundlast alle Arme trifft; den Median zu veröffentlichen hieße, eine Runde zu melden und den Rest wegzuwerfen, einen Mittelwert ohne Streuung zu verschweigen, dass Zahlen zwischen Läufen um ein Viertel wandern.

nodes.label: Alle vier JVM-Arme forken einen frischen Prozess
nodes.rationale: Früher liefen sie in der warmen JVM ihres Build-Tools, während jeder andere Arm frisch startet; isoliert zeigte sich, der Unterschied ist der Fork und war bis zur Hälfte der Ping-Pong-Zahl wert. Der Fork kostet Genauigkeit, bei hundert Runden aber kein Vertrauen.
nodes.norm_label: alle vier jvm-arme forken einen frischen prozess

nodes.label: Keine Spalte "ohne Framework"
nodes.rationale: Sie wurde als 'diese Frameworks sind verschwenderisch' gelesen statt als 'ein direkter Aufruf macht nichts davon', und war zugleich die unzuverlässigste Zahl (16 % Drift zwischen zwei Läufen). 'Gar kein Framework' ist keine der Optionen, zwischen denen man wählt.

nodes.label: Kosten der Scala-Bindung (Allokation pro Nachricht)
nodes.rationale: Bei Batch 1 000 liegen die Scala-Arme 26 % und 36 % hinter ihren Java-Geschwistern (t = 11 und 16), bei Batch 10 000 ist der Effekt weg — die Form, die eine Allokation pro Nachricht annimmt, wenn ein JIT lernt sie zu entfernen.

nodes.label: Warmup gehört zum Workload
nodes.rationale: Der Harness-Default ergibt beim größten Batch drei ungemessene Iterationen — für eine JIT-kompilierte Runtime heißt das mitten in der Kompilierung gemessen; die Korrektur bewegte die tell-Rate des JVM-Arms um 130 %.

nodes.label: Erledigte Arbeit, nie angeforderte
nodes.rationale: Der Report-Generator weigert sich, eine Zeile zu rendern, deren erledigte Anzahl von der angeforderten abweicht — nicht hypothetisch: eine früher veröffentlichte Zahl war rund 10-mal zu hoch, weil die Mailbox Nachrichten still verwarf und der Harness die Anforderung zählte.

nodes.label: Mailbox-Tiefe erklärt die zwei Zahlen
nodes.rationale: Ein Actor arbeitet pro Scheduling-Durchlauf einen Batch ab, eine tiefe Mailbox verteilt das Aufwecken; ein Actor, der eine Anfrage nach der anderen beantwortet, hat zwischen zwei Nachrichten eine leere Mailbox. Keine der Zahlen ist falsch, sie beschreiben verschiedene Lastformen — einige Millionen Nachrichten/s durch einen Actor sind erreichbar, hundert Millionen nicht.

nodes.label: ACTOR_TS_SKIP_FLAKY_MNS wird aus der Kindumgebung entfernt
nodes.rationale: Es zu erben würde eine strikt kleinere Suite messen und dann eine verlässliche Pass-Rate über genau die Tests melden, von denen bekannt ist, dass sie nicht verlässlich sind.
nodes.norm_label: actor_ts_skip_flaky_mns wird aus der kindumgebung entfernt

nodes.label: Die ersten zwei Nächte behielten keinen Beleg
nodes.rationale: upload-artifact hat include-hidden-files seit v4.4 auf false, .stress ist ein Punkt-Verzeichnis, und mit if-no-files-found auf warn in continue-on-error-Jobs wurde nichts rot. Jetzt include-hidden-files: true plus if-no-files-found: error, geprüft von WorkflowHygiene.test.ts; Nächte vor dem Fix zählen nicht.
nodes.norm_label: die ersten zwei nachte behielten keinen beleg

nodes.label: Ein Hänger ist ein Messwert, kein Abbruch
nodes.rationale: --run-timeout tötet den Lauf, verbucht ihn als HUNG und macht weiter; ohne das blieb die Schleife beim ersten Hänger stehen und der Job wurde von seinen timeout-minutes getötet — die eine Messung, für die es das Harness gibt, überlebte genau nicht. Getrennt gezählt werden auch ein fehlender JUnit-Report und ein Exit ≠ 0 ohne roten Test; alle drei lesen sich für eine naive Schleife als grün.
nodes.norm_label: ein hanger ist ein messwert, kein abbruch

nodes.label: DurableStateActor
nodes.rationale: Persistiert einen einzelnen State-Snapshot pro persistenceId statt eines Event-Logs.

nodes.label: persistenceId rules for durable state
nodes.rationale: Non-empty, at most 255 characters, no slashes or control characters. The validator checks in the constructor rather than preStart, because an id that can never address a record is worth refusing before the actor is wired to a store.

nodes.label: StateAdapter for schema evolution
nodes.rationale: The record is wrapped in a versioned envelope and fromJournal migrates older versions on load, the durable-state counterpart of an event adapter.

nodes.label: eventDispatcher builder
nodes.rationale: A typed builder whose Handled type parameter tracks which event kinds have handlers, so build only type-checks once every variant is covered.

nodes.label: EventDispatcherIncomplete marker
nodes.rationale: build returns a non-callable value when kinds remain, and an __unhandled phantom field carries the missing kind so the type error is informative.

nodes.label: FSM base class
nodes.rationale: In-memory state machine over three type parameters - state names, state data, message type. Transitions are configured in the constructor and the base onReceive routes each message to the handler for the current state.

nodes.label: goto and stay
nodes.rationale: goto fires onExitState, sets the new state and data, then fires onEnter; stay updates data without firing either hook.

nodes.label: onEnter and onExitState
nodes.rationale: The natural home for setting up a timer on entry and tearing it down on exit, and for logging transitions without coupling that to message handling.

nodes.label: onTransition listener
nodes.rationale: Fires on every transition with from, to and the new data, so global instrumentation needs no per-state callbacks; multiple listeners append.

nodes.label: when state handler
nodes.rationale: Receives the current data and the incoming message and returns a transition; may be async, in which case it serializes like any onReceive so the next message waits.

nodes.label: applyEvent pure fold
nodes.rationale: The single source of truth for state and data updates. It runs both at persist time and during recovery, so it must be deterministic and free of side effects; transitions and guards are consulted only for live commands.

nodes.label: FsmTransitionMap transition table
nodes.rationale: State by command kind to an entry with an event, a target next and an optional guard. Declared as a class field so per-command type narrowing works at each call site; next is mainly informational since applyEvent drives the transition, but a mismatch is warned to catch table and fold drift.

nodes.label: Multi-event transitions
nodes.rationale: An array of events persists atomically in one persistAll, applyEvent runs once per event, and only the final post-replay state is checked against next; an empty array is a no-op. tagsFor is asked once per event too.

nodes.label: PersistentFSM
nodes.rationale: Table-driven and event-sourced: every command that fires a transition persists its events, and a restart replays them through applyEvent to resume the exact state name and data.

nodes.label: PersistentFSM recovery
nodes.rationale: preStart loads the latest snapshot and reads every subsequent domain event, replays them in order through applyEvent, then fires onRecoveryComplete. A failed recovery stops the FSM before any transition runs or any state timeout is armed.

nodes.label: State timeouts
nodes.rationale: A _timeout entry arms a one-shot timer on entering a state and fires its event through the same persist-then-apply pipeline. On recovery the timer is re-armed relative to wall-clock at recovery completion, so a long-stopped FSM gets a fresh window rather than an immediate expiry.

nodes.label: FSM pattern overview
nodes.rationale: The right modeling tool when an actor has a small named set of states with explicit transitions - connection lifecycles, order workflows, document approvals.

nodes.label: Await persist before acknowledging
nodes.rationale: Without the await the reply happens before the state is durable, so a crash in between leaves the user believing a change was applied that was not.

nodes.label: Build a new state object rather than mutating
nodes.rationale: Mutating the loaded reference works accidentally in some stores but the same object may already have been handed out in a reply, and it was mutated before the persist confirmed.
nodes.norm_label: build a new state object rather than mutating

nodes.label: Durable state versus event sourcing
nodes.rationale: Durable state wins on a simple shape, no projections and read-dominated access; reach for PersistentActor when history matters, when state is large and changes are small, or when read-side projections need the event stream.

nodes.label: Encryption overrides only the object-storage store reads
nodes.rationale: Nine of the ten durable-state stores accept encryption, compression and integrity overrides and never look at them - on in-memory, SQLite, Postgres, Mongo and DynamoDB the override is dropped silently, with no tamper detection and no error saying so.
nodes.norm_label: encryption overrides only the object-storage store reads

nodes.label: Compile-time exhaustiveness
nodes.rationale: ts-pattern exhaustive and assertNever both check at runtime or rely on the author remembering; the builder moves the check to compile time, and the error names the missing kind so the fix is mechanical.

nodes.label: onEvent is pure and testable in isolation
nodes.rationale: It runs on every recovery, so a side effect inside duplicates per restart and belongs in the persist callback in onCommand; being a pure value, the dispatcher unit-tests without an actor instance.
nodes.norm_label: onevent is pure and testable in isolation

nodes.label: A plain switch silently swallows new kinds
nodes.rationale: An unhandled kind falls through to return state, so adding a variant makes replay produce wrong state with nothing failing - the event just never contributes.
nodes.norm_label: a plain switch silently swallows new kinds

nodes.label: Errors in enter and exit hooks are logged, not escalated
nodes.rationale: They are caught and warned rather than reaching the supervisor, and the transition completes regardless.
nodes.norm_label: errors in enter and exit hooks are logged, not escalated

nodes.label: FSM restart resets to the initial state
nodes.rationale: There is no event log to replay, so a restart runs the constructor and starts over at the initial state and data; use PersistentFSM if the state must survive.
nodes.norm_label: fsm restart resets to the initial state

nodes.label: Keep state data serializable and immutable
nodes.rationale: Closures and actor refs do not survive a restart and can leak; treating data as immutable per transition keeps the machine testable and makes a later move to PersistentFSM possible.
nodes.norm_label: keep state data serializable and immutable

nodes.label: DSL-driven FSM versus table-driven PersistentFSM
nodes.rationale: The two variants have different shapes: in-memory FSM is when, goto, stay plus enter and exit hooks; PersistentFSM declares a transitions table and an applyEvent reducer, and every transition is persisted and replayed.

nodes.label: FSM versus become
nodes.rationale: FSM has named states, explicit goto transitions and typed state inspection, where become is anonymous closures that do not expose the current behavior; for two states become is fine, for four or more FSM is easier to read.

nodes.label: When the FSM pattern fits
nodes.rationale: Three or more named states with distinct behaviour, explicit from-X-on-Y-go-to-Z transitions, and side effects that belong to entering a state. One state or a boolean toggle reads cleaner as an ordinary actor; hierarchical or parallel substates want a heavier library.

nodes.label: There is no stay for data-only updates
nodes.rationale: A command with no matching transition entry is dropped and the in-memory data is not mutated as a side channel; a data-only update that must survive a restart is modelled as an event whose next is the same state.
nodes.norm_label: there is no stay for data-only updates

nodes.label: persistenceId collision with another actor
nodes.rationale: PersistentFSM and PersistentActor share the journal, so the same persistenceId is the same event stream; use distinct ids rather than discovering the clash at replay.

nodes.label: Side effects belong in onCommand
nodes.rationale: PersistentFSM has no enter, exit or transition hooks; onCommand never runs during replay, so overriding it and acting after super is what makes a side effect fire once per real transition rather than on every restart.

nodes.label: Re-arming supersedes a queued timeout fire
nodes.rationale: A fired timeout travels through the mailbox like any message, so it can already be queued behind an unprocessed command; re-arming on every transition, including one that stays in the same state, drops the superseded fire instead of expiring a session that was just renewed.
nodes.norm_label: re-arming supersedes a queued timeout fire

nodes.label: Native conditional-write CAS for durable state
nodes.norm_label: native conditional-write cas for durable state

nodes.label: persistenceIds is a full table scan
nodes.norm_label: persistenceids is a full table scan

nodes.label: The integrity tag is required, not merely checked
nodes.norm_label: the integrity tag is required, not merely checked

nodes.label: A shared snapshot store across replicas
nodes.norm_label: a shared snapshot store across replicas

nodes.label: Scala binding cost at small batches
nodes.norm_label: scala binding cost at small batches

nodes.label: spawn to started to stopped measurement
nodes.norm_label: spawn to started to stopped measurement

nodes.label: ts-pattern dispatch costs 18-22 % of tell throughput
nodes.norm_label: ts-pattern dispatch costs 18-22 % of tell throughput

nodes.label: How many actors one process can hold
nodes.norm_label: how many actors one process can hold

nodes.label: Per-message overhead (53 ns tell, 0.9 us ask)
nodes.norm_label: per-message overhead (53 ns tell, 0.9 us ask)

nodes.label: All four JVM arms fork a clean process
nodes.norm_label: all four jvm arms fork a clean process

nodes.label: One harness, literally, on the JavaScript side
nodes.norm_label: one harness, literally, on the javascript side

nodes.label: Warmup is part of the workload
nodes.norm_label: warmup is part of the workload

nodes.label: A mailbox with depth amortises the wakeup
nodes.norm_label: a mailbox with depth amortises the wakeup

nodes.label: A dispatcher hop between wait and assert
nodes.norm_label: a dispatcher hop between wait and assert

nodes.label: Message
nodes.rationale: Konvention: Discriminated Union mit einem kind-Feld.

nodes.label: Counter (Discriminated-Union-Commands)
nodes.rationale: match(command).exhaustive() aus ts-pattern liefert zur Compile-Zeit die Garantie, dass jede Variante behandelt ist: ein neues kind ohne with-Arm bricht den Build ab.

nodes.label: Hello, Actor
nodes.rationale: Die ganze Schleife: definieren, spawnen, tell, terminieren — dieselbe Datei laeuft unveraendert auf Bun, Node und Deno.

nodes.label: Prioritaet und ein Bound zugleich
nodes.rationale: withMailbox und withMailboxCapacity lassen sich nicht kombinieren, die Capacity liegt also auf PriorityMailboxOptions; eine Nachricht, deren priorityFor nicht auswertbar ist, wird zuletzt rangiert und damit als erste abgeworfen - ein defekter Callback zeigt sich als steigendes drop-new, nicht als Fehler (onPriorityError verdrahten).

nodes.label: Router und Supervision
nodes.rationale: Der Router ist ein regulaerer Actor: er supervised und watcht jeden Routee. Ein neu gestarteter Routee tritt am selben Pfad wieder bei, und was waehrend des Restart-Fensters geroutet wurde, bleibt in seiner Mailbox — sie wird suspendiert und wieder aufgenommen, nicht gedrained.

nodes.label: context.stash
nodes.rationale: Parks the currently-handled message and must be called from inside a user-message handler; calling it elsewhere throws StashOutsideHandlerError.

nodes.label: unstashAll
nodes.rationale: FIFO replay — messages return in the order they were stashed, and on a PriorityMailbox they are re-inserted through the priority function so an unstashed message rejoins its tier rather than the absolute front.

nodes.label: onPriorityError hook
nodes.rationale: Nothing else in the system reports a contained failure. Record and return — the hook runs on the sender stack too, so a throw from inside it puts the escape back.

nodes.label: PriorityMailbox
nodes.rationale: Lower numbers first, ties by FIFO insertion. Sorted-insertion array today — O(log n) locate plus O(n) splice per enqueue — open to a heap-backed swap if a sustained 10 000-message backlog shows it in profiles.

nodes.label: withInternal
nodes.rationale: Marks tooling rather than application actors so whole-system instrumentation skips them — without it, DevTools own hub traces itself and every batch comes back as the payload of the next. Application actors should not be marked: hiding real work from the profiler is how a performance problem stays invisible.

nodes.label: withMailbox
nodes.rationale: The factory is called once when the cell is constructed, so the mailbox outlives every restart — only the Actor instance is rebuilt and messages queued before the crash are still there. Cannot be combined with withMailboxCapacity.

nodes.label: withSupervisorStrategy
nodes.rationale: Two strategies are involved in every actor life: the one in its spawn options governs its own failures, the one inside its class governs its children.

nodes.label: Terminate drains mailboxes
nodes.rationale: terminate() drains the mailboxes under /user before stopping anything, so a message told just before shutdown is still handled. It does not wait for un-fired timers, un-awaited promises, throttled or suspended mailboxes; the whole drain is bounded by actor-ts.system.shutdown-drain-timeout (2 s, 0 disables) and the remainder goes to dead letters.

nodes.label: Messages are the only contract
nodes.rationale: Holding only an ActorRef with a tell verb looks restrictive until you see it makes asynchrony, backpressure and location transparency free.

nodes.label: Der Options-Builder verändert sich selbst
nodes.rationale: withX returns this, so branching off a shared base mutates it; options are copied at spawn time, so changing a builder afterwards reconfigures no running actor.

nodes.label: withInternal
nodes.rationale: Marks an actor as tooling so system-wide instrumentation skips it — without it the DevTools hub traces itself and every batch returns as the payload of the next; application actors must not be marked.

nodes.label: One-Shot-Reply-Actor hinter ask
nodes.rationale: Das Framework spawnt unter der Haube einen One-Shot-Reply-Actor, setzt ihn als replyTo UND als context.sender ein und loest das Promise mit der ersten Antwort auf — Aufrufer schreiben nie selbst replyTo hin.

nodes.label: terminate() leert die Mailboxen
nodes.rationale: Der Drain deckt /user-Mailboxen ab, aber nicht Arbeit, die noch in keiner Mailbox liegt (ein ungefeuerter Timer-Tick, ein tell aus einem nicht awaiteten Promise) und nicht eine bewusst geparkte Mailbox. Begrenzt durch actor-ts.system.shutdown-drain-timeout (2 s); was danach in der Queue steht, geht in die Dead Letters.

nodes.label: Batteries-included
nodes.rationale: Die meisten TS-Actor-Libraries hoeren bei der Actor-Abstraktion auf — dem einfachen Teil. Die harten Teile sind die operativen Stuecke rundherum: Clustering, Sharding, Persistenz, verteilte Daten, Integrationen, Observability.

nodes.label: Mentales Modell des Actor-Modells
nodes.rationale: Kein geteilter Speicher und genau eine Nachricht pro Actor in Bearbeitung — das Modell gibt Serialisierbarkeit umsonst. Alles andere (Sharding, Persistenz, verteilte Daten, Membership, Pub-Sub) ist auf diesem einen Primitiv aufgebaut.

nodes.label: Warum ein TypeScript-Port
nodes.rationale: Das Modell ist produktionserprobt (Erlang/BEAM, Akka/Pekko, Orleans), aber das Actor-Toolkit fuer TS war duenn — man schrieb eigene Primitiven oder akzeptierte 'alles ueber ein Spielzeug hinaus braucht die JVM'. Der Port stuetzt sich auf das Typsystem, wo JVM-Ports sich auf Traits stuetzten.

nodes.label: Actors kapseln State
nodes.rationale: Innerhalb von onReceive ist garantiert, dass niemand sonst liest oder schreibt — der Actor ist die Serialisierungsgrenze, count++ braucht keinen Mutex.

nodes.label: Fehlererholung ohne Supervision
nodes.rationale: Vanilla JS beantwortet nicht, was mit dem partiellen State nach einem Throw passiert, ob das Objekt noch sicher ist und ob Aufrufer vom Absturz wissen sollten — man baut es pro Service, meistens inkonsistent.

nodes.label: Nachrichten sind der einzige Vertrag
nodes.rationale: Die scheinbar unnoetige Restriktion macht drei Dinge umsonst: Asynchronitaet (jedes tell ist fire-and-forget), Backpressure (die Mailbox hat eine Laenge und eine waehlbare Policy) und Location Transparency.

nodes.label: Geteilter veraenderlicher State unter Nebenlaeufigkeit
nodes.rationale: Das Promise-/async-await-Modell gibt Parallelitaet, aber kein Synchronisationsprimitiv — zwei nebenlaeufige Einzahlungen lesen beide 0 und eine geht verloren.

nodes.label: Statusbehaftete langlebige Komponenten
nodes.rationale: Die uebliche Antwort — Klasse zustandslos machen, State nach Redis/Postgres — tauscht ein Concurrency-Problem gegen zwei operative: Network-Roundtrips bei jedem Read und denselben Race im Datenspeicher.

nodes.label: Supervisors behandeln Fehler als erstklassiges Anliegen
nodes.rationale: Vier Ergebnisse — Restart, Resume, Stop, Escalate — einmal pro Actor-Klasse konfiguriert, sodass jeder Fehler gleich behandelt wird.
nodes.norm_label: supervisors behandeln fehler als erstklassiges anliegen

nodes.label: Wann Actors die richtige Wahl sind
nodes.rationale: State pro Entitaet, der laenger als ein Request lebt; Fehlerisolierung; Verteilung; alles, was konzeptionell ein Zustandsautomat ist. Pointiert: die Kaestchen auf dem Whiteboard sind meistens Actors.
nodes.norm_label: wann actors die richtige wahl sind

nodes.label: Wann Actors NICHT zu verwenden sind
nodes.rationale: Zustandslose Request/Response-Services, reine Datentransformationen und Code, der synchron blockieren muss — Actor-Overhead ist verschwendet, wo es nichts zu kapseln gibt.
nodes.norm_label: wann actors nicht zu verwenden sind

nodes.label: Stash capacity bound (1024)
nodes.rationale: Bounded to prevent memory leaks from runaway stashing; overflow throws, which is why a stash-on-not-ready branch always needs a timeout beside it.

nodes.label: The stash is lost on restart
nodes.rationale: The instance is thrown away with its buffer, and the new instance has none of the state that made those messages unhandleable — they go to dead letters so the loss is at least visible.
nodes.norm_label: the stash is lost on restart

nodes.label: priorityFor callback
nodes.rationale: An unrankable answer queues at the lowest priority rather than the highest — a priority that could not be determined must not outrank one that was stated — and the failure is contained rather than thrown, because priorityFor runs inside the sender tell and a sender is a bystander to the receiver mailbox configuration. Note the framework calls it with PoisonPill and Kill, which have no fields.

nodes.label: Unstash goes through prependUser
nodes.rationale: PriorityMailbox re-runs the priority function rather than pushing to the front, so unstashAll goes through the same enqueue path and therefore the same bound — replaying the stash on a full bounded priority mailbox can discard messages. BoundedMailbox unstash bypasses the bound instead.

nodes.label: System messages always come first
nodes.rationale: Two queues live side by side and system messages have absolute precedence — which is why supervision reacts instantly. ref.stop() does not jump the queue: PoisonPill is a user message, making stop a graceful drain-then-stop, and a death-watch Terminated is a user message for the same reason — it must arrive after everything already told to the watcher.

nodes.label: Supervisor strategy resolution order
nodes.rationale: Child spawn options, then the parent override, then the default — so one child opts out without affecting siblings. Because the parent applies it, an all-for-one strategy set on a child still widens to every sibling and the restart budget is shared per parent.

nodes.label: MemberWeaklyUp event
nodes.rationale: A non-zero rate in steady state means partitions are happening, or the threshold is set too low for the network.

nodes.label: StableObservation
nodes.rationale: Pollt den Seed-Provider und verlangt, dass die Menge fuer stableMarginMs exakt identisch bleibt; ein fehlgeschlagener Lookup ist keine leere Menge, sondern zaehlt gar nicht als Beobachtung, damit ein DNS-Ausfall nie mit 'ich bin allein' verwechselt wird.

nodes.label: StableObservationError
nodes.rationale: Die Phase wirft, statt trotzdem zu joinen: ein degradierter Fallback waere von genau dem Fehler nicht zu unterscheiden, den sie verhindern soll. Ein lauter Fehlstart ist per Neustart behebbar, ein zweiter Cluster nicht.

nodes.label: DowningProvider
nodes.rationale: Ein winziges Interface: decide(view) liefert die Adressen, die zwangsweise herabgestuft werden; eine leere Menge heisst 'noch keine Entscheidung — abwarten'. Jedes Cluster-Event fuehrt den Provider mit der aktuellen Sicht erneut aus.

nodes.label: KeepMajority
nodes.rationale: Der allgemeinste Default ohne externe Abhaengigkeiten, vorhersagbar bei ungeradem N; bei exaktem N/2-Split fahren beide Seiten herunter, und Mehrheit per Zaehlung ist blind fuer physische Topologie.

nodes.label: KeepReferee
nodes.rationale: Die vorhersagbarste Strategie und fuer jede Cluster-Groesse geeignet, aber der Schiedsrichter ist ein Single Point of Failure — faellt er aus, kann niemand entscheiden, wofuer downAllIfBelowQuorum existiert.

nodes.label: StaticQuorum
nodes.rationale: Strenger als Mehrheit und bewusst fail-stop; erholt sich nicht automatisch, und weil das Quorum bei jeder Mitgliedschaftsaenderung geprueft wird, blockiert eine zu grosse Quorum-Groesse den Scale-Up.

nodes.label: FailureDetector
nodes.rationale: Eine Zustandsmaschine pro Peer (healthy / unreachable / down) auf Basis abgelaufener Zeitschwellen, ohne Tracking statistischer Varianz — ausreichend fuer LAN-Skala.

nodes.label: MemberUnreachable
nodes.rationale: Ein Mitgliedschaftsuebergang, kein lokales Urteil: es feuert auch fuer einen Peer, von dem jemand anderes nichts mehr hoert, und nur fuer ein Member, das up war.

nodes.label: PhiAccrualFailureDetector
nodes.rationale: Varianzbewusst und adaptiv, eine oeffentlich exportierte Klasse — aber noch nicht als auswaehlbarer Detector eingebunden, der Cluster faehrt immer den einfachen FailureDetector, die failureDetector-Option stellt nur dessen Schwellwerte.

nodes.label: ReachabilityChanged
nodes.rationale: Das eigene Urteil des lokalen Detectors, ohne die zwei Einschraenkungen von MemberUnreachable; es feuert nur bei Uebergaengen, kippt bei unreachableAfterMs und ist damit die frueheste Warnung — traegt aber keine Observer-Menge, weil Gossip nur eine flache Member-Liste fuehrt.

nodes.label: SelfUp
nodes.rationale: Feuert einmal, wenn dieser Node auf up uebergeht — das nuetzliche Gate fuer Arbeit, die Cluster-Mitgliedschaft erfordert.

nodes.label: Cluster.bootstrap
nodes.rationale: Buendelt ActorSystem erstellen, Seeds aufloesen, Cluster.join rufen und Signale einhaengen in einen Aufruf; das Low-Level-Paar bleibt fuer volle Kontrolle verfuegbar.

nodes.label: CurrentClusterState
nodes.rationale: Wird nie auf dem Event-Stream veroeffentlicht: es beschreibt den Startpunkt genau eines Subscribers, nicht etwas, das dem Cluster widerfahren ist; unreachable ist eine Teilmenge von members.

nodes.label: Cluster bootstrap phase
nodes.rationale: Runs before Cluster.join so that at most one cluster comes out of a simultaneous start; gossip never repairs two clusters with the same name, each with its own leader, singletons and shard allocations.

nodes.label: StableObservation
nodes.rationale: Polls the seed provider and requires the returned set to be byte-identical for stableMarginMs before acting; a failed lookup is not an empty set and does not count as an observation, so a DNS outage can never be mistaken for 'I am alone'.

nodes.label: Routee discovery from up-members
nodes.rationale: Rebuilt on MemberUp and MemberRemoved and ordered deterministically by address so round-robin counters stay sane across rebuilds.

nodes.label: DowningProvider
nodes.rationale: Re-run on every cluster event with the current view, returning the addresses to forcibly down; an empty set means 'no decision yet - wait'. Without a provider the cluster sees unreachable members forever and operators must call cluster.down() by hand.

nodes.label: KeepMajority
nodes.rationale: The most general default with no external dependencies and predictable behaviour for odd N; it cannot handle an exact N/2 split (both sides down) and is blind to physical topology.

nodes.label: KeepOldest
nodes.rationale: Despite the name it does not track join order - 'oldest' is the lowest host:port, the same rule Cluster.leader() uses - so a node that joined a minute ago beats one up for a week. Pick it for a deterministic agreed tiebreaker and pin the surviving node's address; downIfAlone prevents a one-node winner after a total split.

nodes.label: KeepReferee
nodes.rationale: The most predictable strategy and works for even-sized clusters, but it cannot decide if the referee itself disappears - hence downAllIfBelowQuorum. Useful for two-DC clusters with a neutral tie-breaker.

nodes.label: StaticQuorum
nodes.rationale: Stricter than majority and errs toward fail-stop, but does not recover automatically; the quorum is checked at every membership change including the initial join, so a quorum above the starting size downs the cluster on startup.

nodes.label: MemberUnreachable
nodes.rationale: A membership transition, not this node's observation: it also fires for a peer someone else stopped hearing from, and only for a member that was up - a peer falling silent while joining, weakly-up or leaving produces no reachability event at all.

nodes.label: PhiAccrualFailureDetector
nodes.rationale: A public exported class tracking inter-arrival distribution and producing a continuous suspicion value, but not wired into the cluster as a selectable detector - the cluster always runs the simple FailureDetector, so it is used standalone.

nodes.label: ReachabilityChanged
nodes.rationale: The local detector's own verdict, fired on transition only, without MemberUnreachable's two caveats; comparing it against the gossiped status is how a partition is told apart from a dead peer. It carries no observer set because that would need an observer-to-subject table on the wire and gossip carries a flat member list.

nodes.label: Join handshake
nodes.rationale: The joiner contacts a seed, is added as joining, propagates through gossip and reaches up once the leader sees it plus convergence.

nodes.label: Seed list as a bootstrap hint
nodes.rationale: Seeds are not special after the join - the node learns every other peer via gossip; an empty list means this node bootstraps the cluster itself and auto-promotes to leader.
nodes.norm_label: seed list as a bootstrap hint

nodes.label: SelfUp event
nodes.rationale: Fires once when this node reaches up - the gate for starting work that requires membership, with MemberUp counted after it when other members are needed.

nodes.label: Cluster.bootstrap
nodes.rationale: Packages system creation, seed resolution, join and SIGTERM/SIGINT wiring into one call; discovery defaults to an env-driven chain and local dev with no env produces a single-node cluster.

nodes.label: Cluster.join
nodes.rationale: Resolves once this node has finished joining, but peers' views converge over the next few gossip rounds, so startup logic that needs every peer to know about this node should act in a SelfUp handler.

nodes.label: ClusterOptions
nodes.rationale: host+port is the address peers dial, seeds is the bootstrap hint (empty = 'I am the first'), roles tag the node for routers and shard regions to filter on.

nodes.label: CurrentClusterState
nodes.rationale: Never published on the event stream: it describes one subscriber's starting point, not something that happened to the cluster; unreachable is a subset of members, not a set beside it.

nodes.label: Gossip membership protocol
nodes.rationale: Each member exchanges its view with a random reachable peer every gossipIntervalMs and merges by picking the higher version per member, so every concurrent update converges without a central coordinator.

nodes.label: Membership state machine
nodes.rationale: joining, weakly-up, up, unreachable, leaving, exiting, removed; a removed member is kept as a tombstone for a TTL (default 24 h) so stale gossip from a slow peer cannot resurrect it.

nodes.label: Single-node cluster mode
nodes.rationale: A cluster of one is valid - the local node auto-promotes to leader and every extension works as in a larger cluster, so cluster code can be developed without a Docker Compose setup.

nodes.label: Weakly-up member state
nodes.rationale: A transient state between joining and up that breaks the deadlock where a joiner on a partitioned side waits forever for a leader it cannot see.

nodes.label: weaklyUpAfterMs
nodes.rationale: Default 0 (disabled); 3-10s is typical — high enough that joining to up stays the common path, low enough that a stalled join recovers. Settable from HOCON with the usual explicit-options-first precedence.

nodes.label: requiredContactPoints
nodes.rationale: Die Margin faengt langsame Discovery ab, nur eine Mindestanzahl faengt Discovery ab, die stabil falsch ist — ein Resolver, der konsequent zwei von drei Pods liefert, pendelt sich sonst bereitwillig auf die falsche Menge ein. Default 1 nur fuer Einzelknoten-Entwicklung.

nodes.label: heartbeatIntervalMs / unreachableAfterMs / downAfterMs
nodes.rationale: Defaults 500 / 2000 / 5000 ms ergeben ein 2-Sekunden-Erkennungs- und ein 5-Sekunden-Entscheidungsfenster; ueber Regionen hinweg alle drei erhoehen, denn bei 100 ms RTT ist ein verpasster Heartbeat normales Rauschen.

nodes.label: seedRetryIntervalMs
nodes.rationale: Loest das Problem eines Seeds, der irgendwann erreichbar ist — ein erstes Mitglied kann die Schleife nicht herbeizaubern.

nodes.label: Seed-Liste
nodes.rationale: Nur ein Bootstrap-Hinweis — nach dem Join lernt der Node alle Peers per Gossip, Seeds sind danach nichts Besonderes mehr. Eine leere Liste heisst 'ich bin der erste'.

nodes.label: selfElection
nodes.rationale: Bestimmt, wann ein Node allein einen Cluster bilden darf: immediate nur bei leerer Seed-Liste, never, oder eine Frist in Millisekunden — gesetzt vom Cluster-Bootstrap.

nodes.label: Gossip
nodes.rationale: Jedes Mitglied tauscht periodisch seine Sicht mit einem zufaelligen Peer; beim Merge gewinnt die hoehere Version pro Mitglied, weshalb Konvergenz ohne zentralen Koordinator funktioniert.

nodes.label: Mitgliedschaftszustaende
nodes.rationale: joining, optional weakly-up, up, unreachable, leaving/exiting, removed — removed bleibt fuer eine TTL als Tombstone, damit veralteter Gossip von einem langsamen Peer das Member nicht wiederbelebt.

nodes.label: Single-Node-Modus
nodes.rationale: Ein Cluster aus einem Node ist gueltig: der lokale Node befoerdert sich zum Leader, und jede cluster-abhaengige Extension funktioniert — Cluster-Code laesst sich also ohne Docker-Compose entwickeln.

nodes.label: Getaggter JSON-Tree auf dem Wire
nodes.rationale: Dasselbe Format, das die Persistenz-Stores schreiben, sodass Date, Map, Set, bigint und Uint8Array im Body als sie selbst ankommen; replyTo-Refs serialisieren zu remote-routbaren Handles.

nodes.label: MemberWeaklyUp event
nodes.rationale: A non-zero rate in normal operation means partitions are happening — or the threshold is set too low for the network.

nodes.label: LeaseMajority
nodes.rationale: The split-brain strategy that feature-detects acquireWithToken and is the one caller that reacts to a release() rejection — it fails safe and stops claiming a majority until the partition heals.

nodes.label: Lease.release
nodes.rationale: A no-op when not held, but it REJECTS when the backend was unreachable: a failed release leaves the record claimed on the server while this process has locally given it up, and not knowing whether you own the lease is information you need. Backends must propagate the error; cleanup-only callers wrap it. The flip side of the no-op: release does nothing while an acquire is still in flight, so an abandoned acquire cannot be undone until it reports back.

nodes.label: Failure Detector
nodes.rationale: Phi-Accrual-Detector, der unerreichbare Peers auf Basis fehlender Heartbeats markiert.

nodes.label: crash(role) und leave(role)
nodes.rationale: crash reisst den Transport eines Nodes abrupt weg — die Peers beobachten Unreachable, gossipen die Aenderung und loesen Downing plus Failover aus; leave fuehrt einen sauberen Cluster-Austritt durch.

nodes.label: Deferred self-election
nodes.rationale: The lowest-addressed node still joins the others as seeds and only gets a deadline; addresses are handed out by the platform, so a later-starting node can sort first and immediate self-election would form a second cluster beside the running one.

nodes.label: requiredContactPoints
