nodes.rationale: The envelope has no sender field at all: routing on one let any connected party choose the address this node replied to and opened a connection to. Deleting the field rather than checking it leaves nothing to get wrong next time. It is not authentication - only peer certificates make the claimed address true.
nodes.norm_label: replies follow the connection, not the payload

nodes.label: Redacted ask failure with correlation id
nodes.rationale: A failing actor's text is the same class of string as an HTTP 500's - file paths, SQL fragments, a stack - and a contact point is reachable from outside the cluster's boundary, so the client gets a fixed sentence and an id while the reason stays in the node's log. A path-not-found deliberately omits the node's own address.
nodes.norm_label: redacted ask failure with correlation id

nodes.label: rejectUnauthorized
nodes.rationale: Setting it false defeats authentication entirely - any cert is accepted - and is never acceptable in production.

nodes.label: bun audit gate over bun.lock
nodes.rationale: GitHub's dependency graph records the unresolved ranges from package.json rather than the shipped closure, which is why bun audit reads the lockfile and dependency-review-action is deliberately not used.

nodes.label: In scope - everything the mitigations promise
nodes.rationale: A documented mitigation that does not deliver what it says is a vulnerability, and one that has happened here before; also anything reachable from untrusted input on a socket, missing bounds, crypto mistakes and cross-entity persistence access.
nodes.norm_label: in scope - everything the mitigations promise

nodes.label: Out of scope - documented insecure defaults
nodes.rationale: The framework ships insecure-by-default transports on purpose with the secure configuration documented next to them, so a cluster run on a hostile network without TLS is documented behaviour, not a vulnerability.
nodes.norm_label: out of scope - documented insecure defaults

nodes.label: ClusterClient
nodes.rationale: Laesst einen Prozess ausserhalb des Clusters mit Actors innen sprechen, ohne als Peer beizutreten — der Notausgang fuer externe Services, Bridges und Cross-Cluster-Foederation.

nodes.label: ClusterClientReceptionist
nodes.rationale: Eine Per-System-Extension ohne zu befuellende Service-Registry: sie loest den Ziel-Pfad jedes Envelopes im lokalen Actor-Baum auf und stellt zu.

nodes.label: Kontaktpunkte
nodes.rationale: Der Client probiert die Liste der Reihe nach und faellt bei Ausfall auf den naechsten zurueck; die Cluster-Seite betreibt dafuer typisch einen Receptionist auf einem festen Satz von Nodes.

nodes.label: Cert-Layout
nodes.rationale: Minimum ist ein CA-Cert plus Schluessel und ein von der CA signiertes Per-Node-Cert; jeder Node laedt sein eigenes Cert und die CA, um Peers zu verifizieren.

nodes.label: cert-manager und Secrets
nodes.rationale: cert-manager erneuert Certs automatisch, Pods laden sie beim Neustart neu — Rotation ohne Downtime heisst Rolling Restart, sobald neue Certs bereitliegen.

nodes.label: Cluster-Sicherheit
nodes.rationale: Der Cluster-Transport ist standardmaessig unauthentifiziertes Plain-TCP — in Ordnung in einem privaten Netz, nicht ausserhalb; TLS ist alles-oder-nichts pro Cluster, gemischtes Plain plus TLS funktioniert nicht.

nodes.label: Mutual TLS
nodes.rationale: rejectUnauthorized: true plus eine gemeinsame CA verlangt von beiden Seiten ein gueltiges Cert — keine anonymen Joins, kein Plain-Text-Fallback.

nodes.label: NetworkPolicy als zweite Schicht
nodes.rationale: Nur Pods mit dem passenden Label erreichen den Cluster-Port; kombiniert mit mTLS sind das zwei unabhaengige Schichten.

nodes.label: Bewusst verfasste Ablehnungsantwort
nodes.rationale: Wer als Client auf einen bestimmten Fehlschlag reagieren muss, modelliert ihn als Antwort, die der Actor selbst schreibt — die kommt woertlich an. So bleibt der Domaenenvertrag explizit, statt das, was eine Exception zufaellig sagt, zur API zu machen.

nodes.label: Redaktion von Fehlschlaegen mit Korrelations-Id
nodes.rationale: Den Fehlertext schreibt der Actor, der zufaellig gescheitert ist — dieselbe Klasse String wie bei einem HTTP-500, mit Dateipfaden, SQL-Fragmenten oder Stack. Der Client bekommt einen festen Satz plus Id, der Volltext bleibt im Log des ausfuehrenden Nodes. Auch 'path not found' nennt die Node-Adresse nicht.

nodes.label: Das ist keine Client-Authentifizierung
nodes.rationale: Auf der Verbindung zu routen nimmt die Beliebigkeit heraus, macht die Gegenstelle aber nicht zu dem, was sie behauptet; nur Peer-Zertifikate tun das — unter mTLS muss die behauptete Adresse zum Zertifikat passen.

nodes.label: Antwort geht ueber die Verbindung, nicht ueber ein Absenderfeld
nodes.rationale: Der Client sagt genau einmal im hello, wer er ist; der Transport bindet das an den Socket. Das frueher mitgereiste Absenderfeld liess jede Gegenstelle die Antwortadresse waehlen, also wurde es geloescht statt geprueft — dann bleibt nichts uebrig, das beim naechsten Mal falsch gemacht werden kann. Ein abweichender Wert wird gezaehlt, nicht abgelehnt.
nodes.norm_label: antwort geht ueber die verbindung, nicht ueber ein absenderfeld

nodes.label: rejectUnauthorized: false
nodes.rationale: Hebelt die Authentifizierung aus und akzeptiert jedes Cert — nie in Produktion.

nodes.label: Bedrohungen und Massnahmen
nodes.rationale: Lauschangriff und MITM decken TLS und Zertifikatspruefung ab, unautorisierten Join nur mTLS, ein kompromittiertes Cert nur Rotation und Revocation, und Replay eines Gossip-Frames zusaetzlich die Sequence pro Sender.

nodes.label: TLS-Performance-Auswirkung
nodes.rationale: Rund 5-15 Prozent Overhead pro Byte — bei typischen Actor-Nachrichten unbemerkbar, bei hochfrequentem Cluster-Verkehr messbar, aber selten der Flaschenhals.

nodes.label: DevTools resolved-configuration panel (#553)
nodes.rationale: A merged tree answers 'what is this setting now'; the question that brings someone here is 'why is it not what I wrote', which needs the layer as well as the value — so Config.load keeps the layers it merged and a config built any other way reports that it cannot attribute rather than guessing. Secrets are redacted by key rather than by value: a password that happens to look ordinary is still a password.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Event-sourced actor example
nodes.rationale: State is rebuilt from a journal on every restart, so there is no in-place mutation and no 'did this write commit?' question. The sample shows both style rules at once: onEvent is a fold that computes a value and stays inline, onCommand is a dispatch and every arm delegates.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Typed options with fail-fast validation
nodes.rationale: One fluent XOptions builder per configurable thing, validated once on the merged settings so a bad port, timeout or URL throws an OptionsError at startup rather than deep in a later code path.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Utility primitives and helpers
nodes.rationale: Option/Try/Either/Lazy, BidirectionalMap and BidirectionalMultiMap that survive a snapshot as real instances with no adapter, plus randomString/randomHex/randomId/randomUuid with an optional exists predicate so 'keep drawing until one is free' is the call itself, safeStringify and lazyImportModule.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Spell out abbreviations in identifiers
nodes.rationale: Full words everywhere including locals, params and kind string-literal values. Two exceptions only: single-letter loop/lambda/catch vars, and names mirroring an external API or an established domain acronym (nats.js ack/nak, prom-client inc/dec, amqplib noAck, PubSub, K8s, AMQP, MQTT, SQL, S3, DNS, CBOR).
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Pass the actor class, not a closure around it
nodes.rationale: spawn(() => new MyActor(), 'x') is a leftover from the Props era and reads as noise; actorFactoryOf does the wrapping. The factory form is for constructor arguments only, and per-actor configuration is the third argument, ActorOptions, never a closure.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: pass the actor class, not a closure around it

nodes.label: A builder is structurally its settings
nodes.rationale: OptionsBuilder.set writes each field as an own enumerable property, so consumers read the argument directly with no resolve helper. Keep the union in the signature — a methods-only builder is not assignable to a bare XOptionsType under the TS weak-type check. Never nest a builder into a call; assign it to a contextual local first.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: a builder is structurally its settings

nodes.label: Four-place constant placement rule
nodes.rationale: Checked in order: XOptions.ts default/bound, stays where it is (a closed list of six kinds), src/<subsystem>/Constants.ts, src/util/Constants.ts. A Constants.ts imports nothing from its own subsystem so it is cycle-free by construction; declarations move with their JSDoc, as const and explicit annotations, because dropping them is how a pure move silently widens a type.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: HOCON keys through ConfigKeys with layered precedence
nodes.rationale: explicit options > HOCON > built-in defaults, layered with mergeOptions where undefined on a higher layer means 'not set' and falls through rather than shadowing. A key in reference.conf must be reachable from ConfigKeys and read by something in src/, else NoDeadConfigKeys.test.ts fails; adding a key nothing reads is not an option.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: hocon keys through configkeys with layered precedence

nodes.label: interface for contracts, type for everything else
nodes.rationale: An interface states a contract someone implements and extends reads as a hierarchy where an intersection only reads as conjunction; a data shape states a value's layout, and there type composes with the union aliases the project already uses. A function-typed property is not a function head.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: interface for contracts, type for everything else

nodes.label: The discriminant field is always `kind`
nodes.rationale: `type` collides with the type keyword; `kind` is the single project-wide convention, including the WebSocket/wire protocols of the examples.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Every match arm delegates to a private onXxx handler
nodes.rationale: Keeps the matcher a scannable dispatch table rather than logic. Applies wherever a match dispatches an incoming message, event or command; exempt are matches on internal state or that compute a value in a helper.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: every match arm delegates to a private onxxx handler

nodes.label: Measured-hot-path switch exemption
nodes.rationale: Building a matcher and one closure per arm is free at one call per request and is not at one per actor lifecycle. The exemption is per-site and evidence-carrying: the site must name the benchmark and the measured delta, and that comment is the token the conformance sweep (#494) recognises. Two sites qualify today (ActorCell.handleSystemCommand, BoundedMailbox.enqueue).
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: Discriminated unions as named variant types
nodes.rationale: Each tagged union is a union of named members, never an inline object-literal union; variants are PascalCase(kind) plus a role suffix matching the union, and handlers take the named variant type rather than Extract<Union, { kind }>.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: discriminated unions as named variant types

nodes.label: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.rationale: XOptionsType, XOptionsBuilder and XOptions (both the accepted-input union and the value alias). There is no separate 'Settings' concept. Naming lockstep with no divergence: builder method withX, field x, HOCON leaf x.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: xoptions family — three exports per configurable thing

nodes.label: XOptionsValidator — fail-fast validation at consume time
nodes.rationale: Validation runs once, at consume time, on the merged settings, so builder, plain object and HOCON are all covered and cross-field rules see final values. Helpers take only the field name (typo-checked against XOptionsType) and are a no-op on undefined; rejections throw OptionsError, distinct from BrokerOptionsError and ConfigError.
nodes.community_name: XOptions family — three exports per configurable thing
nodes.norm_label: xoptionsvalidator — fail-fast validation at consume time

nodes.label: Drei Fehlerschichten und ihre Präzedenz
nodes.rationale: Innermost handleErrors first, then the server-wide withErrorHandler, then the framework default; a handler that throws hands the new error to the next layer out.

nodes.label: handleErrors(handler, child)
nodes.rationale: Sees the original throw before any default mapping and may decline with null so an outer handler takes over; nests outside-in like withMiddleware, so wrapping an auth middleware also catches its 401.

nodes.label: Helmet-nahe CSP-Baseline
nodes.rationale: default-src 'self', object-src 'none', base-uri 'self', frame-ancestors 'self'; own directives override per directive, an empty array removes one, withoutDefaults skips the baseline.

nodes.label: completeHtml
nodes.rationale: Sends SafeHtml as text/html; charset=utf-8 with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

nodes.label: escapeHtml
nodes.rationale: Escapes & < > " ' and the backtick. Covers HTML element content and quoted attribute values only - not a script block, CSS, or a URL, which need their own encoding.

nodes.label: html tagged template
nodes.rationale: Escapes every interpolation by default so building an HTML response is safe without thinking about it. SafeHtml values interpolate verbatim so fragments nest, arrays render item-by-item, null/undefined become empty, everything else is coerced and escaped.

nodes.label: SafeHtml
nodes.rationale: A brand marking already-safe HTML, which the template then interpolates verbatim instead of escaping.

nodes.label: Escaping ist kontextspezifisch
nodes.rationale: escapeHtml covers element content and quoted attribute values only — script blocks, CSS and URLs need their own encoding, so never build a javascript: URL or inline script from untrusted input.

nodes.label: rawHtml
nodes.rationale: Inserts the string verbatim and therefore trusts the caller — feeding untrusted input in reintroduces exactly the XSS the template prevents.

nodes.label: Sanitisieren von untrusted Markup
nodes.rationale: Escaping neutralizes markup but does not make attacker-authored HTML safe to render, so rich HTML needs a dedicated battle-tested sanitizer before it goes into rawHtml; a built-in conservative sanitizer is tracked separately.

nodes.label: Injection-Guard für Source-Tokens
nodes.rationale: A source token containing ';', ',' or whitespace throws at construction — no silent header injection.

nodes.label: Per-Request-Nonces fehlen
nodes.rationale: Nonces would need a template/SSR integration to reach the rendered HTML, which the framework does not have; a handler that needs one sets its own header, and the middleware never overwrites a header the handler already set.

nodes.label: rawHtml
nodes.rationale: Inserts its argument verbatim, so it trusts the caller absolutely: passing untrusted input reintroduces exactly the XSS the template prevents. Escaping neutralises markup but does not make attacker-authored HTML safe to render - sanitise with a dedicated library (sanitize-html, DOMPurify) before wrapping.

nodes.label: CborSerializer
nodes.rationale: CBOR (RFC 8949) - typischerweise 20-40 % kleiner als JSON und mit erstklassigem Binaer-Support (kein Base64-Wrapping); JSON bleibt fuer menschenlesbar zu debuggende APIs die bessere Wahl.

nodes.label: completeJson
nodes.rationale: Der 95-%-Fall: Body wird beim Schreiben JSON-serialisiert, Content-Type auf application/json; charset=utf-8.

nodes.label: entity<T>(req)
nodes.rationale: Reduziert den Content-Type auf den reinen Media-Type, waehlt den Serializer, dekodiert und castet. 400 bei fehlendem/malformem Body, 415 wenn nichts diesen Typ dekodiert. Gematcht wird gegen den GEPARSTEN Media-Type - ein bekannter Typ in einem Parameter waehlt keinen Serializer aus.

nodes.label: FormUrlEncodedSerializer
nodes.rationale: Flacher Record aus Strings - Form-Encoding transportiert keine Typen; ein wiederholtes Feld weitet sich zu einem Array, Verschachtelung ist nicht ausdrueckbar.

nodes.label: marshal(req, value)
nodes.rationale: Waehlt den Serializer aus dem Accept-Header - fuer Faelle, in denen IoT-Clients CBOR und Browser JSON wollen; sonst completeJson.

nodes.label: Serializer (Interface)
nodes.rationale: toBinary/fromBinary; das Media-Type-zu-Serializer-Mapping des HTTP-Moduls ist eine private Konstante, eigene Serializer werden vor dem entity-Aufruf manuell verzweigt. Der Cluster-Wire hat gar keinen solchen Hook - er rahmt immer den getaggten JSON-Tree.

nodes.label: HttpExtension / HttpExtensionId
nodes.rationale: HTTP ist als Extension gebaut und bewusst getrennt von den I/O-Broker-Actors - HTTP-Server passen nicht in die Form 'eine Verbindung, viele Nachrichten'.

nodes.label: Route-DSL (path / get / post / concat)
nodes.rationale: Baut einen In-Memory-Routenbaum, der beim Bind zu einer flachen Liste kompiliert und beim gewaehlten Backend registriert wird - identisch fuer alle drei Backends.

nodes.label: 415 statt Rateversuch
nodes.rationale: Die akzeptierte Liste geht als Accept-Response-Header raus - genau das, was RFC 9110 12.5.1 in einer Response bedeutet. Zwei Ausnahmen: ein fehlender Content-Type wird als JSON dekodiert (RFC 9110 laesst dem Empfaenger die Freiheit, und HttpClient setzt den Header nur fuer Objekt-Bodies).

nodes.label: Grosse Bodies im Speicher
nodes.rationale: Die Route-DSL liest den ganzen Body vor dem Handler; fuer grosse Uploads auf die native Streaming-API des Backends absteigen oder Pre-Signed URLs verwenden.

nodes.label: Structured-Syntax-Suffixe (+json)
nodes.rationale: application/vnd.api+json, merge-patch+json und problem+json folgen gemaess RFC 6839 ihrem Basistyp.

nodes.label: entity<T> validiert nicht
nodes.rationale: Der Cast ist vertrauensbasiert - das Framework bundelt keinen Validator; zod/valibot/io-ts auf entity<unknown> legen, sonst liefert {"totally":"wrong"} ein undefined-Feld und Folgefehler.

nodes.label: HTTP-Handler als duenner Adapter zu Actors
nodes.rationale: Request parsen, einen Actor fragen, die Antwort marshallen. Kein geteilter veraenderlicher State in Handlern (sie laufen parallel), und schwere Arbeit in einen Actor auslagern - ein langsamer Handler belegt eine Verbindungslebenszeit.
nodes.norm_label: http-handler als duenner adapter zu actors

nodes.label: addressTerminated
nodes.rationale: Reserviert fuer den Cluster-Fall (ganzer Node unerreichbar); aktuell immer false - Node-weite Unerreichbarkeit loest noch kein Terminated aus.

nodes.label: context.unwatch(ref)
nodes.rationale: Idempotent; Registrierungen eines stoppenden Actors werden automatisch aufgeraeumt - unwatch ist nur fuer Interessenwechsel mid-flight.

nodes.label: context.watch(ref)
nodes.rationale: Opt-in pro Watcher; der beobachtete Actor erfaehrt nichts davon. Einen bereits gestoppten Actor zu beobachten liefert sofort ein Terminated.

nodes.label: context.watchWith(ref, message)
nodes.rationale: Verlegt die Bedeutung eines Todes auf den Zeitpunkt der Registrierung, damit die Nachrichten-Union des Watchers eine Beschreibung seiner Aufgabe bleibt; die Nachricht wird im Watcher gemerkt und reist nie zum beobachteten Actor - kein Serializer, nichts Neues auf der Leitung. Umgeht onSignal bewusst.

nodes.label: DeathPactError
nodes.rationale: Die Runtime wirft ihn nie selbst - einen automatischen Death Pact gibt es nicht, weil ein Pakt Policy ueber DIESEN Watcher ist und onReceive dem Framework kein Signal gibt, einen ignorierten von einem still erledigten Tod zu unterscheiden. Ein Restart ist die falsche Antwort: decideBy auf Directive.Stop.

nodes.label: existenceConfirmed
nodes.rationale: Aktuell immer true - die Implementierung setzt es nie auf false, also nicht als Fehlersignal verwenden.

nodes.label: Terminated
nodes.rationale: Kommt ueber die Mailbox an, damit alle vorher gesendeten tells zuerst verarbeitet werden; feuert nur bei Stop, nicht bei jedem Fehler.

nodes.label: DeadLetter (Event)
nodes.rationale: Publishen ist alles, was mit ihr passiert - nichts loggt sie, nichts bewahrt sie auf; ohne Abonnent ist sie weg.

nodes.label: Mailbox.enqueueSignal
nodes.rationale: Vertrag: reihe es ein, was die Schranke auch sagt. Die Basis delegiert an enqueue - richtig fuer eine Queue, die nichts verwirft, falsch fuer eine, die es tut; wer enqueue zum Abwerfen ueberschreibt, MUSS enqueueSignal ueberschreiben. Delegieren statt direkt in die Basis-Queue zu schreiben ist Absicht: ein Envelope in einem Speicher, den dequeueUser nie liest, waere schlimmer als ein verworfenes.

nodes.label: undroppable-Envelope-Flag
nodes.rationale: removeOldest liest es, eine drop-head-Schranke ueberspringt so ein Envelope gratis und muss nicht wissen, warum.

nodes.label: AllForOneStrategy
nodes.rationale: Nur wenn explizit entschieden wurde, dass die Zustaende der Kinder gekoppelt sind (z. B. ein Producer-Consumer-Paar ueber einen internen Channel).

nodes.label: defaultStrategy / stoppingStrategy / escalatingStrategy
nodes.rationale: defaultStrategy restartet alles, gecappt bei 10/Minute - genau das verhindert unendliche Restart-Loops.

nodes.label: decideBy
nodes.rationale: Baut einen Decider aus {match, then}-Mappings mit Fallback; ein handgeschriebenes (err) => Directive geht genauso.

nodes.label: Directive (Restart / Resume / Stop / Escalate)
nodes.rationale: Restart ist der Default. Resume behaelt den Zustand und ueberspringt die Nachricht - falsch, wenn der Zustand der Ausloeser war; richtig fuer transiente Fehler.

nodes.label: maxRetries / withinTimeRangeMs
nodes.rationale: Durchbricht unendliche Restart-Loops - jenseits der Grenze wird gestoppt statt restartet. Der Zaehler auf der Parent-Seite schliesst den ausloesenden Fehler ein, maxRetries: 10 toleriert also elf Restarts. -1 = unbegrenzt, withinTimeRangeMs 0 = Lifetime-Cap.

nodes.label: OneForOneStrategy
nodes.rationale: Default-Scope; die ueberwaeltigende Mehrheit des Codes verwendet ihn - Geschwister laufen weiter.

nodes.label: ActorKilledError
nodes.rationale: Distinct error type matters when a supervisor uses decideBy to dispatch on error class.

nodes.label: Terminations-Sequenz
nodes.rationale: One code path regardless of trigger: children stop first, postStop runs, watchers are notified, the mailbox drains to dead letters, and the ref starts routing there.

nodes.label: exhaustive() ohne Terminated-Arm wird zur Restart-Schleife
nodes.rationale: ts-pattern wirft einen gewoehnlichen Fehler, der durch die Supervision geht - unter der Default-Strategie restartet der Watcher. Ein Actor.onReceive ohne Branch tut dagegen nichts, ein typed Behavior ohne Signal-Handler schickt das Terminated zu Dead Letters.
nodes.norm_label: exhaustive() ohne terminated-arm wird zur restart-schleife

nodes.label: Eine Registrierung, ein Tod (Inkarnation als Schluessel)
nodes.rationale: Der Schluessel der Buchfuehrung ist die Inkarnation, nicht der Pfad - ein neu gespawnter Name ist ein anderer Actor, und genau das verhindert, dass eine offene Notification der Vorgaenger-Inkarnation gegen ihren Nachfolger zugestellt wird.
nodes.norm_label: eine registrierung, ein tod (inkarnation als schluessel)

nodes.label: Todesbenachrichtigung ist nicht verwerfbar
nodes.rationale: Ein Tod wird genau einmal angekuendigt und kann nicht erneut gesendet werden - deshalb ausgenommen von jeder Mailbox-Schranke und von throttle({onExcess:'drop'}); unzustellbar wird sie zum Dead Letter, damit der Verlust sichtbar statt stillschweigend ist.

nodes.label: Watch ueber Cluster-Nodes hinweg
nodes.rationale: Termination-Notifications propagieren ueber den Cluster-Transport; Node-weite Unerreichbarkeit liefert noch kein Terminated.

nodes.label: Absoluter Vorrang von System-Nachrichten
nodes.rationale: Zwei Queues nebeneinander; nur vom Framework emittierte System-Nachrichten draengeln vor. ref.stop() ist eine USER-Nachricht (PoisonPill) - sauberes Drain-dann-Stop - und ein Terminated ebenfalls, damit ein Handler die Arbeit davor gesehen hat. Nicht verwerfbar heisst nicht vordraengeln.

nodes.label: gracefulStop(ref, timeoutMs)
nodes.rationale: Returns a boolean rather than rejecting because a timeout is a result, not an error; the budget is mandatory because a default would quietly cut somebody's shutdown short, and only a locally hosted actor can be confirmed.

nodes.label: Kill
nodes.rationale: The escape hatch for making a non-failing actor trigger its supervisor strategy from outside without touching its code; under the default restart strategy it does not actually stop the actor.

nodes.label: withSupervisorStrategy
nodes.rationale: Two strategies are in play per actor — the one in its spawn options handles its own failures, the class override handles its children's; resolution is spawn options, then parent override, then defaultStrategy, and because the parent applies it, all-for-one still spreads to siblings and the retry budget is counted per parent.

nodes.label: Eskalations-Kette
nodes.rationale: Laeuft den Parent-Baum hoch bis zum Root-User-Guardian; eskaliert dessen Strategie, tritt das System in einen Fatal-Error-Zustand. Uncaught Errors passieren nur, wenn jede Ebene explizit eskaliert - Stops sind ein normaler Ausgang, Eskalation-zur-Wurzel das 'wir wissen nicht, was wir tun sollen'-Signal.

nodes.label: Behaviors.supervise zaehlt und eskaliert anders
nodes.rationale: Liest maxRetries woertlich und eskaliert jenseits der Grenze statt zu stoppen - der Wrapper sitzt INNERHALB des fehlschlagenden Actors, ein Stopp dort verwuerfe den Fehler unbemerkt. Wrapper verschachteln sich zu einer Supervisions-Hierarchie innerhalb eines Actors, geschichtet ueber die zwischen Actors.

nodes.label: Das Spawn-Kommando einer Verbindung ist nicht verwerfbar
nodes.rationale: Nimmt dieselbe Spur wie ein Terminated der Death Watch: hinten eingereiht, aber von jeder Overflow-Policy ausgenommen. Es wird genau einmal aus dem Upgrade-Callback gesendet und traegt die einzige Referenz auf einen bereits gehandshakten Socket - es zu verlieren liesse den Socket aufgewertet zurueck, ohne Listener, mit belegtem maxConnections-Platz.
nodes.norm_label: das spawn-kommando einer verbindung ist nicht verwerfbar

nodes.label: Idempotency-Key header
nodes.rationale: The client must mint the key once before the first attempt and reuse it on retry; generating one inside the retry loop is the common bug that defeats the whole mechanism.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: cors(...)
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: handleErrors / withErrorHandler
nodes.rationale: Return a generic body and log the detail server-side keyed by the request id; keep 403 and 404 unspecific.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: requestTimeout(ms)
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: dotfiles: deny
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: identity scope and maxScopeLength
nodes.rationale: Folds a per-caller scope into the cache key so an identity-specific response is never replayed to a different caller (security audit HTTP-4). Both key rules apply to it, because it is the other half of the same composed key — a two-character key with a 64 KiB x-account header used to be accepted. Two separate caps rather than one over the composed key, so a tenant with a long id cannot spend an honest client header budget.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: Key validation (length and control characters)
nodes.rationale: The header value is attacker-chosen and lands verbatim in a cache key: CR and LF are the classic header-injection pair, and space plus the control range are command delimiters in Memcached text protocol, so a key carrying one is only safe depending on which Cache is wired in behind the middleware. The rejection names the limit and the offending index, never the key itself.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on by default
nodes.rationale: Written by the backend rather than a middleware, so it also reaches responses no middleware sees. It is the only default because it is the only header of the bundle that cannot change how an existing application is embedded, framed or referred to — X-Frame-Options and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy would break iframes and OAuth popups, so they stay opt-in.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: redactUrlCredentials / redactedUrlLabel
nodes.rationale: The server-side copy needs hygiene too — a password that has reached a log aggregator has to be rotated, not deleted.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering
nodes.rationale: requestId outermost so every log line including errors has an id; securityHeaders above everything that rejects so those responses carry them; cors outside auth because preflights are anonymous by spec; handleErrors outside csrf so it maps that middleware own 403, and inside the header layers so what it returns still flows through them; fallback at the root.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering
nodes.norm_label: recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: securityHeaders() / withSecurityHeaders
nodes.rationale: The middleware covers its own subtree including an HttpError thrown below it, but never a response raised outside that subtree — the backend own 404, the 413, the generic 500. Configure it on the server when the whole server needs it, as middleware when only a subtree does.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: Path-traversal defence
nodes.rationale: The URL remainder is fully decoded before validation (peeling every encoding layer), then every segment is rejected if it is .., empty, a NUL, a backslash or a colon segment (Windows drive / NTFS alternate data stream); absolute forms are refused and the joined path is confined to the root.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: symlinks: within-root confinement
nodes.rationale: Checked on every filesystem hop a request touches, not just the resolved path: a directory index file and each listing entry are canonicalised too, so an escaping link is a 404 whether asked for directly or reached as index.html, and it is left out of the listing entirely — its name, size and mtime are exactly what the policy withholds.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: Every rejection is a uniform 404
nodes.rationale: No information leak about what exists — the response never distinguishes a denied dotfile, an escaping symlink and a missing file.
nodes.community_name: Recommended middleware stack and its ordering

nodes.label: rateLimit handler wrapper
nodes.rationale: Per-key fixed-window limiter answering excess with 429 plus Retry-After; layered limits are composed by wrapping each handler with its own limiter.

nodes.label: cached handler wrapper
nodes.rationale: A cache hit serves the stored response without invoking the underlying handler; which handlers to wrap is a per-handler decision.

nodes.label: Cluster transport threat model
nodes.rationale: Eavesdropping, MITM, unauthorized join, stolen certs, hostile frames, decode amplification, half-open and silent sockets, unbounded registries, pre-claimed addresses, replayed gossip and spoofed discovery — each with its stated mitigation.

nodes.label: Cluster-aware rate limiting
nodes.rationale: Redis-backed cache shares one counter across pods; InMemoryCache gives each pod its own, so a client spread over 4 pods gets 4x the limit.

nodes.label: Do not share the limiter cache
nodes.rationale: A flood travelling through the limiter can never evict its own counter, because incr runs before the max comparison and marks it most-recently-used. A key-minting route on the same Cache that the limiter does not wrap gives no such bump — measured on one shared maxEntries:4 instance, a client answered 429 was answered 200 again after twenty off-limiter Idempotency-Key requests.
nodes.norm_label: do not share the limiter cache

nodes.label: Fixed-window counting via cache incr with TTL
nodes.rationale: The TTL on the counter is what makes fresh windows start cleanly; incr is atomic across pods when backed by Redis.
nodes.norm_label: fixed-window counting via cache incr with ttl

nodes.label: Fixed-window edge effects
nodes.rationale: A burst crossing a window boundary yields double the limit in seconds; no sliding-window or token-bucket variant ships, so implement one manually if strict burst protection matters.

nodes.label: key(request) derivation
nodes.rationale: Key on a value the client cannot forge — socket peer, user id, API key — never a raw x-forwarded-for, or an attacker rotates it per request to bypass the limit.

nodes.label: Trusting X-Forwarded-For
nodes.rationale: Every common proxy appends, so whatever the client typed stays at the left of the header and keying on it is spoofable.

nodes.label: Cache invalidation by TTL or manual delete
nodes.rationale: No auto-invalidation on writes: staleness is bounded by ttlMs, or you delete the prefixed key directly because the cache is just a Cache.
nodes.norm_label: cache invalidation by ttl or manual delete

nodes.label: Cache key composition
nodes.rationale: key(req) is the entire cache-key contract. req.path is the pathname only, so an endpoint that varies by a query parameter must fold it into the key or every page shares one entry and page 2 is served page 1.

nodes.label: cacheStatuses
nodes.rationale: Defaults to [200] so a transient 500 never sticks around for the TTL; add 404 where many lookups miss, to save repeat database hits.

nodes.label: The key-minting side of a shared cache
nodes.rationale: key(request) almost always derives from client-controlled input, so a caller who varies it mints an entry per request. Harmless alone — the LRU bound is exactly what stops the response cache growing — and these plain sets are drained before a rate-limit counter, but the bound is still hard and Memcached and Redis under allkeys-lru have no such policy.
nodes.norm_label: the key-minting side of a shared cache

nodes.label: Per-process single-flight stampede protection
nodes.rationale: On a miss the handler runs once per process and the other concurrent requests await that result; it is not cluster-wide, so with N pods the handler can run N times, and stale-while-revalidate is not built in.

nodes.label: JSON cannot construct a PoisonPill
nodes.rationale: The message is a plain object, so it cannot be a PoisonPill, a Kill or any other class the system treats specially; that bound is structural rather than enforced by a check, which is why it holds.

nodes.label: Firewall the cluster port
nodes.rationale: Even with TLS and auth, expose 2552 narrowly: pods talk to pods, nothing goes through a Service, Ingress or LoadBalancer.

nodes.label: Stall and handshake deadlines
nodes.rationale: An incomplete frame may sit 30 s without another byte, re-armed on every chunk so a slow link is never punished, only silence. The handshake gets 5 s from accept — the case an incomplete frame cannot cover, since a socket sending no bytes is not stalled mid-frame — and the deadline is gone once hello lands, because an established peer between gossip rounds is idle by design.

nodes.label: Inbound connection cap of 1024
nodes.rationale: Far above any realistic fully-meshed topology; what it removes is multiplying per-connection cost by opening sockets in a loop. The newest connection is refused rather than an established one evicted, because eviction would let an attacker push real peers off the node — and the cap is only worth what its slot turnover is worth, which is why the handshake deadline is its pair.

nodes.label: Linear decode buffer
nodes.rationale: The peer chooses the chunk split, and the decoder used to rebuild its accumulator per chunk, so one frame cost work quadratic in the chunk count — a 16 MiB frame in TCP-sized writes is ~12 000 chunks and about 100 GB of copying, roughly 6000x amplification on bytes never sent, reachable before the hello gate. Doubling growth makes it 1x.

nodes.label: Pinning what the resolver may say
nodes.rationale: A seed answer arrives before any certificate has been checked. It cannot let an attacker join where certificates bind the claimed address — but that guarantee is configuration-dependent, so pinnedAddresses is defence in depth and the only discovery-layer control left standing when mTLS is not in place.
nodes.norm_label: pinning what the resolver may say

nodes.label: What the wire edge rejects
nodes.rationale: Frames used to be cast rather than checked, so null alone was an eight-byte remote process kill needing no handshake. Two tiers deliberately: a frame failing validation is dropped and the connection stays up, because one bad frame should not cost a healthy peer its link, while a handler that throws drops the connection because that is the case nobody understands.

nodes.label: ackToken / acknowledgment / negativeAcknowledgment
nodes.rationale: negativeAcknowledgment mit drop: true quittiert ohne Verarbeitung - der Notausgang fuer eine Nachricht, die jedes Mal scheitert.

nodes.label: onProcessed-Modi: markSeen und move
nodes.rationale: markSeen setzt \Seen und braucht ein eigens vorgesehenes Postfach, weil ein zweiter Leser die Bridge Nachrichten ueberspringen laesst; move verschiebt nach moveToMailbox, das beim Verbinden angelegt wird.

nodes.label: At-least-once, quittiert ueber IMAP-Flags
nodes.rationale: Verarbeitet ist eine Tatsache auf dem Server (\Seen bzw. Abwesenheit aus dem Postfach) statt Buchfuehrung im Speicher - genau deshalb sieht ein abgestuerzter Consumer die Nachricht wieder, statt sie zu verlieren.

nodes.label: moveToMailbox muss sich vom beobachteten Postfach unterscheiden
nodes.rationale: Mails in genau das Postfach zu verschieben, aus dem sie gelesen werden, stellt sie endlos erneut zu - und jeder einzelne IMAP-Befehl in dieser Schleife ist erfolgreich, der Validator erzwingt es deshalb.
nodes.norm_label: movetomailbox muss sich vom beobachteten postfach unterscheiden

nodes.label: LibSqlDurableStateStore
nodes.rationale: The first durable-state store in the SQLite family — the local SQLite backend ships journal + snapshot only.

nodes.label: PostgresDurableStateStore
nodes.rationale: The first SQL-backed durable-state store; SQLite and Cassandra ship journal + snapshot only.

nodes.label: SqliteDurableStateStore
nodes.rationale: A remote URL is rejected at construction and points at LibSqlDurableStateStore, because the local driver cannot open one and silently creating a FILE with that name is the confusing outcome.

nodes.label: Range requests (206 / 416)
nodes.rationale: Only the requested window is read, never the whole file — a bytes=0-0 on a 50 MiB file costs one byte.

nodes.label: StaticFilesOptions
nodes.rationale: Per-route code only, with no HOCON layer, because an HTTP handler has no ActorSystem at request time — unlike the WebSocket policy.

nodes.label: Streaming responses from a handler
nodes.rationale: All three backends stream a ReadableStream without buffering. Streams are one-shot, so never wrap one in caching middleware; set Content-Length yourself since a backend has nothing to measure on a stream — and Bun.serve re-frames a stream as chunked regardless.

nodes.label: Streamed bodies break cached() and idempotent()
nodes.rationale: Both serialise a body by checking for Uint8Array, so a streamed response is stored as an empty object and the second hit serves nothing (#674); and the Express backend pipes a stream with no error handler, so a mid-response failure takes the process or the request with it (#979). Streaming being opt-in is why the out-of-the-box static route is unaffected.
nodes.norm_label: streamed bodies break cached() and idempotent()

nodes.label: streamThreshold
nodes.rationale: Setting it retires the 413 without losing a bound: it must be at or below maxFileSize, so nothing can buffer past the threshold and the cap becomes unreachable rather than waived. Content-Length is stated by the handler because a backend has nothing to measure on a stream.

nodes.label: CassandraJournalOptions
nodes.rationale: Das Framework erstellt die Tabellen, aber nicht den Keyspace selbst - der muss extern mit angemessener Replikation provisioniert werden.

nodes.label: Zusammengesetzter Partition-Key (partitionSize)
nodes.rationale: Die Events einer persistenceId werden in Partitions von partitionSize Zeilen (Default 500.000) gebucketet, sodass ein langlebiger Stream mehrere Partitions umfasst und Recovery eine Partition pro Bucket liest. Heisse Tags (jedes Event mit 'audit') werden zu heissen Partitions - Bucketing oder feinkoernigere Tags erwaegen.

nodes.label: ServiceAccount and pod-reader RBAC
nodes.rationale: The K8s API seed provider must list pods matching a label selector; without the grant it gets 403 and the cluster never forms.

nodes.label: terminationGracePeriodSeconds sizing
nodes.rationale: Must cover the preStop sleep plus the pipeline; the pipeline worst case is default-phase-timeout times the phases that actually have tasks, not times twelve.

nodes.label: Broker actor TLS knobs
nodes.rationale: Each broker exposes its own shape: Kafka withSsl plus SASL, MQTT via mqtts, AMQP via amqps, NATS mTLS through the driver, Redis Streams via rediss, gRPC credentials, WebSocket via wss.

nodes.label: Certificate provisioning patterns
nodes.rationale: cert-manager auto-renews before expiry in Kubernetes, Vault Agent pulls certs into the pod filesystem as a sidecar, and non-K8s environments fall back to scheduled cron pulls plus restarts.

nodes.label: Cluster transport TLS configuration
nodes.rationale: TcpTransport takes cert, key, ca and rejectUnauthorized for mutually-authenticated TLS between nodes; defence in depth applies even on internal networks.

nodes.label: HTTP server TLS
nodes.rationale: HTTPS at the application layer via the Fastify backend https option; often terminated at the load balancer instead, so pick by your infrastructure shape.

nodes.label: Management endpoint TLS
nodes.rationale: The management server is internal-only by default, but TLS still protects against lateral movement in a compromised network and is required by some compliance regimes regardless of topology.

nodes.label: Persistence backend TLS
nodes.rationale: SQLite is local-file so TLS does not apply; Cassandra mTLS is configured on the driver client passed via withClient; cloud object storage always uses TLS with no extra configuration.

nodes.label: Code-only upgrade
nodes.rationale: A new binary against the same schemas; gossip, sharding rebalance and coordinated shutdown handle the choreography for zero downtime, given at least two replicas and health checks that gate readiness.

nodes.label: Revision-checked optimistic concurrency
nodes.rationale: A second concurrent writer is rejected with DurableStateConcurrencyError. In practice concurrent writes should not happen - one entity per persistenceId addressed via routing or sharding - so seeing them in production usually means a routing bug.

nodes.label: CassandraJournal
nodes.rationale: Shared across cluster nodes, unlike one SQLite file per node, so any node can append or read any persistenceId. The production choice for sharded entities that move between nodes and for cross-node projections; single-node Cassandra is strictly worse than SQLite.

nodes.label: Composite partition key with bucketing
nodes.rationale: Events are keyed by persistence_id and partition_nr and bucketed at partitionSize rows, so a long-lived stream spans multiple partitions and recovery reads one partition per bucket.

nodes.label: Cassandra journal consistency model
nodes.rationale: Within a pid the order is strict by sequenceNr regardless of which replica responds; across pids, tag-query order is timestamp-bound but not strict, so same-timestamp events may interleave.

nodes.label: CQL identifier validation
nodes.rationale: Identifiers cannot be bound, so keyspace and table names are interpolated and therefore validated against a strict pattern on every path. Data-center names are CQL string values instead, so they keep hyphens and are quote-escaped; everything else travels as bind parameters.

nodes.label: LWT sequence claim on the metadata row
nodes.rationale: A CQL INSERT is an upsert, so without the claim two writers reading head N would both pass expectedSeq and both write N+1, the second silently overwriting the first while both callers are told the event persisted. Relational journals cannot lose that race because their primary key rejects the loser.
nodes.norm_label: lwt sequence claim on the metadata row

nodes.label: serialConsistency on a multi-DC keyspace
nodes.rationale: The driver default SERIAL is a quorum across every DC, dragging each append over the inter-DC link and undoing what LOCAL_QUORUM buys; LOCAL_SERIAL keeps Paxos inside one DC, at the cost of linearizability only within a DC.

nodes.label: events_by_tag side table
nodes.rationale: Optional, off by default, partitioned by tag so a projection query hits one partition; each row carries its own copy of the payload.

nodes.label: Kubernetes deployment recipe
nodes.rationale: Stable identity, seed discovery and a clean shutdown path are the three things K8s must get right for an actor cluster.

nodes.label: TLS everywhere
nodes.rationale: A catalog of every network surface with its own TLS knobs - cluster transport, HTTP, management endpoint, broker actors, persistence backends - and what certificate material each needs.

nodes.label: CQL-Identifier-Validierung
nodes.rationale: Keyspace und Tabellennamen werden als Identifier interpoliert, weil Identifier sich nicht binden lassen - jeder wird gegen /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/ geprueft, bevor er in einem Statement landet. Data-Center-Namen sind CQL-String-Werte statt Identifier und behalten daher ihre Bindestriche (us-east-1), werden aber quote-escaped. Alles andere geht als Bind-Parameter.

nodes.label: preStop sleep for load-balancer drain
nodes.rationale: Without the sleep, SIGTERM races load-balancer deregistration and in-flight requests see draining responses.

nodes.label: Readiness and liveness probe split
nodes.rationale: ready asks whether to send traffic and may depend on external systems; health asks whether a restart would help, so it must depend on nothing outside the process or a shared outage restarts the whole fleet.

nodes.label: Rolling update ordering
nodes.rationale: Terminating, ten second drain, SIGTERM, coordinated-shutdown phases, then a fresh pod rejoins via the seed provider and shards rebalance automatically.

nodes.label: Single-replica cluster hazard
nodes.rationale: A one-replica cluster has nowhere to fail over to and is briefly empty mid-rolling-update, so sharded singletons go down and in-flight requests fail.

nodes.label: StatefulSet versus Deployment
nodes.rationale: StatefulSet buys stable pod names for per-pod identity and volumes; Deployment is fine when persistence is external, such as a shared Cassandra journal or S3 snapshot store.

nodes.label: TLS fields take material, never a path
nodes.rationale: Nothing in the transport touches the filesystem and none of Bun, Node or Deno accepts a filename in these fields, so the example reads the files itself.
nodes.norm_label: tls fields take material, never a path

nodes.label: Separate certificates per component
nodes.rationale: One wildcard cert for everything combines the blast radius; different certs for cluster, HTTP and brokers keep a compromised cert contained.

nodes.label: Compaction must reach the side table
nodes.rationale: It is a real dual-written table, not an index Cassandra maintains, and each row holds its own payload copy - so a row left behind would keep answering tag queries and keep storing the body after the event was compacted away. Its keys are not derivable from persistenceId and toSeq, so delete reads the prefix back first.
nodes.norm_label: compaction must reach the side table

nodes.label: The claim-before-write crash window
nodes.rationale: Claiming first inverts rather than removes the window: a death between the committed claim and the events leaves the head ahead of stored events, a gap. That is the safer trade because a gap is detectable by comparing highestSeq against the highest sequence present, whereas a lost write is not.

nodes.label: Hot tag partitions
nodes.rationale: Every event carrying one tag lands in a single partition, so a blanket audit tag at 10M events a day makes that partition huge; bucket high-volume tags by time window or use finer-grained tags.

nodes.label: What the LWT costs
nodes.rationale: One Paxos round trip per append, not per event - roughly 3 to 4 times a plain quorum write. Cross-pid throughput is unaffected since each claim contends only on its own metadata partition. Claiming on metadata is cheaper than IF NOT EXISTS per event, which a conditional batch could not span anyway.

nodes.label: Set lightweightTransactions uniformly
nodes.rationale: Cassandra only guarantees LWT linearizability when every write to a partition goes through Paxos, so a rolling change leaving some nodes conditional and others plain breaks the guarantee for the duration of the roll. Sharding aims for one writer per pid but does not guarantee it during a rebalance or split brain.

nodes.label: What carries over from any actor framework
nodes.norm_label: what carries over from any actor framework

nodes.label: Different defaults
nodes.rationale: Bun is the primary runtime with Node supported and Deno best-effort, JSON is the default serializer with CBOR and custom available, and Kubernetes is the assumed deployment target - which is why seed discovery, lease and management endpoints are first-class.

nodes.label: Incremental migration
nodes.rationale: Migration is rarely one-shot: run a small actor system alongside existing code, migrate one stateful concept (a registry, a job-runner) while HTTP handlers still call it like a service, then add clustering and persistence as you go. You do not have to rewrite everything to benefit.

nodes.label: Smaller surface than Akka
nodes.rationale: Akka Streams is not ported (use Promise-based patterns or a separate library), FSM exists but with a different API shape, and the framework deliberately targets the 80 percent of features rather than parity.

nodes.label: TypeScript-specific differences
nodes.rationale: No fibers and no JVM: JavaScript is single-threaded per process, so scheduling rides the microtask and macrotask queues. The typed Behaviors API is Akka-Typed-inspired but not identical, and ts-pattern stands in for the native match expressions TypeScript lacks.

nodes.label: Compose is not a production orchestrator
nodes.rationale: It is single-machine and lacks cross-host scheduling, coordinated rolling updates, health-based replacement (it restarts on crash but does not evict from a load balancer during deployment) and cluster autoscaling.
nodes.norm_label: compose is not a production orchestrator

nodes.label: Binding a body to its storage key
nodes.norm_label: binding a body to its storage key

nodes.label: migrateInMemoryJournal
nodes.rationale: Does the whole walk-and-rewrite for the in-memory journal, preserving sequence numbers, timestamps and tags. It relies on an internal _remapForMigration hook only the in-memory journal exposes, so Cassandra / SQLite / Postgres / S3 need their own backend-specific rewrite path around wrapEventAsEnvelope.

nodes.label: InMemoryReEncryptProgressStore
nodes.rationale: A plain re-run re-lists and re-checks every key, which is fine for small buckets; a progress store lets a crashed sweep over a million-object corpus resume near where it stopped.

nodes.label: Keyring-completeness pre-check
nodes.rationale: The sweep samples the first encrypted objects and refuses to start if any payload's key version is missing from the keyring — catching 'operator dropped the retired key too soon' before a mid-sweep decrypt failure leaves the corpus half-rewritten.

nodes.label: reEncryptObjectStorage
nodes.rationale: Lists every object under keyPrefix; already at the active version means skip with no PUT, otherwise decrypt with the matching retired key and rewrite under the active one. Returns { scanned, rewrote, skippedCurrent, skippedUnencrypted, skippedNonAts1 } — the counts are the source of truth, there is no separate 'list stragglers' helper.

nodes.label: encryption() per-actor hook
nodes.rationale: Lets PCI / HIPAA / GDPR-scoped data use a separate master key AND a separate HKDF context from non-sensitive data, so compromise of one keyring does not expose the other.

nodes.label: One-shot bulk migration, not a read-time shim
nodes.rationale: Walk the journal once, wrap every raw event as a version-1 envelope, write it back — a real rewrite of the stored data. It must run before an actor with the new adapter recovers, otherwise the first raw event throws MigrationError. Afterwards a normal adapter replays them; there is no special legacy-wrapping adapter at read time.
nodes.norm_label: one-shot bulk migration, not a read-time shim

nodes.label: Key version embedded in the body manifest
nodes.norm_label: key version embedded in the body manifest

nodes.label: Sweep writes with an ETag compare-and-set
nodes.rationale: If the app wrote a newer version of an object the sweep is rewriting, the CAS fails, the sweep throws ObjectStorageConcurrencyError and aborts. Per-object failures are never swallowed; fix and re-run, since already-rewritten objects are idempotently skipped.
nodes.norm_label: sweep writes with an etag compare-and-set

nodes.label: Rotating the HKDF context (newInfo)
nodes.rationale: Bodies are decrypted under info and rewritten under newInfo. Because the context is not in the manifest the sweep cannot tell a converted body from an unconverted one by reading the header, so while newInfo differs the version fast-path is switched off and every object is decrypted — a full read pass rather than a header scan. Without that, a context-only rotation would report everything as skipped-current and change nothing.

nodes.label: Online master-key rotation flow
nodes.rationale: Generate the new key as active with the old under retired, roll out, run the sweep, wait the rollback window (~7 days, because backups may still reference the old key), then drop the retired entry. Zero downtime and old data stays readable throughout.

nodes.label: Every key version is used once
nodes.rationale: One manifest byte is all a reader has to identify the key with, so two entries claiming the same version are refused at registration, at the store and at the start of a sweep. Without the check the lookup resolves the collision by precedence — active first — so payloads written under the older key are decrypted with the newer one and fail with an authentication-tag error that names nothing. The 32-byte length is checked in the same pass, since a short retired key is otherwise invisible until some payload at that version is read.
nodes.norm_label: every key version is used once

nodes.label: 255 is not a lifetime budget
nodes.rationale: It bounds how many versions may be live in one corpus at once, not how often you may rotate: a completed sweep puts every payload on the active version, the retired entries go away, and every other number is free again. From version 240 registration warns. There is deliberately no wider version field, because the sweep already resolves the only situation one would help with.

nodes.label: Uniform encryption config across cluster nodes
nodes.rationale: Actors must see the same encryption config on every node, or a sharded entity that migrates cannot be read where it lands. Pass key rings from the same source everywhere.
nodes.norm_label: uniform encryption config across cluster nodes

nodes.label: Contention backstop classification (ER_CHECKREAD 1020)
nodes.rationale: Under real contention InnoDB aborts the loser before it reaches the primary key, so the duplicate-key backstop alone would hand back an opaque JournalError. Those aborts (1020, 1213, 1205) are classified too, but only reported as JournalConcurrencyError once a re-read shows the head actually moved — otherwise a lock-wait timeout against an unrelated long transaction would send the caller into a retry spin.

nodes.label: mongodb@7 cannot be imported on Bun
nodes.rationale: Version 7 bundles a bson that calls v8.startupSnapshot.isBuildingSnapshot() at module scope, which Bun does not implement, so the import throws ERR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED before any framework code runs. The peer range is pinned to ^6, which imports cleanly on Bun, Node and Deno alike.
nodes.norm_label: mongodb@7 cannot be imported on bun

nodes.label: Multikey tag index
nodes.rationale: Because tags is an array, MongoDB indexes it as a multikey index — one entry per tag per event — so a query on one tag plus a timestamp lower bound walks a contiguous range instead of scanning. Cross-tag all/any/not are refined in memory, and a filter with only not falls back to the journal-walking scan.

nodes.label: Payloads are JSON text, not BSON documents
nodes.rationale: BSON would reject or mangle a payload whose keys contain a dot or start with $, and would quietly change how undefined and dates come back. Storing JSON text keeps fidelity and makes an event stream mean the same thing on every backend; the framework never queries inside a payload anyway.
nodes.norm_label: payloads are json text, not bson documents

nodes.label: The unique index is load-bearing
nodes.rationale: The unique compound index on (persistenceId, sequenceNr) is not a performance tweak — it IS the journal's optimistic-concurrency backstop, playing the part a primary key plays in the relational backends. Without it a racing writer silently overwrites an event, so autoCreateIndexes:false means 'I created them myself', not 'I don't need them'.

nodes.label: SQLSTATE 23505 concurrency backstop
nodes.rationale: The append runs SELECT MAX(sequence_nr) and the inserts in one transaction; a racing writer that slips through trips the primary key and 23505 becomes JournalConcurrencyError. A contention abort (40001 / 40P01) gets the same treatment, but only once a re-read confirms the head moved — an ordinary lock problem stays a JournalError rather than becoming a retry loop.

nodes.label: Journal.read replay contract
nodes.rationale: Events must come back ascending by sequence number, contiguous, and inside the requested window; delete compacts a prefix, never a hole in the middle. So a gap can only mean a defect — a missing ORDER BY, a half-written append, a store someone else can write — and replay raises JournalIntegrityError instead of folding it.

nodes.label: Chat-Sample
nodes.rationale: Komplette Demo-App: TCP-Cluster aus 3 Bun-Prozessen, sharded Chatroom-Actors, DistributedPubSub, PersistentActor-History auf SQLite, DistributedData-Presence und ein ClusterSingleton als HTTP-Eingangstuer. Jeder Node fuehrt dasselbe Binary aus und findet die anderen ueber einen Port-Scan ab 2551. Demonstriert bewusst KEINE Sharded Daemon Processes und kein Replicated Event Sourcing.

nodes.label: Examples-Uebersicht
nodes.rationale: Lauffaehige Beispiele im Repo: Chat-Sample (Cluster + PubSub + DD + sharded Persistenz), Voice-Sample (ephemeres Pub/Sub + Presence-CRDTs) und eigenstaendige Snippets pro Konzept.

nodes.label: bun run test:examples (Beispiel-Gate)
nodes.rationale: Startet jedes lauffaehige Snippet als eigenen Prozess und prueft dessen Ausgabe; der examples-Workflow laeuft bei jedem Push, der src/ oder examples/ beruehrt. Die Beispiele sind damit ein Gate, keine Dekoration - eine Framework-Aenderung, die eines bricht, wird zum roten Check statt etwas, das erst ein Leser entdeckt.

nodes.label: MultiNodeSpec in Snippets
nodes.rationale: Cluster-bezogene Snippets (Singleton, Sharding, PubSub, DD) simulieren einen Cluster innerhalb eines Prozesses - kein Docker noetig. Nur die Broker-Snippets unter examples/io/ und das K8s-Lease-Snippet brauchen etwas Externes und benennen beim Ausfuehren, was fehlt.

nodes.label: Eigenstaendige Snippets
nodes.rationale: Je eine Datei von 50-200 Zeilen pro Konzept - Counter, Saga, Circuit Breaker, Health-Endpoint, sharded Entity, persistente FSM. Die grundlegenden liegen auf oberster Ebene von examples/, der Rest in themenbezogenen Unterverzeichnissen. Die meisten laufen bis zum Ende; die unter examples/http/ sowie Prometheus- und K8s-Probe-Snippets sind bewusst Server und bleiben oben.

nodes.label: Voice-Sample
nodes.rationale: Verteiltes Walkie-Talkie mit drei Modi (1:1-PTT, 1:N-Gruppe, N:N-Raum) ueber einen WebSocket pro Client. Exerziert bewusst die Primitiven durch, die das Chat-Sample NICHT nutzt, und laesst ClusterSharding und PersistenceExtension weg - Voice ist ephemer per Design, der Server ist ein reiner Audio-Relay. Audio laeuft als binaere Frames ueber den bestehenden WebSocket (kein WebRTC, kein SFU), damit PubSub-Fan-out, Receptionist-Lookup und ORSet-Presence sichtbar die tragenden Teile sind.

nodes.label: tests/examples/examples.manifest.json
nodes.rationale: Every standalone example appears exactly once, either runnable with an output assertion or skipped with the reason it cannot run unattended; the runner fails when the list and the tree disagree in either direction.

nodes.label: HttpIngressActor (voice)
nodes.rationale: Binds in preStart and unbinds in postStop, so singleton failover moves the port to a survivor automatically.

nodes.label: withEntity
nodes.rationale: Public for the test bench: an entity deriving its persistenceId from entityId would otherwise be unspawnable without a cluster standing behind it.

nodes.label: Next static export (output: 'export')
nodes.rationale: A fully static export needs no Node runtime and pairs cleanly with @fastify/static; basePath + assetPrefix retarget internal URLs at /static/next/.

nodes.label: useChat hook (React)
nodes.rationale: useReducer drives multi-room state so messagesByRoom and unreadByRoom update atomically per message action; the WS lifecycle is owned by the hook and the UI only sees plain values.

nodes.label: chat.svelte.ts runes store
nodes.rationale: The .svelte.ts extension activates rune compilation, turning a plain TS class into a reactive store.

nodes.label: canonicalPairId
nodes.rationale: Orders the two usernames so canonicalPairId(alice, bob) === canonicalPairId(bob, alice), giving a DM channel and its DD entry one stable key for both participants.

nodes.label: ChatRoomActor
nodes.rationale: One sharded PersistentActor per room; recovery replays from the latest snapshot (every 100 events) plus the tail, so a 10k-message room cold-starts in O(100 events) regardless of total history.

nodes.label: ChatRoomDirectoryActor
nodes.rationale: Wraps a DistributedData ORSet so user-created rooms converge across nodes; every node spawns its own instance and the DEFAULT_ROOMS seed is idempotent (#98).

nodes.label: backend/auth/credentials.ts (validateCredentials)
nodes.rationale: Scans every user and verifies against a real hash even on a username miss, so response timing does not leak account enumeration.

nodes.label: DirectMessageChannelActor
nodes.rationale: DMs are modelled as virtual @username rooms so no new protocol frames are needed; routing keys on the canonical pair-id and each user subscribes once at login to chat.dm.user.<self>, removing per-channel subscription bookkeeping from the client (#100).

nodes.label: DistributedPubSub (chat.room.<name> topics)
nodes.rationale: One topic per room gives cross-node fan-out with no routing code in the middle — a message posted on node 1 reaches a client on node 3 directly.

nodes.label: Emoji support (server-agnostic)
nodes.rationale: Pure text — the server is agnostic, so each frontend can wire any picker on top without server changes.

nodes.label: test:examples CI gate
nodes.rationale: Runs smoke-test.ts --spawn-backend with every other runnable example on each push touching src/ or examples/, so a framework change that breaks the chat protocol round-trip is a red check rather than a later discovery.

nodes.label: chat failover-test.ts
nodes.rationale: Deliberately excluded from the CI example gate: two of its three backends were observed outliving a clean exit and holding their cluster ports, which poisons whatever runs next.

nodes.label: FastifyBackend.withPlugin
nodes.rationale: The HTTP layer goes through the framework directive DSL: @fastify/static and @fastify/websocket are wired in exclusively via withPlugin, so there is no manual Fastify setup in the sample.

nodes.label: HttpIngressActor
nodes.rationale: A ClusterSingleton owning the public :8080 bind so users keep one URL and there are no per-node ports to remember; a survivor re-binds automatically when the holder dies.

nodes.label: backend/auth/password.ts (scrypt hash/verify)
nodes.rationale: Passwords stored as <salt>:<hash> scrypt digests and verified with crypto.scryptSync + crypto.timingSafeEqual (#99, Option A).

nodes.label: Cluster port auto-discovery
nodes.rationale: Each node walks the cluster-port range from 2551, claims the first free port and treats every occupied port below it as a seed, so three identical commands form a cluster without flags. Explicit --port/--seeds remain for cross-machine deployments where a same-host port scan cannot work.

nodes.label: ReadReceiptsActor
nodes.rationale: Writes read pointers via a DD LWWMap with a monotonic guard so a stale write cannot roll a user pointer backwards; for DMs the entry is keyed on the canonical pair-id so both participants share one view (#103 slice 2).

nodes.label: Reconnect-resume frame
nodes.rationale: On socket close the frontend retries with the stored token via the resume frame, so a singleton failover reauthenticates the client without a fresh login.

nodes.label: backend/auth/sessionStore.ts (HMAC-signed tokens)
nodes.rationale: JWT-style HMAC-SHA256 tokens binding { username, issuedAt, exp }; lookupToken self-validates without a DD lookup and the DD LWWMap chat.session-revocations stores only explicitly revoked tokens. TTL 24 h, secret from CHAT_TOKEN_SECRET with a warned fallback.

nodes.label: chat smoke-test.ts
nodes.rationale: Single-node by design: isolating the protocol round-trip from the cluster lazy shard-allocation timing keeps it deterministic. --spawn-backend uses ports outside the auto-discovery window so a self-spawned run neither joins nor collides with an existing cluster.

nodes.label: TEST_USERS (shared/users.ts)
nodes.rationale: Plain-text demo passwords are intentional and printed under each login form; swapping in a real user store is a one-function change because validateCredentials already verifies against an opaque <salt>:<hash> string.

nodes.label: TLS / WSS
nodes.rationale: Frontends auto-promote ws: to wss: from location.protocol, so one cert/key pair flips the whole stack to TLS with no client-side change; production is expected to terminate TLS at a reverse proxy, with --tls-cert/--tls-key for setups where the Bun process owns the public listener.

nodes.label: Typing indicators (ephemeral PubSub)
nodes.rationale: Demonstrates ephemeral PubSub: a typing frame fans out over the room existing topic with no persistence and no actor in between; the server filters self-echoes, the client debounces to 1/2 s and auto-clears after 3 s (#103 slice 1).

nodes.label: Chat WebSocket protocol (shared/protocol.ts)
nodes.rationale: All client traffic is WebSocket-based with no REST: login, room list, history, presence and chat messages all flow through one /ws endpoint.

nodes.label: DistributedPubSub (voice.group / voice.room topics)
nodes.rationale: At-most-once delivery, so lost frames cause audible pops; production voice would want adaptive jitter buffers and retry layers above it.

nodes.label: frameCodec.ts binary frame envelope
nodes.rationale: Inbound is raw Opus with no header because the server knows the sender from session context; outbound prefixes [u8 nameLen][utf-8 username] so a receiver can demultiplex concurrent speakers instead of interleaving them into one stream.

nodes.label: MediaRecorder capture (Opus, 100 ms timeslice)
nodes.rationale: Each PTT press starts a fresh MediaRecorder so the first chunk carries the WebM init segment, lining up with the fresh MediaSource the receiver creates per voice-incoming-start.

nodes.label: Per-sender MediaSource playback
nodes.rationale: The right primitive for streamed Opus, but its quirks (init-segment-once, updating gates, endOfStream) make the pipeline fiddly, and N concurrent speakers cost N MediaSources so RAM scales linearly — a polished app might move to WebCodecs plus a ring buffer.

nodes.label: Receptionist (voice-user:<name> lookup)
nodes.rationale: Gossip latency is about a second, so a 1:1 PTT press within 1-2 s of the target login may fail; a retry on PTT-down handles it.

nodes.label: N:N room (Teams-style) mode
nodes.rationale: Rooms are pure CRDT presence plus a PubSub topic — entering a room subscribes you to its audio topic but you do not speak until a voice-target frame arrives, so membership and talking are independent.

nodes.label: voice smoke-test.ts
nodes.rationale: Brings its own one-node cluster on isolated ports so it runs unattended in test:examples; walks all three modes with a fake 32-byte payload and verifies the relay path including the room-mode self-filter, but deliberately not audio playback, which is a browser concern.

nodes.label: Voice wire protocol (shared/protocol.ts)
nodes.rationale: JSON discriminated unions for the control plane with auth identical to chat; audio chunks are binary WS frames rather than a ServerMessage variant.

nodes.label: VoiceSessionActor
nodes.rationale: One per WebSocket: text frames are the control plane, binary frames are routed per currentTarget.

nodes.label: Chat sample app
nodes.rationale: A complete demo showing cluster, persistence, pubsub and websocket composing together — the sharded and persistent sibling of the voice sample.

nodes.label: Voice sample (distributed walkie-talkie)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately built to exercise the primitives chat does not: Receptionist lookup, PubSub fan-out and CRDT presence with no database on the hot path.

nodes.label: Chat Angular frontend
nodes.rationale: Angular 21 standalone APIs + Signals with no NgModules and no NgRx, because signals keep chat state flat enough that the bundled ChatService is one readable file.

nodes.label: Angular chat host page (chat-root)
nodes.rationale: Angular own host page; the actor-ts backend never serves it directly, only the built bundle.

nodes.label: Chat Lit frontend
nodes.rationale: Lit 3 loaded as ES modules from the esm.sh CDN so no build step or node_modules is required; the CDN version stays self-contained for the demo, with a Vite bundle noted as the production path.

nodes.label: Chat Next.js frontend
nodes.rationale: Contrasts with the React + Vite variant on project structure — file-based routing, layout component, RSC conventions — while the chat itself runs entirely client-side because the backend is the actor system, not a Next API route.

nodes.label: Chat plain HTML frontend
nodes.rationale: The no-magic baseline: static/plain/index.html is both the source and what is served, and it is committed (unlike the built frontends) because a file nothing generates is source. The directory exists only for symmetry.

nodes.label: Chat React + Vite frontend
nodes.rationale: A pure SPA with no SSR/RSC/file-based routing, deliberately contrasted against the Next.js variant to isolate what the meta-framework adds.

nodes.label: Chat SvelteKit frontend
nodes.rationale: Contrast point versus the React variants is the runes state model: $state lifts plain TypeScript fields into a deep-reactive store and the template re-renders on any field change.

nodes.label: Chat sample (multi-frontend clustered chat)
nodes.rationale: Demonstrates the framework as a real distributed system — clustered backend, persisted history, live cross-node broadcast — paired with six frontends on one WebSocket protocol so their feel can be compared side by side.

nodes.label: Voice Angular frontend
nodes.rationale: Angular 21 standalone components with signals; only the reactivity wrapper differs from the React, SvelteKit and plain HTML siblings — the audio plumbing is the same.

nodes.label: Voice Lit frontend
nodes.rationale: Exists alongside the plain HTML one to show the same audio plumbing driven by reactive properties instead of manual DOM updates; CDN-loaded, with a vite build noted as the production path.

nodes.label: Voice Next.js frontend
nodes.rationale: 'use client' end-to-end with no SSR runtime — the static export is what ships; only the build pipeline differs from the React + Vite sibling.

nodes.label: Voice plain HTML frontend
nodes.rationale: The single-file layout is intentional: it keeps capture, WebSocket I/O and per-sender playback inspectable in one place without bouncing through framework abstractions; the other five factor the same logic into framework-shaped pieces for comparison.

nodes.label: Voice React + Vite frontend
nodes.rationale: Mirrors examples/chat/frontend-react in shape, adapted for voice — useVoice instead of useChat, MediaRecorder plus per-sender MediaSource instead of text broadcast.

nodes.label: Voice SvelteKit frontend
nodes.rationale: Same SvelteKit + adapter-static + copy-build structure as the chat sibling, replacing text-message reactivity with audio-stream reactivity (incomingNames, micPct, activeKey) using the same runes idioms.

nodes.label: Voice sample (walkie-talkie / group / rooms)
nodes.rationale: Three voice modes over one WebSocket per client on a 3-node cluster, chosen to exercise three primitives the chat sample does not: Receptionist lookup, PubSub megaphone fan-out and DD-ORSet room membership.

nodes.label: Same-host port-scan seed discovery
nodes.rationale: Nodes scan the cluster-port range from 2551, so three identical terminals settle on distinct ports with no seeds to configure.

nodes.label: Sharded chat rooms (16 shards)
nodes.rationale: One entity per room spread across the cluster, so killing any node lets the survivors take over its rooms; direct-message channels reuse the pattern keyed on a canonical pair-id.

nodes.label: Example gate (bun run test:examples)
nodes.rationale: Exit code 0 is not enough on its own — a snippet whose external dependency is missing can fail its actual work and still exit 0 — so every runnable case asserts on a substring of its output. The examples are a gate, not decoration.

nodes.label: Ephemeral by design (no sharding, no persistence)
nodes.rationale: The deliberate teaching contrast with the chat sample: the server is a dumb audio relay, so a dropped session simply vanishes from the ORSets and there is nothing to recover.
nodes.norm_label: ephemeral by design (no sharding, no persistence)

nodes.label: Presence via DistributedData ORSets
nodes.rationale: One global set tracks who is online and one set per room tracks who is in it — no sharded entity owns room state, it is pure CRDT membership plus a pubsub topic.

nodes.label: Group and room fan-out via DistributedPubSub
nodes.rationale: A topic fans out to every subscriber including the sender, so receivers drop their own frames with a self-filter on the sender username.
nodes.norm_label: group and room fan-out via distributedpubsub

nodes.label: Real-world voice adaptation
nodes.rationale: DistributedPubSub is at-most-once, so a production relay needs jitter buffers and retransmission above it, server-side mixing for large rooms, and WebRTC or an SFU on the media path.

nodes.label: Local protocol mirror
nodes.rationale: The ~50-line protocol types are duplicated per frontend rather than imported from ../../shared/, because reaching outside the project source root would mean relaxing rootDir and the strict-mode settings each toolchain relies on; self-containment is judged the better trade-off.

nodes.label: Gitignored frontend build output (#559)
nodes.rationale: static/angular|next|react|svelte are build artefacts and are not committed, so those routes 404 until npm ci && npm run build has run; plain/ and lit/ stay committed because a file nothing generates is source.

nodes.label: Production hardening (pointed at, not shipped)
nodes.rationale: CSRF/origin checks, login rate-limiting, a strong shared token secret and a real user store are config-driven through existing middleware slots rather than deeper code changes, so they are documented instead of duplicated in demo code.

nodes.label: HTTP singleton failover
nodes.rationale: A self-contained fallback that needs no external infrastructure; real zero-downtime active/active would put a load balancer in front. In-flight WebSocket frames are lost during the brief outage but persisted history survives.

nodes.label: hydrated flag (hydration-safe first paint)
nodes.rationale: Defers the first paint past hydration so the useEffect-driven phase machine can flip from gate-mic to gate-login without a hydration mismatch.

nodes.label: Server as dumb audio relay
nodes.rationale: No WebRTC, no SFU, no transcoding — deliberately flowing audio frames through actors so the PubSub fan-out, Receptionist lookup and DD-ORSet presence are visibly the load-bearing parts.

nodes.label: End-to-end latency (100-300 ms)
nodes.rationale: The dominant cost is the 100 ms timeslice; pushing it to 20-40 ms tightens latency at the price of CPU on both ends.

nodes.label: No cross-speaker echo cancellation
nodes.rationale: Browser AEC works only against locally-rendered audio, so a room of unmuted participants on one speaker will feed back; headphones are the mitigation.

nodes.label: FilesystemObjectStorageBackend
nodes.rationale: Objects as files under a root directory — the same code path as production with no network, no S3 cost and no MinIO container, for tests, local dev and small single-node deployments.

nodes.label: ObjectStorageBackend
