nodes.rationale: GossipMessage gains a required sequence, so an upgraded peer refuses an old node's frames and an old node ignores the new one: membership does not converge in either direction while both versions run. The guard holds only while the sender is still a member — closing that residual needs #940's incarnation identity.
nodes.norm_label: gossip frame sequence field breaks rolling upgrades (#112)

nodes.label: 50-oldest production-goal wave
nodes.rationale: Triage before code was the expensive half: every issue was read against today's tree asking 'are the acceptance criteria met' rather than 'does the defect still exist', and 277 claims in the issue bodies did not survive it. Unreachability is now deliberately NOT reconciled — on the no-lease path 'hosted somewhere' and 'at most one' cannot both be had, because reaching the incumbent to ask it to stand down is precisely what failed.

nodes.label: Dependabot configuration
nodes.rationale: Two ecosystems, both daily at 06:00 Europe/Berlin: npm (label dependencies, commit prefix chore(deps)) and github-actions (labels dependencies + github-actions, prefix chore(actions)).

nodes.label: Bug report issue template
nodes.rationale: Titled [Bug], labelled bug + priority: medium. Asks up front whether the issue reproduces against an in-memory transport or journal, which rules out a peer-dep mismatch before a maintainer looks.

nodes.label: Documentation issue template
nodes.rationale: Titled [Docs], labelled documentation + priority: low. Asks for a location that points the maintainer at the right place fastest — a README header, a docs/ path, or a fully-qualified JSDoc symbol — and classifies the gap as unclear, wrong, outdated, missing entirely, or a broken link.

nodes.label: benchmarks workflow
nodes.rationale: A smoke-level gate that proves the suite still compiles and still runs against the current src/ API — it measures nothing, because benchmark numbers from a shared CI runner are noise. It triggers on src/** too, since the failure mode is a source change orphaning a benchmark, which is invisible from the benchmark side of the diff.

nodes.label: build workflow
nodes.rationale: Verifies bun run build produces a usable dist/ (entry point plus type declarations) and that the committed DevTools UI bundle was generated from the sources in the tree; skips on docs-only, test-only and README changes so the actions queue stays focused.

nodes.label: docs-checks workflow
nodes.rationale: Fast, dependency-free checks on every docs change, distinct from the slow docs.yml build that only deploys from main at release time.

nodes.label: docs workflow (Astro Starlight to GitHub Pages)
nodes.rationale: Builds and deploys on pushes to main, which only moves when a release is cut, so published docs track released versions. The release: [published] trigger is deliberately not used — its runs execute on the TAG ref and are rejected by the github-pages environment protection rules, which is how the v0.11.0 docs deploy failed.
nodes.norm_label: docs workflow (astro starlight to github pages)

nodes.label: examples workflow
nodes.rationale: Two jobs answering two questions: do the eight bundled frontends still install and build (#903), and do the standalone examples still run (#545). src/** is in the filter because of the snippets job and is the whole point of it — an examples-only filter would produce zero checks for exactly the failure this gate exists to catch.

nodes.label: multi-runtime workflow
nodes.rationale: Verifies actor-ts boots identically across Bun, Node and Deno. It fires on main as well as develop because the release merge is --no-ff rather than a PR, so without main the exact commit users install would have had no Node/Deno signal at all.

nodes.label: nightly-flakes workflow
nodes.rationale: Answers the two questions a single bun test cannot: are the quarantined suites still broken on hosted runners, and which tests are flaky as opposed to which build was red. Both jobs are continue-on-error on purpose — a red required check for a known-red measurement trains people to ignore it, so the signal lives in the step summary, the ::warning:: annotation and the uploaded artifact. 04:00 UTC, after the two other nightlies.

nodes.label: publish workflow
nodes.rationale: Fires when a GitHub Release is published, with a workflow_dispatch fallback because a release-event run uses the workflow file at the tag's commit, so a workflow bug cannot be fixed and re-run through the release event alone. Runs are serialised rather than cancelled — an in-flight npm publish is the last thing to interrupt — because the version guard is a check-then-act that two overlapping runs would both pass.

nodes.label: tests workflow
nodes.rationale: Runs the unit/multi-node/smoke suite plus the README-badge updater on any change that could plausibly affect a test result. Concurrency is grouped by github.ref so develop pushes queue (preserving every commit's README state) while PR re-pushes cancel.

nodes.label: typecheck (dev) workflow
nodes.rationale: Its own workflow rather than a step in test.yml because path filters are per-workflow: a step there would never fire on an examples/** or benchmarks/** change, the very changes this configuration exists to cover, and widening test.yml's filters would run the full suite on every example edit. It is also cheap enough to be a required check.

nodes.label: actor-ts Working Standards
nodes.rationale: One file holds every convention for humans and coding agents alike, so a standard is discoverable in one place rather than re-derived from the diff history.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md repository pointer
nodes.rationale: Holds no standards of its own — it exists only to point every coding agent at AGENTS.md and to @-include it, so there is exactly one source of truth.

nodes.label: SHA-pinned actions with trailing tag comment
nodes.rationale: Every uses: is a full 40-character commit SHA plus a trailing # vX.Y.Z comment (#585). A tag is a mutable pointer - whoever can move actions/checkout@v7 runs arbitrary code inside the publish job that holds id-token: write. The comment is load-bearing, not decoration: Dependabot reads it to learn which version a SHA stands for, and without it the pin is invisible to updates and the repository freezes on a stale, eventually vulnerable action.
nodes.norm_label: sha-pinned actions with trailing tag comment

nodes.label: @types/node major-bump ignore rule
nodes.rationale: @types/node deliberately tracks the engines support floor (24), not latest, so a newer-Node API cannot slip in unnoticed. Nothing in the toolchain catches the violation - with the major bump applied, both typecheck and the full suite stay green, because the pin's whole job is to make those APIs unrepresentable at compile time. Without the rule the same PR kept returning (#334, #336, #340, #374, #481, #906).

nodes.label: Blank issues disabled
nodes.rationale: Every issue must come through a template so the right labels and reproduction context land automatically.

nodes.label: Acceptance criteria field
nodes.rationale: Asks how the requester would verify the feature works, with one-line scenarios preferred; vague acceptance pushes the issue further down the queue. The alternatives-considered field exists to distinguish a missing feature from missing documentation.

nodes.label: Least-privilege workflow permissions (#621)
nodes.rationale: Stated rather than inherited: the repository default is read-only today, but a settings flip would otherwise hand a write token to a job that installs and runs the whole dependency tree.

nodes.label: Fourteen-consecutive-green-nights exit criterion
nodes.rationale: Fourteen rather than a smaller number because the failure is a property of the runner pool, not the code: two calendar weeks spans weekday and weekend pools. Nights count only while the .bun-version pin is unchanged. The first two nights produced no artifact at all because .stress is a dot-directory and upload-artifact defaults include-hidden-files to false — so nothing before that fix can be counted, since the runs happened but their evidence was never kept. Nothing accumulates the streak: a human reads the annotations, which is the same failure that made the quarantine permanent in the first place.

nodes.label: SHA-pinned actions (#585)
nodes.rationale: The actions run in the same job that holds id-token: write, so an action author — or anyone who compromises their account — who repoints a mutable tag executes code next to a credential that can publish actor-ts to npm with provenance. A SHA cannot be repointed; the trailing # vX.Y.Z comment is what keeps Dependabot updating the pin.

nodes.label: Frozen-lockfile install policy
nodes.rationale: An unfrozen install resolves whatever package.json's ranges allow right now, so a required check could pass against a dependency set no lockfile ever recorded and nobody could reproduce. Dependabot does not speak the Bun lockfile format, so its PRs fail here until bun.lock is regenerated — that is the intended signal, and #817 is what removes the manual step.

nodes.label: JUnit test-count parser
nodes.rationale: Bun 1.3.14 stopped printing the trailing summary block under GitHub Actions, so the old console scrape matched nothing — and a `[[ -z $PASS ]] && PASS=0` fallback turned 'the parser found nothing' into a plausible zero and pushed a tests-0 of 0 badge from a green run. Now it reads a contract that does not move between bun releases and treats an unreadable count as an error rather than as zero. Output goes to a FILE, never through a pipe: ~8700 annotation lines through a command-substitution pipe made bun die mid-flush with WriteFailed.

nodes.label: Angular templates always live in a separate .html file
nodes.rationale: Markup and logic are read, reviewed and edited by different motions. An inline template pushes the class off screen, has no HTML tooling, and puts HTML inside a template literal where a stray backtick or ${ surfaces as NG1010 nowhere near the cause — which has happened here twice, both times from a backtick inside an HTML comment. styles may stay inline.
nodes.norm_label: angular templates always live in a separate .html file

nodes.label: Re-measure comparison benchmarks at release time
nodes.rationale: environment.actorTsVersion comes from package.json and the docs tables label their columns with it, so a release that skips re-measuring ships figures attributed to a version that never ran; bump first, then measure, so results carry the new version and a clean commit rather than -dirty. Version labels belong in the docs tables and RESULTS.md, never in README.md (#1322).
nodes.norm_label: re-measure comparison benchmarks at release time

nodes.label: Benchmarks compile + smoke gate
nodes.rationale: The build tsconfig excludes benchmarks/, so nothing else catches an orphaned benchmark; typecheck:bench plus bench:smoke make benchmarks part of the adoption sweep for a breaking change, exactly like tests and examples.

nodes.label: 1:1 bilingual Starlight documentation
nodes.rationale: English docs under docs/src/content/docs/ are mirrored 1:1 under de/; every content change updates BOTH languages, code samples stay identical and prose is translated. The i18n label tracks translation work.

nodes.label: develop / main / features branching model
nodes.rationale: develop is the integration branch and main holds releases only; every unit of work gets a features/ branch, so no change lands on develop without passing through a branch.

nodes.label: Pre-1.0 hard cut for breaking changes
nodes.rationale: No deprecation cycle is required pre-1.0: remove or replace an API directly, flag it BREAKING in the CHANGELOG with a one-line migration note, and update every in-repo caller (examples, tests, docs, benchmarks) in the same change.
nodes.norm_label: pre-1.0 hard cut for breaking changes

nodes.label: check:ui source-hash staleness gate
nodes.rationale: src/devtools/generated/UiAssets.ts is generated but committed, and a stale one is valid TypeScript, so nothing else notices. The check compares a source-hash rather than bundle bytes, because bytes vary with OS and Bun release; review is therefore the only thing that ever looks at the embedded payload, which is why .gitattributes gives the file a plain textual diff.

nodes.label: Commit identity pinning via environment variables
nodes.rationale: Tooling has been observed substituting a work address at commit time, and a wrong author only surfaces afterwards in the log; GIT_AUTHOR_*/GIT_COMMITTER_* outrank both --local config and -c user.email, and the values are read back out of git config so the recipe works unchanged in a fork.
nodes.norm_label: commit identity pinning via environment variables

nodes.label: Conventional Commits policy
nodes.rationale: type(scope): subject with small focused commits, each keeping typecheck + test green so a bisect never lands on a broken tree; the body explains what and why, issues referenced as #NNN.

nodes.label: Coverage floor gate (aggregate + per-module)
nodes.rationale: Two floors from one --coverage run: the aggregate 80% from bun's `All files` row, and src/cluster/ + src/persistence/ at 90% from lcov as sum(LH)/sum(LF) per prefix — a rollup of per-file percentages would average a ten-line barrel against a thousand-line coordinator. Module floors live only in scripts/coverage-gate.mjs, deliberately: an env override in a workflow is a second place the number lives and a way to loosen the gate invisibly.

nodes.label: Coverage ratchet policy
nodes.rationale: A floor may be raised, never lowered silently. The aggregate was 89 until 83b0a4af dropped it to 80 for the worker-thread quarantine, with the reasoning living only in a commit message; both floors are now pinned from below by tests/unit/ci/CoverageGate.test.ts so lowering one means editing that test, in the same commit, on purpose.

nodes.label: Cross-runtime smoke gate
nodes.rationale: tests/smoke/cases/*.mjs run on Bun, Node and Deno. A case must release every handle on every path: a socket abandoned on a timeout keeps Deno's event loop alive and the run hangs after its last green line with no exit code, so the gate stops being a gate (#1196).

nodes.label: Two DevTools UI test runners with disjoint patterns
nodes.rationale: The framework-free half runs under bun test from devtools-ui/tests/*.test.ts; the Angular half runs under Vitest in jsdom from *.ng-spec.ts. The suffix is not a style choice — bun test collects *.spec.ts anywhere in the tree and would try to run specs needing Vitest and a DOM, so renaming them back breaks the root suite (#487).
nodes.norm_label: two devtools ui test runners with disjoint patterns

nodes.label: Nested, un-hoisted DevTools UI toolchain
nodes.rationale: devtools-ui/ is deliberately not a bun workspace — hoisting would put @angular/core in the root node_modules and in Dependabot's view of a manifest that ships two runtime dependencies, and Angular pins a TypeScript the library does not use (#483). typecheck skips the UI half locally and fails hard under CI, which keeps a fresh clone working.

nodes.label: Examples manifest gate
nodes.rationale: Every standalone example is classified in tests/examples/examples.manifest.json as runnable-with-an-output-substring or skipped-with-a-reason, and the runner fails when manifest and tree disagree in either direction. The output assertion is not decoration: `exited 0` is also what a failing example does, so a runnable case without an expect would gate on nothing.

nodes.label: ACTOR_TS_SKIP_FLAKY_MNS quarantine
nodes.rationale: Bun on GitHub's hosted runners cannot respawn functional worker threads after the first worker test, which also starves LeaseMajority's lease arbitration into a false split-brain; three suites are therefore skipped in test.yml, multi-runtime.yml and publish.yml. A local bun test runs them; a green CI check says nothing about them (#538).

nodes.label: Comment on the issue whenever the work changes course
nodes.rationale: The commit message records what was done and why; it is a poor place for what turned out to be wrong on the way there, and it is invisible to anyone reading the issue later. Worth a comment: a stale report, a failed obvious fix, a bound that changed after measuring, a scope move, or a verification step that proved nothing.
nodes.norm_label: comment on the issue whenever the work changes course

nodes.label: Issue-first workflow
nodes.rationale: Check for an existing issue before starting; open one first otherwise, for traceability, using the matching template. Close via `Closes #NNN` in the commit body — GitHub resolves it once the commit reaches develop, the default branch, so there is no release-window in which to reconsider.

nodes.label: Always merge --no-ff, never rebase
nodes.rationale: History stays a true graph; it is never rewritten or flattened, in both directions (features to develop, develop to main).

nodes.label: Agent commits locally, human pushes
nodes.rationale: Nothing is pushed by the agent, so a wrong author or a bad commit is always still fixable by rewinding the branch; the single exception is cutting a release.

nodes.label: Bot-maintained README test/coverage badges
nodes.rationale: A CI workflow pushes the badge numbers directly to develop, measured with the quarantined multi-node suites skipped, so hand-edited figures are overwritten and differ slightly from a local full run.

nodes.label: Pre-1.0 SemVer release strategy
nodes.rationale: Patch is fixes only, minor may break, 1.0.0 is the API-stability commitment; releases are cut on a release/vX.Y.Z branch, tagged vX.Y.Z and published as a normal Latest GitHub Release.

nodes.label: Runtime portability behind src/runtime abstractions
nodes.rationale: Code must run on Bun, Node >= 24 and Deno; runtime-specific primitives (HTTP serve, sockets, workers, SQLite) live behind small abstractions in src/runtime/ and auto-detect at startup.

nodes.label: Repeat-run flake hunting (test:stress)
nodes.rationale: Loops the suite N times and aggregates failures by test identity, splitting flaky from consistently failing. It drops ACTOR_TS_SKIP_FLAKY_MNS from the child environment by default — a harness that inherited it would report a reliable pass rate over exactly the tests known not to be reliable (#290).

nodes.label: typecheck:dev — the caller's-side compile
nodes.rationale: The only gate that sees the library from a caller's side: an exported class narrower than the interface it implements still satisfies `implements`, and an exported type whose properties are all optional is satisfied by nothing. Neither shows up in bun test (which transpiles without checking) or bun run typecheck (which never compiles a call site). Green since #540.

nodes.label: Verification gates before every commit
nodes.rationale: typecheck, typecheck:dev, bun test with a coverage floor, smoke, examples, benchmarks, DevTools UI and security scanning — each gate exists because a distinct class of defect is invisible to all the others.

nodes.label: AI-assisted hobby-project disclaimer
nodes.rationale: Coverage is good but the surface area is enormous and none of it is battle-tested; the badge figures are measured on hosted runners where three multi-node suites are skipped, so the README states that rather than letting the number imply more than it proves.

nodes.label: Kompatibilitäts-Checks (none / backward / sample)
nodes.rationale: Prüft zur Register-Zeit, dass eine neue Version die vorherige noch lesen kann; 'sample' fährt zusätzlich einen Round-Trip dekodieren-upcasten-neu-enkodieren und erwischt latente Upcaster-Bugs vor dem Deploy.

nodes.label: Generated and vendored path exclusions
nodes.rationale: dist, src/devtools/generated, docs/dist, docs/.astro, node_modules and the front-end scaffolding directories are excluded because the fix for an alert there is never an edit to the flagged file. examples/** source stays in scope - it is what a reader copies from, so an injection in it propagates.

nodes.label: Optional peer dependency checklist
nodes.rationale: Thirteen checkboxes naming the optional peers (better-sqlite3, cassandra-driver, ioredis, memjs, @aws-sdk/client-s3, kafkajs, nats, mqtt, amqplib, @grpc/grpc-js, ws, the HTTP backends, @kubernetes/client-node) — reporters check only what their code exercises, because the bug may be in the adapter for that integration.

nodes.label: Pre-filing contact links
nodes.rationale: Three deflection links before the form — the README for scope, the ROADMAP for what is planned and what is explicitly out of scope, and the CHANGELOG because the issue may already be fixed in the latest version.

nodes.label: Exploit walkthrough requirement
nodes.rationale: Attacker capability, input, code path, corrupted or leaked state, realistic worst case. The worked sample is a spoofed cluster hello frame rebinding the peer connection map to an attacker socket.

nodes.label: Severity self-assessment rubric
nodes.rationale: CRITICAL = system-wide compromise possible with a low-skill attacker; HIGH = significant impact, exploitable in the documented closed-group threat model; MEDIUM = requires specific conditions or partial impact; LOW = informational or mitigated by design.

nodes.label: Job-level security-events: write
nodes.rationale: A read-only floor for the file with the one write scope declared on the analyze job alone (#621) - the rule WorkflowHygiene.test.ts enforces, and the reason docs.yml's build job used to hold scopes it never used. Uploading the SARIF is what makes an alert appear; the category keys the upload so a second language could not silently replace this analysis. timeout-minutes: 30 rather than the 6 h default, since a runaway analysis holding a runner for six hours is not a useful failure mode.

nodes.label: broker matrix job
nodes.rationale: fail-fast: false so a single broker regression does not mask the others. The matrix now carries only the display label, the one thing nothing can derive; it is not a second source of truth, because IntegrationBrokerSuites.test.ts fails when matrix and tree disagree in either direction, so a backend added without a leg is a red test rather than a suite that silently never runs.

nodes.label: integration scenarios job
nodes.rationale: The failure path is a relay: a failing scenario exits the controller 1, docker-compose 1 via --exit-code-from controller, the step 1, and the workflow turns red. Container logs are dumped on failure so a flaky scenario is debuggable from the workflow log alone.

nodes.label: bun audit advisory gate (#539)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately bun audit rather than dependency-review-action: GitHub's graph records the unresolved ranges out of package.json and carries no find-my-way entry at all, which is why the only Dependabot alerts this repository ever produced come from the npm lockfiles under examples/. It also runs on a Monday cron, because an advisory is published upstream against a lockfile that did not change, so a push-only gate would not notice. Baselined by --ignore'd IDs listed in SECURITY.md, since an unbaselined gate would land red on its first run and teach everyone to ignore it.

nodes.label: package-health job
nodes.rationale: Each step runs the package.json script rather than repeating the tool invocation, so the flags live in one place and a local `bun run lint:package` checks the same thing. knip-bun rather than knip, because the Node binary exhausts its heap on this module graph. attw runs in the esm-only profile, the honest one, since this package ships no CJS.

nodes.label: Issue label taxonomy
nodes.rationale: priority/severity tiers plus security, i18n, infrastructure, dependencies, production-goal and the standard bug/enhancement/documentation; audit-catalog items carry the [Security] / [Feature] title prefixes.

nodes.label: DevTools dead-letter panel (#553)
nodes.rationale: An undeliverable message throws nothing and logs nothing by default, and that silence is what makes the failure easy to miss. It polls once a second rather than streaming, so DevTools is not on the delivery path of the very failures it watches. The queue being off is said out loud rather than shown as an empty table: 'nothing is broken' and 'nothing is being recorded' are opposite answers an empty table gives identically.

nodes.label: DevTools event-stream panel (#553)
nodes.rationale: Needs EventStream._observe, checked BEFORE the empty-stream early return — an observer placed after it sees nothing on a system nobody else subscribes to, which is exactly the system a developer opens this panel on. The observer installs only while a panel is subscribed, unlike the span tap, because the bus is always live. Events are capped and the panel says how many were dropped: a tail that silently skips is worse than one that admits it.

nodes.label: DevTools send-message action (#553)
nodes.rationale: Every other panel reads; this one writes, so it is off until acknowledged in code. Two switches and only one is a security decision: panels.send hides the view, allowMessageSending grants the capability — and while the acknowledgement is unset the actors.send method is never registered, so a client is told there is no such method rather than being refused by a guard it might argue with. One bound is structural rather than checked, which is why it holds: the body is JSON, so it cannot be a PoisonPill.

nodes.label: One integration-compose driver replaces 34 broker scripts (#559)
nodes.rationale: The list of backends lived in four places at once — both scripts, both aggregate chains and the CI matrix — and missing one meant the suite simply never ran, silently. The driver discovers suites from the tree; IntegrationBrokerSuites.test.ts fails when matrix and tree disagree in either direction and pins the compose argument vectors, --exit-code-from runner included, since without it a failing scenario inside the container would leave every broker suite green forever.
nodes.norm_label: one integration-compose driver replaces 34 broker scripts (#559)

nodes.label: actor-ts framework
nodes.rationale: A batteries-included actor-model runtime for TypeScript running natively on Bun, Node.js and Deno; Apache 2.0, pre-1.0, experimental.

nodes.label: Actors and supervision
nodes.rationale: Single-threaded per-mailbox processing, lifecycle hooks, stash, timers, become/unbecome and supervision (restart / resume / stop / escalate).

nodes.label: Ask pattern (request/response)
nodes.rationale: tell is fire-and-forget; ref.ask<Reply>(msg) spawns a one-shot reply actor, wires it as both replyTo and context.sender, and resolves the promise when the target replies.

nodes.label: Pluggable cache
nodes.rationale: One Cache interface over in-memory, Redis and Memcached backends.

nodes.label: Cluster membership and failure detection
nodes.rationale: Gossip membership, phi-accrual failure detection, split-brain resolvers, weakly-up, and multiple transports (TCP, MessageChannel, in-memory).

nodes.label: Cluster sharding
nodes.rationale: The framework routes per-entity messages to the owning node and migrates entities as nodes come and go; ShardKey declares identity on the actor class so neither the type name nor the entity-id extractor is repeated at the call site.

nodes.label: Cluster singleton
nodes.rationale: One node hosts it, the rest hold a forwarding ref, and failover moves it without callers changing anything; start() is get-or-create so calling it from several modules is safe.

nodes.label: Dead letters and the dead-letter queue
nodes.rationale: Every undeliverable message is published on the event stream; opting in to system.deadLetterQueue also keeps them in a bounded ring or a journal-backed one, replayable by id with a replay cap so a poison message cannot be retried into an ever-growing queue.
nodes.norm_label: dead letters and the dead-letter queue

nodes.label: DevTools embedded web UI
nodes.rationale: Reads only by default — sending a message into the system is a separate, off-by-default acknowledgement. Angular and ECharts are build-time only so neither appears in the package's dependencies and the served page loads nothing over the network; loopback-only and unauthenticated by default, and it refuses a routable bind without a gate.

nodes.label: Distributed Data (CRDTs)
nodes.rationale: Nine CRDTs (counters, registers, sets, maps) with a durable-storage backend, quorum reads/writes and automatic gossip.

nodes.label: Message-broker integrations
nodes.rationale: A single BrokerActor base with Kafka, MQTT, AMQP, NATS, Redis-Streams, gRPC, SSE, raw TCP/UDP and IMAP/SMTP integrations; reconnect-with-backoff, outbound buffer and subscriber fan-out are baked into the base rather than repeated per adapter.

nodes.label: Multi-sink logging
nodes.rationale: One record fans out to several destinations at once, each with its own minimum level, bounded queues, batched delivery and a flush on shutdown; every integration is dependency-free (Sentry is a passthrough to your own SDK) and a transform hook redacts once, before fan-out.

nodes.label: Object storage with compression and encryption
nodes.rationale: S3 / MinIO / R2 / filesystem with optional gzip or zstd compression and client-side AES-256-GCM encryption, using per-tenant subkeys derived via HKDF.
nodes.norm_label: object storage with compression and encryption

nodes.label: Observability — metrics, tracing, management endpoints
nodes.rationale: Prometheus exporter, OTel tracing, management HTTP endpoints (/health, /ready, /cluster/members, /sharding/regions) and out-of-the-box stock metrics.

nodes.label: Persistence — event sourcing and durable state
nodes.rationale: PersistentActor, DurableState, snapshots, projections with a per-projection handler-failure strategy, persistence-query and replicated event sourcing, over journals for in-memory, SQLite, libSQL/Turso, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, MS SQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cloudflare D1 and Cassandra/ScyllaDB.
nodes.norm_label: persistence — event sourcing and durable state

nodes.label: TestKit
nodes.rationale: TestProbe, ManualScheduler and MultiNodeSpec for deterministic tests including cluster scenarios.

nodes.label: Bigger threads (L/XL, own design phase)
nodes.rationale: A Streams DSL subset (#147) that is a deliberate ~5% subset rather than a replacement for the full Source/Flow/Sink composition DSL (#54), plus a WASM/edge subpackage (#209), distributed transactions (#171) and multi-DC clustering (#149).

nodes.label: Core-only root export (#414)
nodes.rationale: One barrel re-exporting every subsystem shipped the testkit in the production entry (#685) and made `import { ActorSystem }` pay for whatever any subsystem pulled in eagerly (#1005); eighteen subsystems now get their own entry, and the smoke suite loads every declared entry on all three runtimes.

nodes.label: Feature-parity quick wins
nodes.rationale: Inbox for non-actor callers (#181), DeathWatch.watchWith (#159), and the ShardCommand types (#151).

nodes.label: 50-oldest bug/security wave
nodes.rationale: 42 of the 50 oldest open defects resolved. Two of the fifty were not defects at all, five entries are BREAKING, and independent verification found five regressions the wave itself introduced — the worst being #588's own fix, where a new inbound-connection cap armed no handshake deadline, so 1024 silent sockets saturated it and refused every real peer: a defence that became the attack.

nodes.label: Logging sink architecture (#1150)
nodes.rationale: The logger wrote to exactly one place; it now fans one record out to as many destinations as configured, each dependency-free, with nothing about the existing surface changed — a system whose config nobody edited logs exactly what it logged yesterday.

nodes.label: Novel differentiators
nodes.rationale: Deterministic simulation testing with seeded virtual-time replay (#200), LLM agents as supervised durable actors (epic #421) and per-entity chaos injection (#206) — each gets its own plan slot.

nodes.label: Planned production features
nodes.rationale: Persistent reminders (#168), stateless workers (#170), saga / process-manager with compensations (#179) and placement strategies (#169).

nodes.label: v0.16.0 — entry points, logging and old defects
nodes.rationale: The largest window so far at 181 commits, landing three things together plus a packaging-surface cleanup: no more dangling source maps (#1007), NodeNext resolution (#1008), and @types/node no longer a silent requirement for reading the public API (#1006).
nodes.norm_label: v0.16.0 — entry points, logging and old defects

nodes.label: Wave 3 residuals (#1211–#1228)
nodes.rationale: Eighteen tracked residuals, each a defect the wave measured rather than inferred and deliberately did not fold in. Four of them are behaviour the wave shipped that no test binds — found by reverting one line at a time, not by reading — and they are the honest measure of what a green suite did not prove.

nodes.label: CodeQL analysis configuration
nodes.rationale: Named actor-ts, referenced by codeql.yml through config-file:; carries the path exclusions and the query-suite decision (#539).

nodes.label: Feature request issue template
nodes.rationale: Titled [Feature], labelled enhancement + priority: low. States up front that this is a hobby project where features land when a concrete need surfaces, and that pull requests are not accepted — well-shaped issues are how features get prioritised.

nodes.label: Security finding issue template
nodes.rationale: Defaults to bug + security + severity: medium + priority: high; a maintainer adjusts the severity label after triage.

nodes.label: codeql workflow
nodes.rationale: Until it landed, code-scanning answered 404 no analysis found - the repository had never been analysed once (#539). Everything here parses somebody else's bytes: cluster wire frames, HOCON, HTTP requests and WebSocket payloads, persisted snapshots - exactly the input surface CodeQL's default queries are written for, and no other gate looks for a taint path. Runs on PRs so a finding attaches to the change that introduced it, on long-lived branches so the baseline stays current, and weekly because CodeQL ships new queries and a file clean in March can be flagged in June untouched. javascript-typescript is one language covering .ts/.mts/.mjs/.js; build-mode: none extracts from source, so no dependency install.

nodes.label: integration-brokers workflow
nodes.rationale: Seventeen live-broker suites in Docker, matrix-parallel so wall clock equals the slowest suite rather than the sum. Nightly at 03:30 UTC, offset from integration.yml's 03:00 so the two do not fight for the same runner pool; the nightly catches upstream-image regressions, since each suite tracks :latest for its broker on purpose.

nodes.label: integration workflow (real-network multi-node)
nodes.rationale: Runs the exact same command that works locally with Docker Desktop; all compose and scenario logic lives in tests/integration/ so the file is intentionally thin and there is no CI-only drift. Nightly at 03:00 UTC catches transport-level flakes that fast PR runs would not show.

nodes.label: package-health workflow
nodes.rationale: Checks the shape of what gets published, which the test suite cannot see (#416): publint for the exports map, attw for declarations that resolve for the author but not a consumer, knip for unreachable modules and undeclared imports. All three failure modes are invisible locally and only bite after npm publish.

nodes.label: Keep a Changelog record
nodes.rationale: Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 plus SemVer, with an [Unreleased] section carrying Added/Changed/Fixed/Removed/Security; twenty released versions from 0.1.0 (2026-04-27) to 0.16.0 (2026-08-15). Every minor is potentially breaking because the project is pre-1.0.

nodes.label: Quick start
nodes.rationale: bun add / npm install / npm: specifier for Deno, then a Greeter actor in a dozen lines; the same file runs unchanged on all three runtimes.

nodes.label: Roadmap status
nodes.rationale: A sketch, not a contract — nothing in it is committed work; README names the current scope and CHANGELOG names what landed.

nodes.label: Default query suite, not security-extended
nodes.rationale: No queries: key on purpose. A first analysis of a codebase this size produces an alert set of unknown volume, and every alert must be fixed or dismissed with a recorded reason before the baseline means anything; a wider suite makes that first triage larger without making it more valuable. Widen once the default baseline is clean, not before.

nodes.label: Security-relevance flag on the bug template
nodes.rationale: Points reporters at the [Security] template, which asks for the exploit walkthrough, affected files and disclosure status; either way a maintainer adds the security and severity: labels, because GitHub Forms cannot add them conditionally.
nodes.norm_label: security-relevance flag on the bug template

nodes.label: Pre-disclosure routing to SECURITY.md
nodes.rationale: Undisclosed findings go privately through the repository Security tab per SECURITY.md; the public form is for audit follow-ups and defense-in-depth items outside the responsible-disclosure window.

nodes.label: Deliberately no paths filter
nodes.rationale: Unlike build.yml and package-health.yml. Code scanning treats the newest analysis of a branch as the truth about that branch, so skipping a push would leave the alert set describing a commit that is no longer there.

nodes.label: Optional peer dependency declaration policy
nodes.rationale: Lazy import() with a clear install error, declared in peerDependencies + peerDependenciesMeta.optional, then a SECOND time in exactly one of root devDependencies (justified by a test importing the real module and asserting the shape the adapter destructures) or tests/integration/brokers/package.json. A peer in neither context is the defect (#676): the structural stub standing in for its types is checked against nothing and no gate notices. Three silent traps: bun add no-ops on an existing optional peer, a package shipping no types needs its @types/*, and a root devDependency enters bun audit's surface.

nodes.label: production-goal label as a gate
nodes.rationale: It is a gate, not a batch marker, so it belongs on any issue that blocks or defines the path to production regardless of which review found it — filtering on it should answer 'what is still between us and running this for real', which is why it is applied to existing issues rather than duplicating them.

nodes.label: Security-first posture
nodes.rationale: Cap untrusted input (WebSocket / wire-frame size limits), never trust client-supplied integrity fields, use crypto-grade randomness for wire identifiers; a security-relevant change gets a Security CHANGELOG entry and a severity: label.

nodes.label: CI-side security scanning with one local half
nodes.rationale: lint:audit reads bun.lock deliberately: GitHub's dependency graph resolves only the ranges in package.json, so Dependabot and dependency-review-action are blind to the shipped closure. Suppressed advisory IDs live in the script AND in SECURITY.md, with tests/unit/ci/SecurityPolicy.test.ts failing if the two sets differ.
nodes.norm_label: ci-side security scanning with one local half

nodes.label: Tagged JSON tree wire format
nodes.rationale: The same format the persistence stores write, so Date, Map, Set, bigint, Uint8Array, RegExp, URL and Error arrive as real instances (#450). Functions and symbols are refused with an error log naming the peer rather than silently stripped, so a callback in a message stops being invisible data loss; class identity is lost and only the tag string travels. A registered custom serializer changes none of this - the cluster wire never consults the registry.

nodes.label: Pull requests are not accepted
nodes.rationale: The issue tracker is the contribution channel: well-shaped issues are accepted, patches are not.

nodes.label: Explicitly out of scope
nodes.rationale: Auto-magic cache invalidation by tag or pattern is a known bug-source, so invalidation stays explicit via cache.delete; and backwards-compatibility guarantees of any kind are out, because the project is pre-1.0.

nodes.label: Supported versions (latest 0.x.y only)
nodes.rationale: Pre-1.0 with no maintenance branches: fixes land on develop and ship in the next release, nothing is backported.

nodes.label: Ask
nodes.rationale: Request/Response ueber Actors — ref.ask(message, timeout) gibt ein Promise fuer die Antwort zurueck.

nodes.label: Broadcast
nodes.rationale: Eine Router-Strategie oder ein Broadcast<T>-Wrapper, der eine Nachricht an jeden Routee sendet.

nodes.label: DeadLetter
nodes.rationale: Der synthetische Empfaenger fuer Nachrichten ohne lebendes Ziel.

nodes.label: randomId
nodes.rationale: Die richtige Wahl beim Benennen eines Aktors: ein Aktorname landet in einem Pfad, und ein Pfad ist eine Adresse — auf dem Cluster-Wire kann alles, was einen Pfad erzeugen kann, auch dorthin senden. Ein Zaehler macht die Adresse erratbar. randomId(12) sind ~48 Bit: unerratbar unter den Namen, die ein Prozess gleichzeitig haelt.

nodes.label: randomUuid
nodes.rationale: 122 Zufallsbits am anderen Ende der Entropie-Skala als randomId — so viel braucht ein Bezeichner, der in einem anderen Prozess, auf einer anderen Maschine, Jahre spaeter und ohne Abstimmung erzeugten unterscheidbar bleiben muss. Nicht durch randomHex(32) mit Bindestrichen ersetzen: sechs der 128 Bit sind Versions- und Variantenfeld nach RFC 9562.

nodes.label: Die fuenf Routing-Strategien
nodes.rationale: round-robin (Default), random, broadcast, smallest-mailbox und cluster-only consistent-hashing. Alle fuenf sind One-Shot: der Router waehlt, leitet weiter, fertig — die Antwort ist Sache des Routees und des urspruenglichen Senders.

nodes.label: Stop-Verhalten im Vergleich
nodes.rationale: Ein Pool-Router faltet sich beim System-Shutdown sauber zusammen; ein Group-Router hinterlaesst Routees auf anderen Nodes, die nicht wissen, dass dieser Aufrufer weg ist — dafuer gibt es Coordinated Shutdown.

nodes.label: Broadcast-Router plus Reply-to-Ref
nodes.rationale: Die Broadcast-Strategie faechert die ROHE Nachricht aus, inklusive jeder Reply-to-Ref darin: jeder Routee antwortet, der Aufrufer sieht N Responses. Manchmal gewollt (replizierte Reads mit Quorum), meist ein Bug.

nodes.label: Broadcast<T>-Wrapper
nodes.rationale: Wickelt eine Payload; der Router packt sie aus, ignoriert die Strategie und sendet die innere Nachricht an JEDEN Routee — fuer gelegentliche Fan-Out-Nachrichten, die nicht ins Routine-Routing passen.

nodes.label: Router-Factories
nodes.rationale: Fuenf One-Shot-Factories (roundRobin, random, broadcast, smallestMailbox, custom) geben eine ActorFactory<TMessage | Broadcast<TMessage>> zurueck, die wie jeder andere Actor gespawnt wird; der Typ-Parameter des Routees fliesst durch.

nodes.label: Ein gestoppter Routee bleibt im Pool
nodes.rationale: Der Router entfernt eine tote Ref nie: Round-Robin teilt ihr weiterhin etwa jede N-te Nachricht zu, die bis zum Neustart des ganzen Routers in Dead Letters landet. Fuer selbstheilende Pools den Routee in eine bei Stop restartende Strategie oder den ganzen Pool in einen BackoffSupervisor wickeln.
nodes.norm_label: ein gestoppter routee bleibt im pool

nodes.label: RouterActor
nodes.rationale: Zur Spawn-Zeit erstellt die Runtime eine RouterActor-Instanz am angegebenen Pfad, spawnt in preStart size Kinder namens routee-1..N und watcht jedes.

nodes.label: AggregateError als einziger Fehlertyp
nodes.rationale: Jeder Fehlschlag rejected mit AggregateError; errors haelt einen Fehler pro Routee in Scatter-Reihenfolge und die message benennt die Ursache (niemand rechtzeitig, alle fehlgeschlagen, keine Routees mehr, Router gestoppt). Ein Aufrufer, der auf den Fehlertyp verzweigen muesste, erfuehre nichts, was das errors-Array nicht schon traegt.

nodes.label: Der Antwort-Vertrag
nodes.rationale: Der Router braucht ein Ziel fuer die gewinnende Antwort: ask oder tell mit explizitem Sender. Ein nacktes tell streut gar nichts, verwirft die Nachricht und loggt eine Warnung — es WIRFT nicht, denn ein Wurf liesse den Router ueber die Supervision fehlschlagen und der Restart risse jeden anderen laufenden Scatter mit. Die Antwort wird dem Routee zugeschrieben, der sie produziert hat, was fuer Hedged Reads beantwortet, welche Replica gewonnen hat.

nodes.label: Scatter/Gather-Metriken
nodes.rationale: router_scatter_gather_resolved_total (Counter, Label outcome: first | timeout | all-failed | stopped | no-reply-target) und router_scatter_gather_latency_seconds (Histogram ueber die Latenz des GEWINNERS). timeout und all-failed sind getrennt, weil das eine 'zu langsam fuers Budget' und das andere 'kaputt' heisst. Keine der Familien traegt einen Router-Pfad, mehrere Router aggregieren also.

nodes.label: Broadcast-Strategie
nodes.rationale: Gibt alle Routees zurueck. N-Wege-Fan-Out mit N-Wege-ARBEIT — das ist kein Load-Balancing, jeder Routee tut dieselbe Arbeit und sieht die volle Nachrichten-Last. Fuer Cache-Invalidierung, periodischen Refresh, Heartbeat.

nodes.label: Smallest-Mailbox im Cluster (gecachte Tiefen)
nodes.rationale: Eine entfernte Mailbox ist von hier nicht lesbar, und pro Nachricht zu fragen wuerde die gesamte Router-Mailbox hinter einen Netzwerk-Roundtrip parken. Also wird die Tiefe jedes Nodes gecacht und auf einem Hintergrund-Tick aufgefrischt; die Entscheidung liest den Cache synchron. Zwei Konsequenzen: die Tiefe kann ein Refresh-Intervall alt sein, und ein Node ohne Meldung wird uebersprungen statt als untaetig angenommen.

nodes.label: Eigene Strategien
nodes.rationale: Eine eigene Strategie sieht nur die Routee-Refs und den Message-Index. Die Mailbox-Tiefe ist runtime-interner Zustand und liegt bewusst NICHT auf ActorRef — eine last-bewusste Eigenbau-Strategie braeuchte jeden Routee, der seine Last an einen gemeinsamen Gauge meldet. Fuer die kuerzeste Queue das eingebaute smallestMailbox nehmen, das die Tiefe von innerhalb des Frameworks liest.

nodes.label: Random
nodes.rationale: Gleichverteilt zufaellig; gleiche statistische Verteilung wie Round-Robin auf lange Sicht, aber kein geteilter Zustand und resilienter gegen synchronisierte Sender. Nicht deterministisch in Tests — dafuer einen seedbaren RNG in einer eigenen Strategie.

nodes.label: Round-Robin
nodes.rationale: Zykelt per Modulo durch die Routee-Liste. Gleichmaessig nach Nachrichten-COUNT, nicht nach Kosten; deterministisch und inspizierbar. Richtiger Default fuer homogene Workloads; kein Load-Balancing nach Arbeitskosten und keine Stickiness-Garantie.

nodes.label: Smallest-Mailbox
nodes.rationale: Die einzige eingebaute Strategie, die auf den tatsaechlichen Rueckstau reagiert: sie waehlt den flachsten Routee, korrigiert sich nach einem Stall ohne Timer oder Health-Check und rotiert bei Gleichstand ueber den messageIndex. Bezahlt mit einer Tiefenabfrage pro Routee pro Nachricht (O(N)-Scan gegen ein Modulo), kennt nur Anzahl statt Kosten und uebt keine Backpressure aus.

nodes.label: Mailbox (glossary)
nodes.rationale: The per-actor message queue; unbounded FIFO by default, boundable per actor, or replaceable with a priority mailbox.

nodes.label: Pool (glossary)
nodes.rationale: A router that creates its routees from an actor class or factory.

nodes.label: Routee (glossary)
nodes.rationale: An actor that receives messages routed by a Router.

nodes.label: Router (glossary)
nodes.rationale: An actor that forwards each message to one (or all) of its routees per a strategy.

nodes.label: ExistsPredicate
nodes.source_location: ### Drawing until you get a free one
nodes.rationale: The optional collision check all four random helpers take, where true means 'taken, draw again'. It is named exists and inverted that way because the callback IS the while condition of the do/while loop it replaces - an accept-predicate would read as that loop's negation and put a ! on every Map- or Set-backed call site. After 1000 draws it throws rather than looping forever, because a call that never returns is the worse failure.

nodes.label: randomString / randomHex / randomId / randomUuid
nodes.rationale: The first three draw from globalThis.crypto and correct the modulo bias a plain byte % alphabet.length introduces. randomId is the one for naming an actor, because an actor name ends up in a path and a path is an address - a counter makes that address guessable, which is why anonymous actors and ask reply refs are named from here. randomHex exists separately because W3C trace-context mandates its alphabet. randomUuid's 122 random bits are what it takes to stay distinct from an id minted in another process years later.

nodes.label: RingBuffer<T>
nodes.rationale: A FIFO queue whose removal from the front is O(1). It exists because Array.prototype.shift() reindexes every element still queued, so taking one item costs more the deeper the queue - invisible at ten, expensive at a hundred thousand, which is what a mailbox becomes when it falls behind its producers. Four operations and nothing else, deliberately: every extra operation is another index-wrapping edge case in a type on the message path of every actor. drain() releases the backing store so a queue that grew to a million gives the memory back.

nodes.label: ClusterRouter form
nodes.rationale: Across cluster nodes; routees are derived from up-members plus a routee path rather than created.

nodes.label: The five routing strategies
nodes.rationale: round-robin, random, broadcast, smallest-mailbox and cluster-only consistent-hashing. All five are one-shot: the router picks, forwards and is done, with the reply between routee and original sender.

nodes.label: Local Router form
nodes.rationale: One node, one actor system; routees are children of the router created at spawn time from the same actor.

nodes.label: Routing overview
nodes.rationale: A router is an actor whose only job is to forward each incoming message to one or more routees. You spawn it once, N workers sit behind it, and senders tell the router without knowing how many routees exist.

nodes.label: Pool vs group
nodes.rationale: Two ways a router acquires routees, encoding very different lifecycle relationships. The local Router is always a pool; ClusterRouter is always a group.

nodes.label: Broadcast<T> message wrapper
nodes.rationale: Wraps a payload; the router unwraps it, ignores the strategy and sends the inner message to every routee. For occasional fan-out (cache invalidation, schema-update notifications) that does not fit the routine pattern. Note it fans out the RAW message including any reply-to ref, so the caller sees N replies.

nodes.label: Per-routee ActorOptions
nodes.rationale: withSupervisorStrategy, withDispatcher and the rest apply to routees individually via the routee options argument.

nodes.label: Router (local pool router)
nodes.rationale: Routees are children of the router actor, created when it is spawned and supervised by it. Five one-shot factories - roundRobin, random, broadcast, smallestMailbox, custom - each returning an ActorFactory you spawn like any other actor, with the routee's type parameter flowing through.

nodes.label: Router.custom
nodes.rationale: Takes a RoutingStrategy of your own; an empty iterable means drop this message, silently and with no dead-letter routing.

nodes.label: What happens at spawn time
nodes.rationale: One RouterActor is created at the path you gave; its preStart spawns `size` children named routee-1..N and watches each so it can react if one stops.

nodes.label: RoutingStrategy (local)
nodes.rationale: (routees, state) => Iterable<ActorRef> - one ref for single-target routing, several for fan-out, none to drop.

nodes.label: Router.smallestMailbox
nodes.rationale: Each message goes to the routee with the shortest queue. Three things before switching the default: it costs a depth read per routee per message against round-robin's one modulo, ties rotate so an idle pool does not pin routee-1, and the strategy never refuses to route - what happens to a message that does not fit is the mailbox's own overflow policy. Local only, because mailbox depth is in-process state.

nodes.label: Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted
nodes.rationale: Sends every message to all routees and answers the caller with the first reply; the losers keep running and their replies are discarded. This is the hedged-request pattern: it does not increase throughput, it lowers the tail - N routees each do the whole job, so you pay N times the work for the minimum of N latencies. It pays only when the slow tail is much slower than the median, and it is for idempotent READS: there is no cancel message, so N-fold work means N side effects.

nodes.label: ScatterGatherOptions
nodes.rationale: A builder or a plain { timeoutMs } object, both validated at the Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted(...) call so the stack still points at the caller.

nodes.label: Scatter/gather metrics
nodes.rationale: router_scatter_gather_resolved_total (labelled first / timeout / all-failed / stopped / no-reply-target) and a latency histogram observing the WINNER's latency. timeout and all-failed are split because they call for different responses - too slow versus broken. Neither carries a router path, so several routers in one system aggregate and the log's actor path is what tells them apart.

nodes.label: RoutingStrategy
nodes.rationale: (routees, state) => Iterable<ActorRef>, where state carries only the monotonic message index. The local router ships four implementations plus a custom slot; the cluster router has a counterpart for each and adds consistent-hashing.

nodes.label: Hinweis 'Kein Scatter-Gather'
nodes.rationale: Ein Aside auf dieser Seite behauptet, actor-ts liefere keinen Scatter-Gather-Router aus und man muesse ihn selbst bauen — was der Seite Scatter/Gather widerspricht, die Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted als ausgelieferte sechste Factory dokumentiert. Vermutlich veralteter Text.

nodes.label: Wann zu einem Router greifen
nodes.rationale: Vier Muster: CPU-lastige Arbeit parallelisieren ohne das Ordering INNERHALB eines Routees zu brechen; Last ueber role-gefilterte Nodes verteilen; Arbeit per Consistent-Hashing deterministisch an einen Routee pinnen; und N Routees um dieselbe Antwort rennen lassen — letzteres zielt auf Tail-Latenz, nicht auf Durchsatz.

nodes.label: size = 0 ist ein Bug
nodes.rationale: Ein Pool mit null Routees gibt ein leeres Iterable zurueck, jedes tell wird still verworfen — kein Dead-Letter-Routing. Das Framework validiert size > 0 nicht; die Verantwortung liegt beim Aufrufer.

nodes.label: Hedged-Request-Pattern
nodes.rationale: Erhoeht nicht den Durchsatz, sondern senkt den TAIL: N Routees machen jeweils die ganze Arbeit, man zahlt das N-Fache und bekommt das MINIMUM aus N Latenzen. Lohnt nur, wenn der langsame Tail deutlich langsamer ist als der Median — redundante Replica-Reads, Multi-Source-Lookup, spekulative Ausfuehrung. Sonst schlicht N-fache Verschwendung.

nodes.label: instanceof traegt nur in-process
nodes.rationale: AggregateError uebersteht die Cluster-Leitung samt intaktem errors-Array (#450), aber seine Mitglieder behalten ihre Klassen nicht: ein AskTimeoutError kommt als einfacher Error an, dessen name weiterhin AskTimeoutError ist. Ueber Knotengrenzen hinweg also den Namen vergleichen, nicht instanceof.

nodes.label: Fan-Out ohne await im Handler
nodes.rationale: Die Runtime awaitet den Handler eines Actors, bevor sie die naechste Nachricht entnimmt — ein async onReceive um Promise.any wuerde die gesamte Router-Mailbox fuer die Dauer eines Scatters parken, ein einziger haengender Routee hielte jeden anderen Aufrufer das volle timeoutMs auf, und gleichzeitige Asks liefen nacheinander. So wie es geschrieben ist, ueberlappen sich Hunderte Scatters frei.

nodes.label: postStop laesst offene Scatters fehlschlagen
nodes.rationale: Statt den Aufrufer erst beim Ask-Timeout merken zu lassen, dass der Router weg ist. Die Routees sind zu dem Zeitpunkt schon gestoppt, ihre Antworten koennen nicht mehr ankommen; timeoutMs abzuwarten machte den Shutdown nur so langsam wie die laengste konfigurierte Deadline. Ein Restart macht dasselbe, weil preRestart auf postStop faellt.

nodes.label: Der Timeout-Abstand ist der Punkt
nodes.rationale: Default 4500 knapp unter den 5000 von ActorRef.ask: der Router kann erst berichten, WELCHE Routees gescheitert sind, wenn seine eigene Deadline verstrichen ist und er deren Fehler eingesammelt hat. Waere sein Budget so gross wie das des Aufrufers, haette dessen ask laengst mit AskTimeoutError aufgegeben — man bekaeme sein eigenes Timeout statt des AggregateError, fuer den es diesen Router gibt.

nodes.label: Verlierende Antworten landen nicht in Dead Letters
nodes.rationale: Der Router fragt per ask, eine verlierende Antwort ist also an die One-Shot-Reply-Ref des Routers adressiert. Diese Ref ist kein Actor; einmal gesettled verwirft sie still. Nichts taucht in Dead Letters auf und keine Metrik zaehlt es — wer sehen muss, wie oft ein Routee verliert, instrumentiert den Routee.
nodes.norm_label: verlierende antworten landen nicht in dead letters

nodes.label: Verlierende Routees werden nicht abgebrochen
nodes.rationale: Es gibt keine Cancel-Nachricht: ein Routee, der das Rennen verliert, laeuft zu Ende und antwortet auf eine laengst verworfene Reply-Ref. N-fach bedeutet damit auch N Seiteneffekte — das Pattern ist fuer IDEMPOTENTE READS, nicht fuer Writes.

nodes.label: Was als Tiefe zaehlt
nodes.rationale: Zwei Faelle ohne brauchbare Queue-Laenge, bewusst gegensaetzlich behandelt. Ein GESTOPPTER Routee wird nie gewaehlt: seine Mailbox ist dauerhaft leer, weil eine terminierte Zelle direkt an Dead Letters zustellt — als blosse Zahl waere er das attraktivste Mitglied, bis der Router den Tod bemerkt, und unter Last ist dieses Fenster so tief wie die Router-Queue. Ein Routee mit UNLESBARER Tiefe zaehlt als leer statt uebersprungen zu werden, denn Ueberspringen wuerde ihn aushungern, solange irgendein lokaler Routee Rueckstau hat; der Balance-Fehler korrigiert sich, das Aushungern taete das nicht.

nodes.label: Routers and supervision
nodes.rationale: The router is a regular actor with its own supervisor strategy that watches each routee. A restarted routee re-joins at the same path and messages routed during the restart window stay in its suspended mailbox. But a routee configured to STOP on failure leaves a dead ref in the pool - round-robin keeps handing that slot 1-in-N messages that land in dead letters until the whole router restarts.

nodes.label: When to reach for a router
nodes.source_location: ## When to reach for a router
nodes.rationale: Four patterns: parallelize CPU-heavy work past one actor's one-at-a-time guarantee, spread load across nodes by role, pin work to a routee deterministically for per-key state, and race N routees for the same answer - the last being a tail-latency goal rather than a throughput one.
nodes.norm_label: when to reach for a router

nodes.label: Cluster-aware pool routers are not exposed
nodes.rationale: Other toolkits have a cluster-pool that spawns its own routees across nodes; actor-ts does not - the cluster router is always group-shaped. The equivalent is a per-node deployment actor spawning local routees plus a ClusterRouter targeting them by path.
nodes.norm_label: cluster-aware pool routers are not exposed

nodes.label: Group router (cluster only)
nodes.rationale: The router finds routees rather than creating them, so lifecycle is independent and sizing follows topology - add a node and it is picked up with no restart. The costs: you must spawn the routees on every node, an empty pool drops messages into dead letters with a warning, and supervision is per-node with the router having no authority. Right shape for fixed-name workers across a cluster.

nodes.label: Pool router
nodes.rationale: The router owns its routees as children, so lifecycle is coupled (stop the router and all routees stop, no orphans), supervision is straightforward and a crashed routee is restarted. The costs: routees are stateless from the router's perspective, size is fixed at spawn time, and their names are auto-generated routee-1..N. Right shape for homogeneous worker pools.

nodes.label: Stopping behavior compared
nodes.rationale: The asymmetry matters for graceful shutdown: a pool router folds cleanly when the system terminates, while a group router leaves behind routees on other nodes that do not know this caller is gone.

nodes.label: Three questions to decide between them
nodes.source_location: ## Three concrete questions to decide between them
nodes.rationale: Do the routees hold per-instance state that matters, does the pool size need to change at runtime, and should stopping the router cascade-stop the routees. If two of three point one way that is the model; if they conflict, the mismatch is telling you something about how the routees should relate to the router.
nodes.norm_label: three questions to decide between them

nodes.label: The original sender is preserved through the router
nodes.rationale: this.sender inside a routee is the original caller, not the router, by design - the routee should be indistinguishable from a non-routed actor.
nodes.norm_label: the original sender is preserved through the router

nodes.label: size = 0 is a bug
nodes.rationale: A zero-routee pool returns an empty iterable from the strategy, so every tell is dropped silently with no dead-letter routing. The framework does not validate size > 0 - the docs say it should, and until then the responsibility is the caller's.

nodes.label: Stopping the pool
nodes.rationale: Stopping the router cascade-stops every routee. When a single routee stops, the router watches it and does nothing by default - its ref stays in the pool and round-robin keeps handing it roughly 1-in-N messages, which land in dead letters until the whole router restarts. Self-healing needs a restart-on-stop supervisor strategy or a BackoffSupervisor around the pool.

nodes.label: Losing routees are not cancelled
nodes.source_location: ## What it buys, and what it costs
nodes.rationale: A routee that loses the race runs to completion and answers into a reply ref that has already been discarded.

nodes.label: The fan-out is not awaited in the handler
nodes.rationale: The runtime awaits an actor's handler before dequeuing the next message, so an async onReceive around Promise.any would park the router's whole mailbox for the duration of one scatter - a single stalled routee would hold up every other caller for the full timeoutMs and concurrent asks would serialize. As written, hundreds of scatters overlap freely.
nodes.norm_label: the fan-out is not awaited in the handler

nodes.label: postStop fails every open scatter
nodes.rationale: Rather than leaving the caller to discover the router is gone when the ask eventually times out. The routees are already stopped so their replies cannot arrive, and waiting out timeoutMs would make shutdown as slow as the longest configured deadline. A restart does the same, since preRestart defaults to postStop.

nodes.label: The reply contract
nodes.rationale: The router must intercept routee replies to pick a winner, so it needs a reply target: ask, or tell with an explicit sender. A bare tell has none, so nothing is scattered, the message is dropped and the router logs a warning rather than throwing - a throw would fail the router through supervision and the restart would take every other in-flight scatter down with it. The winning reply is attributed to the routee that produced it, which for hedged reads answers 'which replica won'.

nodes.label: withTimeoutMs (default 4500)
nodes.rationale: The deadline for one whole scatter, applied as the timeout on each routee's ask. The default sits just under ActorRef.ask's 5000 deliberately: the router can only report which routees failed after its own deadline passes, so a matching budget would leave the caller already timed out with an AskTimeoutError instead of the AggregateError this router exists to produce. In-flight routee asks are not cancelled when a scatter ends early.

nodes.label: Broadcast strategy
nodes.rationale: N-way fan-out with N-way work: cache invalidation, periodic refresh, heartbeats. It does not parallelize work - every routee does the same work - and makes no sense for request/response, where the caller sees N replies. For occasional fan-out, keep the router non-broadcast and wrap the message in Broadcast<T>.

nodes.label: Cluster smallest-mailbox on cached depths
nodes.rationale: A remote routee's mailbox is not readable from here and asking per message would park the router's whole mailbox behind a network round-trip, so each node's depth is cached and refreshed on a background tick while routing reads the cache synchronously. Consequences: a depth can be one refresh interval stale so a node may be chosen just after filling up, and a node that has not reported is skipped rather than assumed idle.

nodes.label: Custom strategies
nodes.rationale: A custom strategy sees only the routee refs and the message index and must carry any other state in a closure. Notably it cannot reach mailbox depth: that is runtime-internal state and deliberately not on ActorRef, so a load-aware strategy of your own would need routees reporting into a shared gauge - which is why the built-in smallestMailbox reads it from inside the framework where the state legitimately lives.

nodes.label: Aside claiming actor-ts ships no scatter-gather router
nodes.rationale: This page's caution says actor-ts does not ship a scatter-gather router and that you would build one as a custom router actor - but Router.scatterGatherFirstCompleted is documented as a shipped sixth factory on its own page and in routing/overview and router. Flagged as an apparent stale/contradictory statement for review rather than omitted.
nodes.norm_label: aside claiming actor-ts ships no scatter-gather router

nodes.label: Random strategy
nodes.rationale: Same long-run distribution as round-robin but with no shared state, and more resilient to synchronized senders that would otherwise hammer the same routees. It gives up deterministic test behavior - inject a seedable RNG in a custom strategy if reproducibility matters.

nodes.label: Round-robin strategy
nodes.rationale: Even distribution by message COUNT, deterministic and inspectable. It does not load-balance by work cost - the router does not know a message is heavy - and gives no 'stick to the same routee' guarantee. The right default for homogeneous workloads.

nodes.label: Smallest-mailbox strategy
nodes.rationale: The only built-in strategy that reacts to what routees are actually doing: it balances by backlog rather than by turn, is self-correcting after a stall (a blocked routee drains no queue, so it simply stops being chosen - no timer, no health check), and rotates ties. Costs an O(N) scan per message, knows count not cost, and applies no back-pressure, because a strategy that refused to route would be inventing back-pressure the caller never configured.

nodes.label: What counts as a depth
nodes.rationale: Two unusable cases handled as opposites. A stopped routee is never chosen: its mailbox is permanently empty because a terminated cell dead-letters instead of enqueueing, so read as a plain number it would be the most attractive member of the pool until the router learns of the death - a window as deep as the router's own queue under load. A routee whose depth is merely unreadable counts as EMPTY, because skipping it would starve a remote routee for as long as any local one has a backlog; a balance error corrects itself, starvation does not.

nodes.label: Deterministic per-index behaviour
nodes.rationale: The factory must produce the same behaviour for the same index, or a failover hands you a different daemon 3 than before.

nodes.label: numDaemons becomes numShards
nodes.rationale: Fixed at init and identical on every node, because the value becomes the sharded type's numShards and the coordinator refuses a diverging node. A rolling deploy that changes it leaves not-yet-updated nodes registered and updated ones refused until the last one is through.

nodes.label: KubernetesLeaseOptions
nodes.rationale: In-cluster pods need only namespace and name plus the base LeaseOptionsType fields; API URL, token and CA come from the standard mount paths.

nodes.label: KubernetesLease required fields enforced at construction
nodes.rationale: Not cosmetic: without owner the Lease is written with no spec.holderIdentity (the undefined key falls out of the JSON body) and a holderless lease reads as free to every pod — every acquire() returns true and the single-holder guarantee is gone with no error logged. A missing ttlMs reaches the same result via NaN expiry.
nodes.norm_label: kuberneteslease required fields enforced at construction

nodes.label: The three connection fields are one credential
nodes.rationale: apiServerUrl, authToken and caCert are all-or-nothing; a partial set throws OptionsError. Previously each fell back to the in-cluster mount individually, so supplying only an apiServerUrl sent the pod's own ServiceAccount token to that host. The TLS pin limited the damage but a cluster credential has no business at an address it was not issued for. apiServerUrl must be https — the client builds a node:https request regardless, so an http:// URL was never plaintext, only confusing.
nodes.norm_label: the three connection fields are one credential

nodes.label: Reply-Type-Generics
nodes.rationale: ActorRef<unknown> swallows the reply type; a discriminated union for the reply lets the caller match success and failure the way it dispatches its own commands.

nodes.label: Reply-to-Ref
nodes.rationale: Clumsier than a method call but decouples request from reply in time, lets a different actor answer, and works identically locally and across the cluster.

nodes.label: Keine Funktionen in Nachrichten
nodes.rationale: No process boundary carries function pointers: the tagged JSON tree rejects them, JSON.stringify drops them silently, and structured clone throws DataCloneError — so a callback works in-process and breaks the moment the actor moves node.

nodes.label: redirectExternal(url, status?)
nodes.rationale: Eine eigene Funktion ist Absicht: grep redirectExternal listet jede Stelle auf, an der der Service den Browser an jemand anderen uebergibt — genau die Liste, die ein Security-Review sehen will.

nodes.label: Same-Origin-Regel gegen Open Redirects
nodes.rationale: Einen ?next=-Parameter ungeprueft in einen Redirect zu reichen, ist der Lehrbuch-Open-Redirect. Das Framework kann Handler nicht zur Pruefung zwingen — also prueft der Helper, zu dem sie ohnehin greifen: absolute URLs, protokollrelative //host-Ziele und Steuerzeichen werfen HttpError(400).

nodes.label: jsonCodec
nodes.rationale: Default-Codec; nimmt optional ein validate, um eingehende Frames gegen ein Schema zu pruefen.

nodes.label: rawCodec
nodes.rationale: Fuer Binaerprotokolle - TOut = TIn = WebsocketFrame.

nodes.label: WebsocketDecodeError / onInvalidMessage
nodes.rationale: Policy close (1003), drop oder hook - 'hook' leitet Dekodier-Fehler an den Actor weiter statt zu schliessen.

nodes.label: Resolver-Upgrades sind Schema-Änderungen
nodes.rationale: Snapshots nicht über Replicas mit unterschiedlichen Resolvern teilen — sonst sieht die Recovery inkonsistenten State; über Standard-Migrationsmuster ausrollen.

nodes.label: Split-Brain: Downing-Strategien plus optionale Leases
nodes.rationale: Ohne Downing-Strategie ist das Default-Verhalten 'unbegrenzt warten' und Operatoren müssen Nodes manuell downen — für Produktion eine wählen.

nodes.label: Single-Writer-Lease
nodes.rationale: Der Mittelweg: genau eine Replica hält das Lease und schreibt, andere lesen; fällt der Halter aus, erwirbt eine andere. Verwandelt Replicated ES in ein failover-fähiges Single-Writer-System.

nodes.label: Kausalität ist partiell geordnet
nodes.rationale: Vector Clocks geben keine Totalordnung; die Journal-Reihenfolge zweier nebenläufiger Events ist zufällig. Das ist der ganze Punkt — Clocks verfolgen Kausalität, nicht Wall-Clock-Zeit. Für eine Totalordnung mit einem Single-Writer-Lease paaren.

nodes.label: HOCON-Durations und -Sizes
nodes.rationale: Einheiten ns/us/ms/s/m/h/d und B/K/M/G/T (binär, 1024); nackte Zahlen parst HOCON als Zahlen, Duration-Keys brauchen also eine explizite Einheit.

nodes.label: distributed-data.max-gossip-bytes
nodes.rationale: Wird immer auf remote.max-frame-bytes heruntergeschnitten, weil die Fehlerbilder unvergleichbar sind: ein Frame über dem Wire-Cap kostet die komplette Peer-Verbindung, ein Budget verteilt denselben Zustand nur über mehr Ticks. Ein Key, dessen eigene Kodierung das Budget überschreitet, wird übersprungen, gezählt — und konvergiert nicht.

nodes.label: max-pending-quorum-requests / max-quorum-timeout
nodes.rationale: Jeder offene Quorum-Request hält Promise, Timer und Ziel-Set bis zur Deadline; ablehnen macht aus einem späteren Timeout-Sturm sofortige Fehler, die den Knopf beim Namen nennen. Das Timeout-Cap begrenzt die andere Achse, damit ein stundenlanges timeoutMs nicht das Budget parkt.

nodes.label: File-Sink: Rotation und Retention
nodes.rationale: Ein Roll öffnet immer eine NEUE gestempelte Datei — die aktive wird nie umbenannt, was Windows bei geöffneter Datei ohnehin verbietet; Retention löscht nur Dateien, die zu Prefix, Extension und Zeitstempelform dieses Sinks passen.

nodes.label: GELF-Sink (Graylog)
nodes.rationale: Nativ statt über OTLP, weil Graylogs OpenTelemetry-Input nur gRPC spricht; TLS für tcp ist code-only, weil die Felder Schlüsselmaterial tragen und keinen Pfad.

nodes.label: Multi-Sink-Logger-Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Jeder Sink ist per Default aus; mindestens einer eingeschaltet ersetzt den ConsoleLogger durch einen MultiSinkLogger. logger.level gatet VOR den Per-Sink-Min-Levels. Ein explizit übergebener Logger ersetzt den Block statt zu mergen — ein Sink gehört einer Konstruktionswelt oder der anderen. Der Sentry-Sink hat keinen Block, weil er einen eigenen Import braucht.

nodes.label: redactedUrlLabel
nodes.rationale: Reduziert eine URL auf eine stabile Identitaet: Schema, Host, Port und Pfad, ohne Userinfo und ohne Query-String — ein WebSocket-Endpunkt wird ueblicherweise mit ?token=… authentifiziert. Der Pfad bleibt, weil er zwei Verbindungen zum selben Host unterscheidet. Fuer wiederholt ausgegebene Zeilen, etwa eine Warnung pro Frame im WebsocketClientActor.

nodes.label: redactUrlCredentials
nodes.rationale: Maskiert die Userinfo und aendert SONST NICHTS — keine Normalisierung, kein angehaengter Schraegstrich, kein kleingeschriebener Host —, damit ein Betreiber den getippten Wert wiedererkennt. Auf allem ohne scheme://…@-Authority ein striktes No-op, also sicher auf einen Wert anwendbar, der nur vielleicht eine URL ist.

nodes.label: safeStringify
nodes.rationale: JSON.stringify wirft bei zyklischen Strukturen und BigInt — beim Bauen einer Logzeile riskiert man damit, das gerade gemeldete Problem durch ein anderes zu ersetzen, geworfen aus dem meldenden Code heraus. Zyklen kollabieren zu [Circular], das Ergebnis ist bei 8 KiB gedeckelt. Bewusst verlustbehaftet und kein gueltiges JSON — nichts sollte es zurueckzulesen versuchen.

nodes.label: Dispatcher-Hop zwischen Warten und Prüfen
nodes.rationale: Der Default-Dispatcher schedult über setImmediate, der Zug des zweiten Actors steht also vor dem nächsten Timer des Pollers in der Queue und gewinnt jedes Mal; das Rennen ist konstruktionsbedingt real, isoliert nie reproduzierbar und fällt nur im großen Parallel-Lauf um.
nodes.community_name: Was Wiederholung findet — und was nicht

nodes.label: Eine Assertion über prozessweiten Zustand
nodes.rationale: bun test führt den ganzen Baum in einem Prozess aus, alle Suiten teilen sich also jede static-Collection; expect(transportA.peers()).toEqual([]) behauptet, nirgends im Prozess sei ein anderer Transport registriert, und 75 Testdateien erzeugen einen. Entfernt man registry.delete aus shutdown(), bleibt die alte Assertion allein laufend grün — sie hat ihre Geschwister erkannt, nicht ihren Gegenstand; die verengte Form wird bei dieser Mutation in beiden Fällen rot.
nodes.community_name: Was Wiederholung findet — und was nicht

nodes.label: Was Wiederholung findet — und was nicht
nodes.rationale: Eine Schleife treibt lastabhängige Flakes hoch, sagt über deterministische Reihenfolge-Fehler aber nichts: die kaputte Bedingung lief 200-mal mit 0 Fehlschlägen bei 5 ms und bei 1 ms Poll-Intervall. Die zweite Familie findet man durch Lesen — liegt zwischen dem gewarteten und dem geprüften Zustand ein Message-Send?
nodes.community_name: Was Wiederholung findet — und was nicht
nodes.norm_label: was wiederholung findet — und was nicht

nodes.label: redirect
nodes.rationale: Sets Location and a status (default 302 Found), but the target must stay on this origin - a relative reference. An absolute URL, a protocol-relative //host target, or a control character throws HttpError(400).

nodes.label: Open-redirect defence
nodes.rationale: Forwarding a ?next= parameter into a redirect is the textbook open redirect: the attacker sends app.example/login?next=<look-alike>, the victim logs in against the real app and the browser lands on a page asking for the password again. The framework cannot make handlers validate, so the helper they already reach for validates instead, failing closed.

nodes.label: redirectExternal
nodes.rationale: The same helper without the origin rule, kept as a separate function on purpose: grep redirectExternal enumerates every place the service hands the browser to somebody else, which is precisely the list a security review asks for. Hand it a constant or an allowlisted value, never a raw request parameter; control characters are still rejected.

nodes.label: MigrationChain
nodes.rationale: Built with MigrationChain.for<E>(manifest, currentVersion) and .add(step); steps must move forward and intermediate shapes need not match any historical event — they are stepping stones the chain walks from the stored version's cursor to currentVersion.

nodes.label: InMemorySchemaRegistry (recipe 3)
nodes.rationale: For schemas not owned by one actor — several services writing one Kafka topic or shared journal, each possibly on a different version. Registration is a first-class step, so a service version can refuse to start when its schema breaks the configured compatibility level. Not worth it for single-service single-actor evolution.

nodes.label: Chain gap raises MigrationError
nodes.rationale: No upcaster registered for the cursor before currentVersion is reached throws a MigrationError naming the missing fromVersion — which is why skipping a version (1 to 3 with no 2 to 3 step) breaks as soon as a v2 payload exists. A step that throws surfaces through onRecoveryFailure and stops the actor unless the hook rethrows into supervision.

nodes.label: zstd compression
nodes.rationale: Best ratio at competitive speed and very fast decode at every level, which makes it a strong default for read-heavy state. Writing requires native support (Bun or Node); there is no pure-JS fallback for compression.

nodes.label: Detect zstd by calling it, not by feature-checking
nodes.rationale: Deno's node:zlib exports zstd entry points with no binding behind them, so a presence check would pass and then fail cryptically. Both directions pick an implementation by calling it, which keeps the framework's own capability message accurate and leaves the fzstd fallback reachable.
nodes.norm_label: detect zstd by calling it, not by feature-checking
